title: LOGIV: Graph-Verified Execution with Causal Local Repair for Long-Horizon Robot Tasks
authors: Enqiao Lu,Yuxiang Xie,Xingrui Yu,Yuyang Wang,Yipeng Gu,Zhenglin Wan,Pengfei Zhou,Wangbo Zhao,Yang You,Yuxiang Gao,Ivor Tsang
abstract: 未获取到摘要
introduction:
Agentic robots combine goal-directed planning, perception, and physical action in a feedback loop Qin et al. (2026). Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models Octo Model Team et al. (2024); Kim et al. (2024); Physical Intelligence et al. (2025) and World Action Models (WAMs) Yuan et al. (2026); Cai et al. (2026) provide increasingly capable execution policies, while an agent-level controller must decide how their actions contribute to a longer task. A distinctive difficulty in physical execution is that an intermediate result can cease to hold after the action that produced it has succeeded. A support placed during bridge assembly may be displaced before the beam is installed (Fig. 1). The placement remains a completed action, yet the support condition needed by the remaining plan is no longer valid. Reliable long-horizon behavior therefore requires tracking both action completion and the continuing validity of its consequences.

Existing work provides important components for this execution loop. LLM- and VLM-based systems select skills, interpret feedback, and organize multistep behavior Ouyang et al. (2025); Huang et al. (2024); Feng et al. (2025); Chen et al. (2025c); Ji et al. (2026); Peng et al. (2026a); Zhang et al. (2026a); Huang et al. (2026). Symbolic and program-based methods make action constraints explicit Yang et al. (2025); Kwon et al. (2025); Chen et al. (2025b); Chu et al. (2025), building on established work in plan monitoring and repair Pollack and McCarthy (1999); Van Der Krogt and De Weerdt (2005). Graph-based agent frameworks expose subtask dependencies for reuse and repair Zhang et al. (2026b); in robotics, AgentChord augments task graphs with anticipatory recovery branches before execution Xu et al. (2026). These advances raise a question: when observations invalidate an earlier condition, which support should the robot restore while preserving a usable unfinished plan?

We approach this question through graph engineering: constructing, checking, and revising an explicit dependency graph as the interface between planning and robot execution. We present LOGIV (Long-Horizon Online Graph-based Inference and Verification for Plan Repair). Its task graph records which conditions each action supplies to later actions, together with resource-ordering constraints. The key design is to separate a node’s completion status from the current validity of the support it provides. When that support fails, unfinished consumers can remain in the plan while repair re-establishes their prerequisites. The retained continuation then constrains the repair goal. This gives graph structure an operational role in deciding what to check, what to preserve, and what to change.

LOGIV implements this interface as a closed-loop execution and repair layer above an existing VLA or WAM policy. Before execution, it validates a high-level plan and compiles its dependencies into a task graph. During execution, visual observations and robot feedback check the selected action and the support required by pending actions. After a confirmed failure, dependency tracing identifies affected actions; repair synthesizes a continuation constrained by retained operators and expands the replacement scope when validation fails. The combined plan is checked under the symbolic model before the graph is rebuilt and execution resumes. In the bridge example, the robot restores the displaced support while retaining the remaining beam operations. This design adds no trainable components and focuses on online repair from the observed state, with the validity of the repaired continuation checked explicitly. We evaluate LOGIV on 20 simulated dual-arm tasks from RoboTwin V2 and BiCoord using π0.5\pi_{0.5}, AHA-WAM, and Light-WAM. Without injected perturbations, mean success across the three backbones increases from 71.67% to 82.33% on RoboTwin V2 and from 42.33% to 57.67% on BiCoord. Under predefined perturbations, LOGIV achieves higher task completion and condition restoration than three adapted recovery baselines for every backbone on both benchmarks. On three real-robot tasks, successful trials increase from 12/30 to 17/30. Ablations support the role of graph structure: removing dependency checks reduces perturbed-task success from 60% to 48%, and replacing local repair with replanning all remaining actions increases repeated valid actions from 0.2 to 1.6. These results support graph engineering for the evaluated tasks. Our contributions are:

A graph engineering formulation of agentic robot execution that separates completed actions from the continuing validity of their condition support during physical task execution.

A closed-loop implementation combining observation-based graph checks, dependency-guided repair constrained by retained actions, and symbolic validation of the full continuation.

Evaluation across two simulation benchmarks, three execution backbones, and real robots, with ablations examining how graph verification and repair design affect task success and redundant execution.

1. A graph engineering formulation of agentic robot execution that separates completed actions from the continuing validity of their condition support during physical task execution.

2. A closed-loop implementation combining observation-based graph checks, dependency-guided repair constrained by retained actions, and symbolic validation of the full continuation.

3. Evaluation across two simulation benchmarks, three execution backbones, and real robots, with ablations examining how graph verification and repair design affect task success and redundant execution.

title: Humanoid Dodgeball: Learning Fast Dynamic Obstacle Avoidance Motions for Humanoids
authors: Aoqian Zhang,Chunzheng Wang,Haoran Chen,Annan Tang,Cheng Xiang,Fan Shi,Shuzhi Sam Ge
abstract: Humanoids have become increasingly agile and capable in real-world environments. To operate safely in dynamic scenarios, they must rapidly evade fast-moving obstacles while maintaining stability and physically feasible whole-body motion. Learning such behaviors remains challenging due to the high-dimensional dynamics of humanoid systems and the need to jointly balance reactive obstacle avoidance, motion naturalness, and control robustness. In this work, we present Humanoid Dodgeball, a reinforcement learning (RL) framework for agile dynamic obstacle avoidance in humanoids. Our method enables highly dynamic whole-body evasive maneuvers against incoming projectiles through threat-aware reward shaping, while multiple direction-specific adversarial motion priors regularize the learned behaviors toward stable and diverse human-like motions. Extensive simulation and hardware experiments demonstrate that the proposed framework substantially improves dynamic obstacle avoidance performance across diverse obstacle speeds and launch distances, while preserving robust and physically plausible humanoid motions. Supplementary videos are available at https://humanoid-dodge.github.io/.
introduction:
Recent advances in reinforcement learning for humanoids have significantly improved humanoid whole-body motion tracking and control through training on large human motion datasets [1, 2, 3]. These developments have enabled humanoids to acquire a wide range of dynamic and human-like skills, including athletic sports behaviors such as soccer [4] and tennis [5], highly dynamic parkour locomotion [6], and complex whole-body tasks such as skateboarding [7]. To further improve the safety and robustness of humanoid deployment in complex and human-centered environments, recent research has explored protective falling strategies that reduce damage to both the robot and its surroundings during unavoidable failures [8], as well as collision-free navigation and traversal in cluttered environments with static obstacles [9]. These advances represent important steps toward deploying humanoids in real-world environments where safety, robustness, and physical interaction are critical.

Despite these remarkable advances, humanoids still lack the ability to safely and robustly react to fast-moving dynamic objects. The capability to evade incoming obstacles is a fundamental and natural behavior observed in legged animals, including humans, and is essential for agile operation in real-world settings. However, learning such reactive whole-body avoidance behaviors for humanoids remains highly challenging due to the need for rapid reaction, dynamic balance maintenance, and coordinated whole-body motion generation.

To address these challenges, we present Humanoid Dodgeball, a novel humanoid whole-body control framework for dynamic obstacle avoidance. The main contributions of this work are as follows:

We design a reinforcement learning framework that enables humanoids to evade fast-moving projectiles through coordinated whole-body evasive maneuvers while maintaining stability.

We design a reinforcement learning framework that enables humanoids to evade fast-moving projectiles through coordinated whole-body evasive maneuvers while maintaining stability.

We combine threat-aware rewards, direction-specific motion priors, and capture-point guidance to promote effective avoidance, diverse natural motions, and stable recovery.

We validate our proposed method through simulation experiments on two humanoid platforms and hardware experiments on the EngineAI PM01 humanoid.

1. We design a reinforcement learning framework that enables humanoids to evade fast-moving projectiles through coordinated whole-body evasive maneuvers while maintaining stability.

2. We combine threat-aware rewards, direction-specific motion priors, and capture-point guidance to promote effective avoidance, diverse natural motions, and stable recovery.

3. We validate our proposed method through simulation experiments on two humanoid platforms and hardware experiments on the EngineAI PM01 humanoid.

title: How Much Should a VLA Trust Its Reasoning? Step-Level Guidance as a Measured Action-Value Function
authors: Dabin Seo,Eunhyek Joa
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Machine Learning (cs.LG)
abstract:
Reasoning vision–language–action (VLA) policies write a reasoning trace and
then decode the action from it. A wrong trace yields a wrong action, and even a
correct-looking trace can mislead the plan. Existing remedies ask whether the
reasoning is right. We ask how strongly it should steer.
CoC-CFG applies classifier-free guidance between the policy’s context
and the same context without the reasoning span. One weight per Euler step
attenuates or amplifies the reasoning, and w=1w{=}1 recovers the original policy.
We treat the choice of this weight as a Markov decision process whose action values
are measured, not bootstrapped. With the expert frozen and the noise fixed, applying a
weight for one step and finishing the plan under the current controller returns
that weight’s value exactly. Q-adaptive guidance fits these values with
small critics and improves the controller conservatively. In the Alpasim
driving simulator it outperforms every fixed weight and online RL (SAC, GRPO) in open loop,
and in closed loop it passes 262 of 300 scenes, against
252 for the original policy. On held-out frames of the Waymo
end-to-end driving benchmark, its first three stages outperform every fixed
weight, four adaptive-guidance methods, SAC and GRPO. On the hidden test set,
a frozen Alpamayo 1.5 with rule-based camera and vehicle conversions and
Q-adaptive guidance sets a new state of the art among published methods:
8.135159 rater feedback score, against 8.079 for the
best published method.
introduction:
Vision–language–action (VLA) models increasingly reason before they act: a
vision–language model (VLM) writes a reasoning trace, and an action expert
decodes the action conditioned on it
[23, 38, 11]. In the Alpamayo
driving planners [23], the VLM writes a Chain-of-Causation
(CoC) into its key–value cache, and a flow-matching expert decodes the
trajectory from that cache in a few Euler steps. The trace is not a caption but
part of the condition: editing it moves the trajectory
[22].

The trace is often wrong. Fewer than half of a driving VLA’s traces match the
scene [20], VLMs answer driving questions from the text
rather than the image [31], and hallucination has
statistical causes [14]. A wrong trace becomes a wrong plan: in
Fig. How Much Should a VLA Trust Its Reasoning?
Step-Level Guidance as a Measured Action-Value Functionb the trace calls for a lane change the scene does not
offer, and the unmodified policy follows it off the logged path. A trace that
reads correctly can mislead too: followed in full, the plan of
Fig. How Much Should a VLA Trust Its Reasoning?
Step-Level Guidance as a Measured Action-Value Functionc runs far past the log.

The obvious fixes ask whether the reasoning is right. Alpamayo 1.5 is already
post-trained with reinforcement learning for reasoning–action consistency
[23], and its traces still err; detecting hallucinations
remains unsolved, at 0.51 IoU for the best system of a recent
shared task [29], and a detector only keeps or drops the
trace. Neither helps when the trace reads correctly yet misleads the plan.

We ask instead how strongly the trace should steer. CoC-CFG,
Chain-of-Causation classifier-free guidance [10], runs
the frozen expert on the policy’s own context and on the same context with only
the reasoning span removed, and moves each Euler step along the line through the
two velocities. The position on that line, the guidance
weight wkw_{k}, sets how strongly the trace steers step kk: wk=1w_{k}{=}1 is the
unmodified model, lower weights attenuate the trace and higher weights amplify it
(Fig. How Much Should a VLA Trust Its Reasoning?
Step-Level Guidance as a Measured Action-Value Functiona). Trusting and rejecting the trace are two points on this
axis.

The weight acts before the plan exists, so we treat its choice as a Markov
decision process over the Euler steps whose only reward is the score of the
finished plan (Sec. 4). Because the expert is frozen and the noise fixed,
generation is deterministic and can be reset to any step: applying one weight
for one step and finishing the plan under the current controller returns that
weight’s value exactly. Learning becomes supervised regression on measured
values, where online reinforcement learning would bootstrap what can be
measured. Q-adaptive guidance
(Fig. 2) fits small critics to these measurements with a cost
for leaving a reference weight, re-measures under the improved controller and
refits on every measurement so far.

In Alpasim, a driving simulator reconstructed from real drives, the controller
lowers the open-loop displacement cost of Alpamayo 1.5 by 16.5 %
against w=1w{=}1, above soft actor-critic (SAC) and group-relative policy
optimization (GRPO) trained on the same signal, and passes 262 of
300 closed-loop scenes against 252 (Sec. 5.1).
On the Waymo end-to-end driving benchmark [32], its first three
stages clear every fixed weight, four adaptive-guidance methods, SAC and GRPO
on the held-out frames, and Alpamayo 1.5,
converted to the Waymo vehicle by rule-based conversions and steered by Q-adaptive
guidance, sets a new state of the art among published methods on the hidden
test set: 8.135159 rater feedback score (RFS) against
8.079 (Sec. 5.2).

Our contributions are three.
(i) CoC-CFG, a guidance axis over the reasoning span of a VLA’s
context that attenuates or amplifies the trace and is exact at w=1w{=}1: an
unreliable trace becomes an influence to control rather than a defect to detect.
(ii) Step-level guidance as a Markov decision process with measured
action values, each obtained by a one-step branch, and Q-adaptive
guidance, a controller that chooses the weight at every Euler step from critics
fitted to these values.
(iii) Evidence on a frozen driving VLA: open-loop gains in Alpasim
above fixed weights and online RL, closed-loop gains over fixed weights,
held-out Waymo gains over fixed weights, adaptive-guidance methods and online RL, and
a new state of the art among published methods on the hidden test set of the
Waymo end-to-end driving benchmark.

title: Gaze-Assisted Supervisory Control for Lunar Robotic Arm Teleoperation Under Concurrent Monitoring
authors: Jiayu He,Yifan Li,Oliver R. Runswick,Ernest N. Kamavuako,Yunjie Jia,Peter D. Hodkinson,Yang Gao
abstract: Rover-mounted robotic arms can extend human reach during lunar sample handling, but continuous joystick teleoperation requires repeated visual–motor alignment while operators may also need to monitor system states. This paper presents a gaze-assisted supervisory control framework in which gaze nominates a rock or placement target, explicit confirmation authorizes the action, and the robot performs bounded autonomous grasp-and-place execution. The framework was evaluated against manual joystick teleoperation in a mission-analog virtual reality study with 16 participants. The study used a 2×2×32\times 2\times 3 within-subject design varying control mode, placement difficulty, and concurrent monitoring load. Mean recorded task completion time decreased from 47.6547.65 to 18.43​s18.43\,\mathrm{s} per rock, with 72.5% of this difference arising during grasping. Under the tested auditory monitoring conditions, gaze-assisted supervisory control showed less average proportional slowing, with no detected control-mode difference in monitoring-response accuracy or speed. The rate of gaze shifts between core areas of interest decreased from 49.98 to 27.73 shifts/min, while the raw NASA Task Load Index score decreased from 32.54 to 18.26. However, the benefit was task dependent. In precision placement, manual control yielded lower mean placement error and a higher placement success rate. These findings support a mixed-initiative allocation in which gaze enables rapid task-level intention specification and autonomous execution, while precision-critical stages retain manual refinement.
introduction:
Rover-mounted robotic arms can extend human operational reach, enabling operators to collect samples and deploy equipment beyond areas that can be safely or practically accessed directly 1, 2. Such support is needed because rugged terrain, abrasive dust, extreme temperatures, and severe lighting contrasts make direct crew operations hazardous and demanding 3, 4, 5. Nevertheless, keeping humans in the control loop remains important for interpreting task context, adjusting priorities when new samples are encountered, and responding to environmental or system uncertainties that may invalidate predefined plans 6, 7.

Manual robotic arm teleoperation typically uses a handheld controller or joystick to command end-effector motion, as illustrated in Fig. 1 6, 8. The operator must continuously compare the target, end-effector, and placement region and translate visual feedback into corrective manual inputs. However, limited crew availability and operational time during lunar surface missions may require operators to manage other tasks concurrently. These tasks include observing the environment, monitoring life-support and other system states through auditory or visual feedback, communicating with the crew or mission control, and confirming procedural steps, placing substantial demands on cognitive performance 9. These concurrent demands may interfere with continuous arm control because manual arm control and concurrent duties can draw on overlapping perceptual, central-processing, and response resources. Multiple Resource Theory (MRT) further suggests that presenting monitoring information acoustically may reduce modality overlap but does not eliminate competition at central-processing and response-selection stages 10. These challenges highlight the need for a control approach that retains the operator’s task-level judgment and intervention authority while reducing reliance on continuous low-level alignment and adjustment.

Supervisory control provides a way to redistribute these responsibilities. Rather than commanding each arm movement, the operator specifies what action is required and monitors its outcome, while the robot determines how to execute it 7. Under this allocation, the operator retains authority over target selection and command authorization and monitors autonomous execution, while autonomy is confined to bounded motion-execution stages. For lunar manipulation, this allocation allows the operator to focus on target assessment and exception monitoring, while the robot handles repeated end-effector approach, trajectory planning, and execution. By reducing the need for continuous low-level visual-motor alignment and manual input, this division may mitigate competition for perceptual, central-processing, and response resources during concurrent crew duties without removing the operator from the control loop. However, this allocation requires an efficient way for the operator to specify task-level goals without continuous manual control.

Gaze offers a potential interface for communicating task-level goals without continuous manual control. Objects or spatial regions receiving the operator’s visual attention can be identified as candidate targets 11. Explicit confirmation can then distinguish intentional target selection from incidental visual attention before autonomous execution 12. Previous studies have explored gaze-based target selection and command input in assistive systems, wheelchairs, and mobile robots 11, 13. In spaceflight research, eye tracking has primarily been used as a measurement tool to examine sensorimotor adaptation, workload, and telerobotic performance 14. However, gaze remains underexplored as an active task-level input for lunar surface robotic manipulation. In particular, limited evidence directly compares gaze-assisted supervisory control with continuous manual joystick teleoperation under varying placement tolerances and concurrent monitoring demands.

To address these gaps, we propose a novel gaze-assisted supervisory control framework for lunar robotic arm teleoperation. Lunar rock collection and placement are selected as a representative manipulation scenario. For this task, the proposed framework allows the operator to select the rock and placement target through gaze and explicit confirmation, while the robot is responsible for target interpretation and autonomous grasp-and-place execution. To evaluate this control allocation, we compare the framework with continuous manual joystick teleoperation in a controlled mission-analog VR study using a within-subject design that varies placement difficulty and concurrent monitoring load and assesses task performance and operator workload.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews related work on space telerobotics, supervisory control, and gaze-based interaction. Section 3 presents the proposed gaze-assisted supervisory control framework, while Section 4 describes the user study. Section 5 reports the experimental results, Section 6 discusses the findings and directions for future work, and Section 7 concludes the paper.

title: Compressed Orientation Reachability Maps for Sub-Second Robotic Needle Entry Point Planning
authors: Prabhu Nithin Gollapudi,Andreas Maier,Franziska Mathis-Ullrich,Water Zhao,Jia Wang,Siming Bayer
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computational Geometry (cs.CG); Systems and Control (eess.SY)
abstract: In the context of multi-stage trajectory planning for robotic percutaneous liver interventions, identifying a kinematically feasible entry point remains a critical computational bottleneck. Existing methods rely on exhaustive inverse kinematics or randomized searches, incurring delays of 13 to 27 seconds per target and limiting real-time intraoperative adaptation. This paper introduces an Orientation-Based Reachability Map (ORM) that precomputes the kinematic feasibility of a 6 Degrees of Freedom (DoF) serial manipulator across 188,873 workspace positions and encodes orientation feasibility into a compact, indexed 83 MB map. A Just-In-Time (JIT) compiled runtime pipeline replaces live optimization with near-instantaneous array lookups. Experimental evaluation demonstrates a reduction in planning latency from 13.5–26.9 s to 0.289–0.349 s per target while maintaining high geometric fidelity, achieving a mean convex hull volume overlap ratio of 0.933 and a mean alpha-shape volume ratio of 0.976 relative to the baseline reachable point cloud. The proposed ORM framework enables sub-second entry point planning and provides an efficient computational framework for robotic needle insertion in percutaneous liver ablation.
introduction:
Liver cancer remains one of the leading causes of cancer-related mortality worldwide, with approximately 865,000 new cases and 757,948 deaths reported in 2022 [1], and a 5-year survival rate of only 22% [2]. For patients with underlying liver disease who are not eligible for surgical resection, percutaneous thermal ablation techniques such as radiofrequency ablation (RFA) and microwave ablation (MWA) are established first-line therapies for small hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) and selected liver metastases [3, 4, 5]. These minimally invasive procedures offer reduced morbidity, shorter hospital stays, and tissue preservation, but their effectiveness depends critically on accurate needle placement to ensure complete tumor coverage with an adequate safety margin (typically 5–10 mm) while avoiding major vessels and bile ducts [5, 6, 7, 8].

Robotic assistance offers clear advantages over freehand techniques by reducing tremor, operator variability, and radiation exposure [4, 7, 8, 6]. In image-guided ablation, treatment success depends on a multi-stage planning pipeline that includes tumor targeting, ablation volume simulation, and needle trajectory selection [9, 10]. Within this pipeline, identifying a kinematically feasible skin entry point is a necessary prerequisite, since even a clinically optimal anatomical trajectory cannot be executed if the manipulator cannot reach it [11, 9].

However, existing intraoperative entry point planning methods often rely on exhaustive inverse kinematics (IK) verification or randomized search to evaluate manipulator reachability over large candidate sets. This leads to latencies of 13–27 s per target [10, 4], which is slow for responsive intraoperative replanning under respiratory motion and soft-tissue deformation.

To address this limitation, we propose an Orientation-Based Reachability Map (ORM) framework for fast kinematic feasibility evaluation in robotic needle guidance. The specific contributions of this paper are:

An ORM representation that precomputes reachability for a 6 Degrees of Freedom (DoF) serial manipulator over 188,873 workspace positions, storing orientation feasibility in a compact 83 MB indexed structure.

An ORM representation that precomputes reachability for a 6 Degrees of Freedom (DoF) serial manipulator over 188,873 workspace positions, storing orientation feasibility in a compact 83 MB indexed structure.

A Just-In-Time (JIT) compiled query pipeline that replaces repeated online inverse kinematics (IK) evaluations with indexed lookups.

An experimental evaluation demonstrating a reduction in entry point planning latency from 13.5–26.9 s to 0.289–0.349 s per target (a 60–90×\times speedup), while preserving high geometric fidelity with a mean alpha-shape volume ratio of 0.976 and a mean convex hull volume overlap ratio of 0.933.

These results support the use of the proposed ORM as a practical foundation for sub-second, workspace-aware entry point planning in robotic percutaneous liver ablation.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section II reviews related work in reachability analysis and robotic surgery. Section III details the proposed ORM generation and runtime pipeline. Section IV presents the experimental setup and results. Finally, Section V concludes the paper and discusses future work.

1. An ORM representation that precomputes reachability for a 6 Degrees of Freedom (DoF) serial manipulator over 188,873 workspace positions, storing orientation feasibility in a compact 83 MB indexed structure.

2. A Just-In-Time (JIT) compiled query pipeline that replaces repeated online inverse kinematics (IK) evaluations with indexed lookups.

3. An experimental evaluation demonstrating a reduction in entry point planning latency from 13.5–26.9 s to 0.289–0.349 s per target (a 60–90×\times speedup), while preserving high geometric fidelity with a mean alpha-shape volume ratio of 0.976 and a mean convex hull volume overlap ratio of 0.933.

title: PASA-KV: Attacking Action-Facing Visual Routes in World Action Models
authors: Zhongbo Wu,Jiakai Huang,Zheng Zhang,Siyu Xu,Kaixiang Chen,Xiaohong Liu,Shan You,Chang Xu,Tao Huang
abstract: World action models (WAMs) increasingly couple internal visual or world representations with action generation, making their world-to-action pathways a critical yet poorly understood source of robustness. We investigate when perturbations to these internal representations actually become behaviorally consequential, and uncover a pronounced mismatch between representation perturbability and closed-loop vulnerability: attack effectiveness varies sharply across visual K/V routes, while larger representation displacement does not reliably imply stronger control failure. Our analysis attributes this mismatch to the action-conditioned readout, where keys determine where action queries read and values determine what content they receive. This motivates an action-facing view of vulnerability, in which the effect of a perturbation depends on how it is routed into action generation rather than on representation-space magnitude alone. We instantiate this view with Tail-AV, a short-probe signal for identifying vulnerable routes, and operationalize it in PASA-KV, which selects action-facing K/V targets before training a fresh task-shared attack. Experiments across multiple WAM systems and a physical robot validate readout-informed target selection, demonstrate strong closed-loop attacks, and reveal substantial system-level differences in resistance.
introduction:
World action models (WAMs) are emerging as a promising paradigm for robot control by coupling visual world representations and dynamics with action generation (Ha and Schmidhuber, 2018, Hafner et al., 2019, Li et al., 2026, Kim et al., 2026, Yuan et al., 2026); latent-imagination methods provide an earlier route from learned world models to control (Hafner et al., 2020, Hafner et al., 2021). Generalist robot policies include RT-1, RT-2, and Octo (Brohan et al., 2023, Zitkovich et al., 2023, Octo Model Team et al., 2024), while MimicGen scales demonstration generation for robot learning (Mandlekar et al., 2023). Across direct, cascaded, and joint WAM architectures, action generation ultimately depends on internal visual or world representations. This coupling introduces a security question that cannot be answered by studying input perturbations alone: when does a change in an internal visual representation actually propagate to the action generator and alter closed-loop behavior? Existing attacks on robot policies expose vulnerabilities at the input, representation, attention, denoising, or action level (Chen et al., 2024, Wang et al., 2025, Lu et al., 2026, Tae and Lee, 2026, Zhang et al., 2026), but they do not reveal which world-to-action routes make WAMs behaviorally vulnerable.

A natural view is that routes whose representations can be perturbed more strongly should provide more effective attack targets. Our layerwise study shows that this view is incomplete. Under the same attack objective and training budget, perturbing different visual K/V layers of FastWAM leads to sharply different closed-loop outcomes (Figure 1(a,c)). More strikingly, stronger or broader internal perturbation does not necessarily produce stronger behavioral failure. Jointly attacking K and V broadens the set of effective targets, yet does not dominate either route at every layer; at L20, for example, K-only reduces policy success to 0.0%, whereas joint K/V leaves it at 91.5%. Across layers, the magnitude of K/V displacement likewise fails to determine eventual attack effectiveness. These results reveal a fundamental mismatch: representation disruption is not action disruption.

The missing information lies in how a perturbation interacts with the action-conditioned readout. In attention-based WAMs, visual keys determine where action queries read, whereas visual values determine what content they receive. A large K displacement can therefore have little effect when it poorly aligns with the directions to which action queries are sensitive, while a large V displacement may remain inconsequential when the altered content receives little attention. K- and V-induced changes can also reinforce or partially oppose one another, providing a mechanism for the non-monotonic behavior above. This suggests that vulnerability should not be characterized solely in representation space, but through the interaction between an internal perturbation and the action-facing pathway that consumes it. We refer to this view as action-facing vulnerability: the behavioral relevance of a perturbation depends not only on how much the representation changes, but also on how that change is routed into action generation.

This perspective changes how vulnerable routes should be identified. Rather than ranking layers by how far their representations move, we measure how a short perturbation changes the visual contribution received by action queries. This motivates Tail-AV, which combines action-query routing with the magnitude of visual content being read and, from short probes, identifies layers that later become strong attack targets (Figure 1(b)). Importantly, this signal is computed without closed-loop rollout outcomes. The resulting characterization naturally leads to the Probe-and-Select Action-facing K/V Attack (PASA-KV): probe candidate routes cheaply, select those with the strongest action-facing responses, and train the final task-shared patch only on the selected routes. In this way, PASA-KV operationalizes the action-facing view without exhaustively training and evaluating full attacks at every candidate layer.

Our experiments support this interpretation at both the mechanism and system levels. Under matched FastWAM controls with the same final K/V objective, target count, geometry, and training budget, Tail-AV-selected layers achieve 1.5% policy success, compared with 47.5% when layers are selected directly by probe K/V displacement and 18.5–86.5% for evenly spaced or random selections (Section 6.3). The resulting PASA-KV Top-5 attack reduces FastWAM success from 92.4% to 0.0%. Yet the same construction produces substantially smaller degradation on LingBot-VA and Cosmos Policy, reaching 87.2% and 89.2% SR, respectively, exposing pronounced architecture-dependent resistance rather than a universal vulnerability (Table 5). Finally, rerunning the complete procedure on a separately trained Piper FastWAM checkpoint yields a task-shared Top-5 patch with 0/10 successes on each of the three evaluated tasks with nonzero clean success (Section 9).

Our contributions are:

We characterize visual K/V vulnerability in WAMs and reveal a systematic mismatch between representation perturbability and closed-loop behavioral vulnerability: attack effectiveness varies sharply across layers, and stronger internal perturbation does not necessarily imply stronger control failure.

We identify action-facing readout as the missing link between internal perturbation and behavioral consequence. This view explains the distinct roles of K and V and motivates Tail-AV as a short-probe signal for locating vulnerable visual routes.

We operationalize this understanding through PASA-KV, whose readout-informed selection substantially outperforms matched representation-based and uninformed controls. Cross-architecture and real-robot evaluations further reveal large differences in how WAMs expose and resist action-facing attacks.

1. We characterize visual K/V vulnerability in WAMs and reveal a systematic mismatch between representation perturbability and closed-loop behavioral vulnerability: attack effectiveness varies sharply across layers, and stronger internal perturbation does not necessarily imply stronger control failure.

2. We identify action-facing readout as the missing link between internal perturbation and behavioral consequence. This view explains the distinct roles of K and V and motivates Tail-AV as a short-probe signal for locating vulnerable visual routes.

3. We operationalize this understanding through PASA-KV, whose readout-informed selection substantially outperforms matched representation-based and uninformed controls. Cross-architecture and real-robot evaluations further reveal large differences in how WAMs expose and resist action-facing attacks.

title: Surrogate Uncertainty for Black-box Visual Grounding
authors: Hanbo Zhang,Tianrun Hu,Cedar Site Bai,Anxing Xiao,David Hsu
comment: A preprint rejected by RSS 2026 AND CoRL 2026
abstract:
Visual grounding is crucial for robots to understand language instructions with visual observations.
This paper addresses the problem of visual grounding uncertainties, where a robot uses a black-box vision-language model (VLM) to ground free-form natural-language instructions to target objects. Prevailing methods derive uncertainty from the VLM itself. Yet, outputs of the VLM, e.g., generated uncertainties, are from the same parameters and structures producing the predictions, and inherit the bias. We give a formal Bayesian definition of the problem that treats the VLM prediction as an observation. An external surrogate Bayesian model then quantifies per-query uncertainty over a local neighborhood of a held-out calibration set, decomposed into aleatoric and epistemic components. A hierarchical retrieval across input modalities realizes a compact joint-space neighborhood, mitigating the curse of dimensionality. The estimator further integrates with conformal prediction or model-based planning for active visual grounding, where robots are allowed to take verbal or physical actions to ground targets. Across grounding benchmarks and state-of-the-art VLMs, it consistently improves both calibration and task performance. On a real Fetch robot under open-world instructions, it enables principled trade-offs between confident action and information gathering, substantially improving robustness.
introduction:
Reliable uncertainty estimation is crucial for robots acting in physical environments. In safety-critical scenarios, overconfident actions can cause harm, e.g., confusing “disinfectant” with “hairspray” (Fig. 1). Modern vision-language models (VLMs) are widely integrated into robot systems [1], yet remain prone to grounding errors, hallucinations, and overconfidence under out-of-distribution (OOD) objects, clutter, or ambiguous instructions. They typically operate as black boxes, with no accessible confidence. More fundamentally, any uncertainty derived from the VLM itself, whether raw logits, verbalized probability, or self-consistency, is a function of the same parameters θvlm\theta_{\mathrm{vlm}} that produced the prediction. It therefore inherits the VLM’s biases rather than providing an independent assessment [2, 3]. This raises a critical question: how can we derive reliable uncertainty for black-box VLMs that are decoupled from VLM-internal biases, to safely bound their behaviors in the open world?

To address this, we propose an external surrogate Bayesian model. It formulates uncertainty estimation as an external statistical test on the VLM prediction, rather than a self-reported confidence drawn from θvlm\theta_{\mathrm{vlm}}. Assuming continuity of neural networks, the surrogate treats a held-out set 𝒟cal\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{cal}} as empirical evidence. For each query, it estimates the posterior-predictive correctness within a local neighborhood via Beta-Bernoulli conjugacy, structurally decoupled from θvlm\theta_{\mathrm{vlm}}. The neighborhood is built by a hierarchical retrieval successively filtering in textual, cross-modal, and visual spaces, approximating a local neighborhood in the joint space without the curse of dimensionality. The surrogate yields two components. Aleatoric uncertainty arises from local prediction-label inconsistency, indicating regions where the VLM systematically fails. Epistemic uncertainty arises from neighborhood sparsity, a principled signal for OOD queries in deterministic VLMs.

Such uncertainty enables two active uncertainty alleviation extensions for visual grounding. Interactive visual grounding [4, 5] asks clarification questions to disambiguate the referring expression. We couple our per-object posterior with conformal prediction to form a (1−α)(1{-}\alpha)-coverage prediction set, querying regions inside it until the target is identified. Active visual grounding [6, 7] additionally takes physical actions, such as clearing obstacles or confirming targets, to actively gather evidence. We drive these decisions with a model-based policy that trades information gain against action cost. Under high uncertainty, both policies default to information-gathering rather than risky commitment.

Experiments show consistent gains across state-of-the-art VLMs, in both discrimination and calibration. On a real Fetch robot, the system identifies OOD queries and improves robustness by resolving uncertainty before acting. Our core contribution is an external surrogate Bayesian model that decouples uncertainty from the VLM itself, estimating closed-form aleatoric/epistemic components over a hierarchically retrieved neighborhood in 𝒟cal\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{cal}}. This, combined with conformal prediction and a model-based policy, realizes the robust uncertainty-to-action framework for active visual grounding in the open world.

title: Data-Driven or Model-Constrained? Comparing Airflow Estimation Methods under Sparse Sensing
authors: Dominik Aigner,Thomas Wiedemann,Javier Monroy,Achim J. Lilienthal
abstract: Airflow-driven advection is the primary mechanism for gas and aerosol dispersion in real-world scenarios, making accurate airflow estimation essential for ventilation monitoring, gas source localization, and contaminant spread analysis. Since obtaining airflow maps via high-resolution spatial sensing is usually infeasible in practice, flow field estimation methods must cope with sparse measurements by introducing statistical or physical priors to compensate for limited data. Existing approaches mainly differ in how they incorporate fluid-flow constraints and environmental geometry. However, due to the lack of systematic comparisons across this spectrum of methods, the potential benefits of physics-based priors for airflow estimation under sparse sensing remain underexplored.
introduction:
The transport of airborne substances is overwhelmingly driven by advection; while molecular diffusion takes hours to spread gases or aerosols over a few meters, even subtle air currents (<0.1 m/s<$0.1\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\text{/}\mathrm{s}$) achieve this in seconds [1]. Consequently, accurate airflow estimation is important for applications ranging from industrial leak monitoring to ventilation assessment in clinical settings [2, 3]. However, obtaining dense airflow maps through high-resolution spatial sensing is often impractical and costly, while Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) simulations require detailed boundary conditions and substantial computational resources.

In practice, neither may be fully available, i.e., only partial boundary knowledge and sparse, noisy airflow measurements, such as those collected along a mobile robot’s trajectory, are accessible. Estimating a dense airflow field under such circumstances is central to this work (see Fig. 1). We consider this problem under two simplifying assumptions: (1) we target the mean flow and therefore neglect short-term fluctuations by assuming steady state; (2) we restrict the flow field to two dimensions, as in prior work [4, 5].

Yet, this estimation task is inherently ill-posed, as the available data underdetermine the unknown flow variables. Existing approaches tackle this challenge through regularization, ranging from statistical smoothness priors to constraints imposed by domain geometry and fluid dynamics. This raises a fundamental question: to what extent can physical priors improve airflow estimation accuracy under practically relevant sampling densities, given their increased computational complexity and the inevitable mismatch between idealized physical models and real-world flow behavior?

To assess the role of physical priors, we compare four estimators spanning this spectrum: a purely data-driven Gaussian Process Regression (GPR) [6]; a graph-based Gaussian Markov Random Field (GMRF) [5] incorporating simplified flow dynamics; and two approaches based on partial differential equations (PDEs) – an existing weak-form Navier-Stokes Minimization (WFNS) [4] and a novel strong-form Navier-Stokes Residual Minimization (SFNS) variant introduced in Section II. In summary, our contributions are twofold: (i) the novel SFNS estimator, and (ii) a systematic comparison across this spectrum using OpenFOAM CFD simulations under varying sampling densities (Section III).

title: Teaching a Tree to Recover: Online Distillation of an LLM Supervisor with Counterfactual Replay
authors: Kristian Ceder,Kilian Freitag,Knut Åkesson
abstract: Autonomous mobile robots commonly pair a global planner with a local model predictive controller (MPC), but nonconvex obstacle avoidance and a limited horizon can make the robot freeze in complex layouts. Deciding whether to replan, wait, or call for help is a supervisory decision. Recent work queries a large language model (LLM) supervisor on every anomaly, which is slow and costly. We instead distill the LLM online into a decision tree. After each training episode, counterfactual replay labels recoveries as needed, unnecessary, or harmful. These labels retire unhelpful rules. In simulation, on 20 unseen layouts where the MPC alone freezes, the tree handles at least 18 correctly across all seeds, either by reaching the goal or by calling for help when no feasible path exists. The tree matches both an always-query LLM supervisor and expert-designed rules, while issuing no LLM queries at test time. Handwritten rules cannot anticipate the long tail of situations a physical robot will encounter. Online distillation is a promising remedy: the tree handles familiar cases, and the LLM is consulted only for new ones, whose validated recoveries become new rules. Language models can thus also serve as designers of supervisors rather than only as runtime supervisors.
introduction:
Autonomous Mobile Robot (AMR) navigation is commonly split into two layers. A global planner computes a path over a map, typically with Dijkstra’s algorithm or A*, treating the robot as a point and ignoring its kinematic and dynamic constraints. A local controller, often a model predictive controller (MPC), tracks this path while respecting those constraints, and may deviate from it temporarily to avoid static and dynamic obstacles. Such deviations must stay small, because obstacle avoidance makes the optimization problem nonconvex: with a finite horizon, the solver is prone to local optima, slow or failed convergence, and exceeding its computation budget. When the path is blocked by a large or non-convex obstacle that is missing from the map, such as a blocking object across an aisle or a U-shaped arrangement of pallets, a way around it lies beyond what the controller can find, and the robot comes to a standstill. Whether it should then replan, wait, or call for help depends on the cause. This decision belongs to a supervisory layer above the controller. Navigation stacks typically implement this layer as hand-written recovery behaviors triggered when the planner or controller fails [9]. In this work, we investigate how to learn this recovery behavior. Recent work places a large language model (LLM) in the loop as a supervisor [6, 14, 7] and queries it on every anomaly, at a latency of seconds.

This paper studies a similar approach where an LLM is used to find effective failure recoveries for an MPC-controlled mobile robot based on our previous work [19, 3]. Unlike other approaches, we study where a decision should reside once it has been made a few times by abstracting and refining recurring events into a decision tree. Further, in subsequent loops, the decision tree is first queried, and only when no fitting decision is present the LLM is queried again for additional labels. Therefore, the cost of decisions drastically decreases over time. To refine and verify decisions in the tree, we use counterfactual replay of each action after an episode finishes, which enables in-context learning for the LLM supervisor. Through this, the LLM can continuously improve its decisions and update the decision tree.

In various simulated scenarios, we find that our method complement and assist the MPC controller, leading to a near-perfect success rate in our tests. Importantly, it performs on par with hand-designed rules specifically created for the tested scenarios, showing that our framework can adapt to and learn from observed scenarios without human supervision.

In 20 held-out test layouts where the MPC alone fails, we show that our method instead succeeds in reaching the goal position in more than 90% of the cases. Furthermore, when comparing our method with a baseline of scripted rules specifically designed for those scenarios, we find that our method automatically finds equal or better decisions while reaching the goal in 10% fewer steps, thus verifying its effectiveness at finding reasonable interventions.

Our contributions are:

Online distillation of an LLM for AMR failure recovery into a decision tree. At a regular interval, a language model reads the current status report and decides whether an intervention is needed and picks a predefined recovery action, which acts only through the reference of an MPC tracker, the robot never waits for the LLM. To reduce the cost of repetitive interventions, we distill the LLM supervisor’s actions online into a decision tree when they occur more than once.

Counterfactual replay for in-context learning and rule-retirement. We show that when having access to a simulator then re-simulating each situation without the supervisor’s intervention gives labels if the action was needed, unnecessary, or harmful. Those are then used to retire existing rules and train the LLM in context to improve future decisions.

The code, data and videos are available at: 
https://github.com/kristianceder/Counterfactual-Tree-Teaching.

title: AFast Robot Localization Method Based on Monte Carlo Sampling
authors: He Zhaoqing,Hang Li,Xian Pu,Li Wang
abstract: 未获取到摘要
introduction:
Robots are the carriers of artificial intelligence and should possess three essential elements: perception, motion, and cognition [1, 2]. Nevertheless, current robots generally do not yet exhibit genuine intelligence and instead provide only basic programming and operational functions. Despite this limitation, their advantages in replacing humans for high-risk work have become increasingly evident [3, 4]. In regions where the Global Positioning System (GPS) is denied, such as disaster zones and caves, performing fast localization and navigation using on-board sensors is an important problem for improving robot intelligence [5, 6]. Closely related is the path-planning task, for which metaheuristic optimizers such as heuristic hybrid particle swarm optimization have been developed to compute feasible quadcopter trajectories efficiently in complex environments [7]; however, reliable path execution still presupposes accurate self-localization.

At present, common localization systems can be divided into external localization, such as GPS and motion capture, and on-board localization, such as visual navigation and radar navigation [8, 9]. Owing to the high computational cost and power consumption of visual navigation [10, 11], it is not well suited for robot exploration in unknown environments. In radar navigation, filtering techniques are generally adopted to achieve localization, such as the Kalman filter, the bootstrap filter, the H∞H_{\infty} filter, and the particle filter [12, 13, 14, 15]. Each filtering technique has its own advantages and disadvantages. The Kalman filter is well suited for handling Gaussian distributions [12, 16]; the particle filter is chosen for large-scale environments [17], because compared with the Kalman filter that has a complexity of O⁡(n2)O(n^{2}), its computational complexity is logarithmic; the H∞H_{\infty} filter is used to improve the convergence of Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) systems [18].

To achieve fast localization in unknown and complex environments, this paper selects the particle filter because it imposes relatively minimal requirements on the system (it requires neither that the system model equations be linear nor that the system noise be Gaussian) [19], and thus offers better algorithmic scalability and generality. In this work, the robot is placed in a complex maze, and its position and heading are inferred by the particle filter. Four sensors are mounted on the front, rear, left, and right sides of the robot, and these sensors are used to measure the perpendicular distance between the robot and the nearest wall. By comparing the observation data with the sampled data, the distribution of the pose estimate is revised, followed by state transition and resampling. Experiments show that an accurate localization of the robot can be obtained after several rounds of resampling.

Recently, the integration of large language models with multi-agent systems and reinforcement learning has opened new directions for autonomous agents and swarm intelligence [20, 21]. For example, language-model-based agents have been used to automate the configuration and training of multi-agent reinforcement learning pipelines for drone swarms [22]. These advances complement classical probabilistic localization by enriching high-level reasoning and coordination, while methods such as the one proposed here remain crucial for the low-level state estimation upon which higher-level autonomy depends.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 introduces the theoretical foundation and operating mechanism of the particle filter; Section 3 evaluates the proposed algorithm in a simulation environment; and Section 4 draws the conclusion.

title: AI for Science in Space: Orbital Laboratories, Planetary Fieldwork, and Embodied Autonomy
authors: Zizhe Wang,Jia Deng,Xin Lu,Zehao Jia,Yi Huang,Yao Zhu,Jianing Li
abstract: Artificial intelligence for science (AI4S) is extending from interpretation of existing data to the design and execution of experiments. Space offers distinctive scientific opportunities while restricting physical support. Microgravity and extraterrestrial environments expose phenomena that terrestrial experiments cannot fully reproduce; finite samples, constrained resources, and limited opportunities for intervention complicate sustained investigation. This critical review examines orbital laboratories and planetary in situ science across biology, materials, fluid and thermal physics, and adaptive exploration. We distinguish learning from space-derived data, selecting scientific actions, executing them, and preserving experimental validity. Terrestrial self-driving laboratories provide complementary evidence on optimization, dedicated automation, robotic manipulation, and the support needed for unattended operation. The synthesis connects scientific gains already demonstrated by bounded AI systems to gaps in observation, executable actions, and continuity of valid evidence. Space robots can expand the attainable scope of autonomous science when necessary interventions exceed validated instrument capabilities and timely human support is unavailable. Their value must be established against dedicated mechanisms, redundancy, and human-supported operation. We develop a framework connecting sample history, scientific decisions, physical execution, and claim-specific validity. A worked orbital design, a planetary extension, and matched evaluation schemes separate the contributions of sensing, decision policies, and physical actions. The resulting agenda measures autonomy through valid scientific return, task coverage, intervention costs, and evidence integrity across complete campaigns.
introduction:
Artificial intelligence for science (AI4S) uses computational methods for learning, inference, search, and decision-making to advance scientific understanding. Its contributions include extracting observables from complex data, constructing predictive models, proposing candidate mechanisms or materials, and selecting informative experiments [1]. These functions occupy different positions in the scientific process. A model that predicts a molecular property can be scientifically valuable without controlling an instrument; a system that chooses an experiment must additionally connect its prediction to a feasible intervention and an interpretable outcome. The transition from analyzing evidence to actively producing it is therefore an integration problem involving scientific reasoning, experimental design, and physical execution.

Space provides a distinctive setting for this transition. Orbital laboratories make altered gravity and prolonged exposure accessible as experimental conditions. Planetary missions investigate materials and environments whose context cannot be reproduced completely on Earth. These opportunities coexist with restricted experimental resources, limited access to equipment, and variable opportunities for human intervention. The space biological and physical sciences decadal survey emphasizes both the scientific questions enabled by these environments and the infrastructure needed to investigate them [2]. AI4S can help make individual experiments more informative, but its longer-term value depends on whether a scientific program can continue producing trustworthy evidence between opportunities for external support.

Robot scientists and self-driving laboratories have developed experimental feedback on Earth [3, 4]. Spacecraft planning and execution research has addressed resource constraints and changing conditions for decades [5, 6, 7]. Mars instruments have demonstrated bounded scientific choices onboard [8, 9]. Orbital biology has established substantial dedicated automation and an explicit agenda for AI-supported deep-space laboratories [10]. These traditions connect scientific inference, experimental feedback, and resource-aware execution across terrestrial and space settings.

This review focuses on orbital experimentation and planetary in situ science. Orbital coverage includes biology, materials and crystal growth, fluid and thermal physics, combustion, soft matter, and a bounded cold-atom comparison. Planetary coverage includes target selection, adaptive spectroscopy, sample acquisition and handling, field surveys, and astrobiology. Sounding-rocket, parabolic-flight, terrestrial analogue, and laboratory studies are included where they clarify the experimental lineage or the transfer problem, with their settings explicitly identified. Astronomy and remote sensing are adjacent AI4S domains; they are not the main evidence base here. Generic spacecraft control, manufacturing, and servicing enter only where they explain a scientific workflow or its continued availability.

Three distinctions organize the synthesis. First, we separate the origin of data from the locations of computation and action. An AI model trained on ISS images on Earth is different from a model selecting an observation aboard a spacecraft. Second, we distinguish scientific decisions from operational decisions. Choosing an observation that discriminates hypotheses is different from maintaining a thermal set point, although both may be needed for the same experiment. Third, we separate action completion from experimental validity. A pump may execute its command while the delivered volume remains unknown; a spectrometer may return data from an unintended target. Validity depends on whether the evidence answers the intended question under known conditions.

These distinctions also clarify terminology. We use automation for execution of defined procedures, which can include feedback, branching, and designed recovery. We use scientific autonomy for delegated decisions about acquiring or interpreting evidence within specified objectives and constraints. We use embodied autonomy for the capacity to estimate relevant physical state and act on it through sensing, movement, manipulation, or reconfiguration, with outcome verification. Embodiment is functional: a microfluidic device can have a useful restricted action space, while a mobile manipulator can access a broader range of interfaces. The question is which physical capabilities are available, which decisions are delegated, and how their consequences are checked.

Our central argument is that space robots can expand the attainable scope of autonomous science when scientifically necessary interventions exceed validated instrument capabilities and timely human support is unavailable. Many scientific loops can be closed through valves, optical settings, or instrument pointing. Others require access to a new measurement geometry, sample transfer, interface exchange, or preservation after an interruption. The relevant comparison is whether an added capability improves valid scientific return under mission constraints relative to dedicated mechanisms, redundancy, and human-supported operation.

Three questions make the proposition testable: what scientific question is blocked, which observation or physical action is missing, and why cannot the existing apparatus or available support supply it? Scientific decision authority, physical action repertoire, and dependence on external support are separate dimensions. A broader repertoire may enable a new class of experiment without increasing decision authority; a better policy may improve an existing instrument without adding mechanics.

The contribution is an account of this boundary across orbital laboratories and planetary fieldwork. Existing space-laboratory perspectives motivate AI-supported deep-space biology, while terrestrial reviews analyze experimental optimization, laboratory integration, and robotics [10, 4, 11, 12]. Table 2 locates our synthesis relative to those contributions. We jointly examine scientific function, sample and measurement history, executable actions, external support, and the scientific outcome of intervention. This connects demonstrated capabilities to a choice among competing designs. A worked orbital design, a planetary extension, and matched comparisons in Section 7 make the resulting propositions operational. The search, selection, and source-access limitations of this structured critical narrative review are documented in Appendix A.

title: Kinematic-Tactile Aligned Dexterous Retargeting with Contact Wrench Space Alignment
authors: Xinyuan He,Ziheng Xu,Yueyuan Chen,Yufan Ye,Yuanshuo Tan,Huiming Pan,Jianjun Meng,Shuo Jiang,Peter B. Shull
abstract:
Human demonstrations provide a natural and scalable source of data for learning dexterous manipulation policies.
However, existing retargeting methods primarily transfer human kinematics, while the tactile information underlying physical interaction is rarely preserved across embodiments.
To address this limitation, we present a hierarchical three-stage framework for kinematic-tactile aligned dexterous retargeting.
We use object-centric contact wrench space as a physical representation for tactile alignment between human and robot hands.
The framework first aligns hand kinematics and contact geometry, and then constructs a human wrench support profile from tactile forces and contact geometry.
Robot fingertip force targets are subsequently optimized to cover the human wrench support and converted into joint position corrections, yielding directly replayable robot hand trajectories.
We evaluate the framework in simulation and real robot experiments across three pouring conditions. In the real robot experiments, our method achieves a 96.7% replay success rate and higher wrench transfer fidelity than representative retargeting baselines.
The framework enables physically grounded transfer of kinematic and tactile information from human demonstrations to robot hands, providing a path toward scalable learning of contact-rich dexterous manipulation.
introduction:
Dexterous manipulation has long been challenging due to the complex kinematics of dexterous hands [1].
Human demonstrations provide a natural and scalable source of data for learning dexterous manipulation policies, motivating growing efforts to transfer human manipulation skills to anthropomorphic robot hands [2].
Retargeting plays a critical role in converting human data into robot hand trajectories and has been widely used in both teleoperation and robot-free data collection [3, 4].
However, existing retargeting methods primarily focus on aligning the kinematics of human and robot hands, while largely overlooking tactile alignment, which plays an important role in reliable and physically consistent manipulation [5].
Therefore, effective dexterous retargeting should consider both kinematic and tactile alignment to faithfully transfer human manipulation skills across embodiments.

Recent studies have made encouraging progress in functional retargeting, yet the explicit use of human tactile information remains limited.
Conventional kinematic methods align human and robot hand kinematics through predefined task-space correspondences, such as fingertip positions and relationships between fingers [6].
More recent interaction-aware methods further preserve contact regions or hand–object interaction structures, improving the consistency of transferred contacts [7, 8].
However, these objectives remain geometric and provide no direct constraint on contact forces.
Modern approaches increasingly employ reinforcement learning to refine retargeted motions through interaction with simulated environments [9, 10, 11].
Although these methods can achieve strong performance in simulation, they primarily recover executable motions through policy optimization and task-specific objectives rather than through explicit tactile alignment across embodiments.
Therefore, existing retargeting methods still lack an explicit physical representation to align both kinematic and tactile information for faithful skill transfer across embodiments.

In this letter, we present a hierarchical three-stage retargeting framework that jointly aligns kinematic and tactile information across human and robot embodiments (Fig. 1).
Our key insight is to use object-centric contact wrench space as a shared physical representation for tactile alignment across different hand embodiments.
This learning-free formulation enables stable and physically consistent retargeting in real-world manipulation with varying payloads and object deformation.

Specifically, our framework progressively aligns hand kinematics, contact geometry, and object-centric wrench support.
First, the kinematic alignment stage matches corresponding human and robot task-space vectors frame by frame to generate an initial robot hand trajectory.
Second, the contact alignment stage uses tactile-activated contact regions to refine the human and robot hand–object configurations at an anchor frame in simulation, and propagates the resulting contact residuals throughout the trajectories.
Finally, the wrench space alignment stage constructs the human object-centric wrench support profile from contact geometry and tactile forces, and optimizes robot fingertip force targets to cover this profile.
These force targets are then converted into joint position corrections, yielding the final directly replayable robot hand trajectory.

We evaluate our approach in both simulation and physical experiments on a paper cup pouring task under three payload conditions with different materials and masses.
The results demonstrate that our framework produces directly replayable robot hand trajectories while preserving human-derived wrench support characteristics across payload conditions.
In real-world trajectory replay, our method achieves a 96.7% success rate over 60 trials, outperforming both baselines.
Our method also achieves higher wrench transfer fidelity than the baselines in both the global and task-relevant wrench spaces.

In summary, our main contributions are:

1. We introduce contact wrench space as a physical representation for tactile alignment in dexterous retargeting.

2. We develop a hierarchical three-stage retargeting framework that progressively aligns kinematic, contact, and wrench information from human demonstrations and produces directly replayable robot hand trajectories.

3. Extensive real robot experiments show that our method achieves higher replay success and wrench transfer fidelity than representative retargeting baselines.
The framework also produces replayable robot demonstrations with human-derived wrench support, providing a practical data source for future contact-rich manipulation learning.

title: SimTO-Robust: Automated Design of Soft Grippers Robust to Grasp Pose and Object Geometry
authors: Kurt Enkera,Joshua Pinskier,Marcus Gallagher,David Howard
abstract: Robotic grippers operating in unstructured environments must robustly grasp objects of different shapes and sizes despite perception and positioning errors. Soft grippers that can achieve this robustness through intelligent mechanical design rather than sophisticated control software offer a promising solution. However, no existing computational design framework explicitly optimises soft gripper morphology for robustness across object geometries and grasp poses. We introduce SimTO-Robust, a generalisation of simulation-driven topology optimisation (SimTO) that simulates grasps across multiple objects and poses and aggregates their contact forces to guide gripper morphology optimisation. We generate 6,646 designs and physically evaluate 24 of them alongside 10 specialised SimTO designs, two rigid baseline grippers, and a baseline generalist soft gripper produced using conventional topology optimisation. All 37 grippers are tested in a pick-and-place task involving five feature-rich objects and six grasp poses, with external disturbances of increasing magnitude applied during the task. On average, SimTO-Robust designs complete pick-and-place more reliably than specialised SimTO designs and the rigid baselines. The best SimTO-Robust designs also withstood more of the applied disturbances than any other tested gripper. These results show that incorporating diverse grasp conditions into simulation-driven topology optimisation is a simple and effective approach to improving real-world soft gripper robustness. More broadly, they show that robust robotic grasping can be achieved through intelligent mechanical design rather than sophisticated sensing and control.
introduction:
While robotic grasping has become ubiquitous in logistics and is rapidly expanding into unstructured settings such as fruit harvesting [19], coral farming [17] and household cleaning [3], its reliance on visually tracking defined object classes limits both its success and robustness. In unstructured environments, objects vary widely in shape and size, making it difficult for perception-based grasping systems to recognise and accurately localise every object encountered [9]. Even when objects are successfully detected, positioning errors can introduce uncertainty in grasp pose. Therefore, to enable the automation of laborious manual handling tasks in unstructured environments, robotic grippers must be robust to variations in object geometry and grasp pose.

Soft robotic grippers offer a promising approach to robust grasping. Unlike conventional rigid grippers, which have limited passive adaptability and often rely on sophisticated vision-based control algorithms to achieve robustness [9, 3], soft grippers made from compliant materials can deform around objects and passively adapt to different object geometries and grasp poses [19], reducing the reliance on complex sensing and control through embodied intelligence [6]. However, designing soft grippers is challenging as their complex material properties and continuous deformability give rise to high-dimensional design spaces [19].

Soft gripper design methods range from manual, bioinspired approaches [16, 7] to highly automated computational design methods [19]. Manual approaches rely heavily on designer intuition and repeated prototyping, and become increasingly difficult as the number of target objects and grasp poses grows. Computational design methods, such as parametric and topology optimisation (TO), use physics-based simulations to systematically explore and evaluate a larger range of candidate designs than manual approaches [19]. However, parametric optimisation requires designers to specify an initial geometry (e.g., a Fin Ray finger) and an often limited set of parameters to optimise (e.g., finger length or width), heavily constraining the range of achievable morphologies [22]. In contrast, TO does not require a predefined parameterised geometry, instead optimising the distribution of material within a general design domain to achieve a specified objective, producing more freeform morphologies with fine-grained geometric features [11, 18].

Despite their ability to efficiently search large design spaces, to our knowledge, no existing computational method explicitly optimises soft grippers for robustness across a specific set of object geometries and grasp poses. Instead, parametric approaches typically optimise grasp strength [13, 14, 21], while TO frameworks optimise generic flexibility-based objectives [11, 20, 4, 12, 18]. In both cases, robustness to variations in object geometry and grasp pose is not explicitly represented in the design objective.

TO is a promising candidate for robust soft gripper design as it produces freeform morphologies while requiring less human input than parametric approaches. However, expressing grasp robustness, which depends on contact-rich interactions across many objects and poses, as a tractable optimisation objective remains challenging. Simulation-driven topology optimisation, or SimTO [5], offers a solution for a single object in a single pose. It simulates soft grasping and uses the resulting gripper-object contact forces to define an object-specific, flexibility-based objective. However, as it only models one object and pose, the resulting designs are specialised to that object-pose combination and lack robustness.

To improve the robustness of SimTO, we develop SimTO-Robust, which simulates soft grasping of multiple objects and multiple poses and aggregates the resulting contact forces into a single flexibility-based objective that accounts for every simulated grasp. The designer can therefore control what the gripper is robust to simply by choosing which objects and poses are simulated. Our contributions are:

A generalised TO framework which explicitly incorporates variations in object geometry and grasp pose into the topology optimisation of robust soft grippers;

A dataset of 6,646 robust designs generated with SimTO-Robust, and an analysis of how their geometric features differ from those of specialised SimTO designs.

1. A generalised TO framework which explicitly incorporates variations in object geometry and grasp pose into the topology optimisation of robust soft grippers;

2. A dataset of 6,646 robust designs generated with SimTO-Robust, and an analysis of how their geometric features differ from those of specialised SimTO designs.
