title: Assuring Learning-Enabled Cyber-Physical Systems with Foundation Models: A Neuro-Symbolic Agenda for Testing, Verification, and Runtime Assurance
authors: Xi Zheng,Ivan Ruchkin,Hong Jin Kang,Tevfik Bultan,Vijay Ganesh,Taylor T. Johnson,Ziyang Li,Lei Ma,Aloysius K. Mok,Daniel Neider,Ruzica Piskac,Nalini Venkatasubramanian,Simon Thompson,Sanjoy Baruah
abstract: Learning-enabled cyber-physical systems (CPS), including autonomous vehicles and UAVs, increasingly incorporate foundation models, yet fragmented assurance practices provide insufficient support for system-level guarantees. We argue that restoring engineering control across stochastic neural, symbolic, and physical boundaries requires a shift from model-centric evaluation to system-level assurance. We introduce the Foundation Model Assurance Stack, connecting three directions: (i) neuro-symbolic architectures that constrain foundation models through explicit symbolic world models, reasoning layers, and interfaces; (ii) semantically grounded, conformance-based testing that combines formal specifications and symbolic world models with foundation-model-assisted specification mining, scenario generation, and test synthesis; and (iii) compositional verification and runtime assurance that target formally tractable components and interfaces through modular contracts, equivalence checking, verified synthesis, uncertainty-aware reasoning, and runtime monitoring and enforcement. Symbolic abstractions establish assurance boundaries between stochastic learning and formal reasoning, connecting testing, verification, and runtime evidence across the system lifecycle. Foundation models serve as constrained assistants whose outputs are independently checked wherever correctness can be formally specified. We identify research challenges in specification engineering, abstraction fidelity, evidence composition, and lifecycle certification, and outline a staged agenda toward trustworthy, deployable, and certifiable learning-enabled CPS.
introduction:
Learning-enabled cyber-physical systems (CPS), including autonomous vehicles,
unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), and embodied robotic systems, increasingly
integrate foundation models such as large language models (LLMs),
vision-language models (VLMs), and vision-language-action models (VLAs).
These models provide powerful capabilities for perception, semantic
understanding, reasoning, planning, and system engineering. At the same time,
their stochastic, opaque, and data-driven behaviour challenges fundamental
software engineering assumptions about explicit specifications, predictable
interfaces, traceable execution, and independently checkable correctness.

The resulting assurance problem extends beyond the reliability of individual
models. In a learning-enabled CPS, information flows from physical sensors
through neural perception and learned representations to world models,
reasoning and planning, and ultimately back to physical actions. Uncertainty,
semantic information, and behavioural assumptions may be lost or transformed
at each boundary. Consequently, strong benchmark performance of an individual
model does not establish that the integrated system behaves correctly, remains
within its operational constraints, or fails safely under distribution shift
and unforeseen environmental conditions. Even formally verified model
properties provide practical assurance only when they are connected to the
requirements of the systems in which those models are
deployed (Johnson, 2025). Establishing this connection requires
relating model-level guarantees to formal system specifications and
environmental assumptions, consistent with the broader verified-AI
agenda (Seshia et al., 2022). The central challenge is therefore
one of regaining engineering control over learning-enabled systems whose
behaviour cannot be completely specified or analysed at the model level.

This challenge motivates a fundamental question for software engineering:

How can we systematically test, verify, and assure learning-enabled
cyber-physical systems that incorporate foundation models?

Discussions at Shonan Seminar No. 235
(Zheng et al., 2026) on LLM-Guided Synthesis, Testing, and
Verification of Learning-Enabled Cyber-Physical Systems highlighted several
limitations of existing assurance approaches. Testing based primarily on model
accuracy, input diversity, or neural coverage provides limited evidence about
system-level safety properties. Formal verification, meanwhile, faces severe
scalability and specification challenges when applied directly to large
foundation models and open-ended neural components. Treating such models as
black boxes further obscures the semantic relationships between perception,
reasoning, and physical behaviour. A more tractable direction is to expose
explicit intermediate representations and interfaces, use foundation models as
constrained assistants rather than trusted oracles, and concentrate formal
reasoning on components and properties for which correctness can be specified
and independently checked.

Therefore, we argue for a shift from model-centric evaluation toward
system-level assurance. Rather than attempting to make the foundation
model itself the trusted core of a CPS, software architecture should establish
explicit assurance boundaries around learning-enabled components. In
particular, neuro-symbolic decomposition and symbolic world models provide a
bridge between stochastic neural perception and formally analysable reasoning,
while specifications, contracts, and interfaces provide shared artefacts for
testing, verification, and runtime monitoring. Assurance can then be built
compositionally by combining empirical evidence, formal guarantees, and
runtime enforcement.

Based on this perspective, we introduce the Foundation Model Assurance
Stack shown in Figure 1. The stack consists of three
complementary assurance pillars, connected through cross-cutting neuro-symbolic
integration, together with a distinct runtime assurance layer that operationalises
their outputs during system execution:

Foundation Models as Assistive Components focuses on
system construction. Foundation models support structured perception,
symbolic world-model construction, symbolic reasoning, and planning and
control, but do not directly control the CPS. The resulting world models,
specifications, interfaces, and system structure expose explicit artefacts for
downstream assurance.

Foundation Models as Assistive Components focuses on
system construction. Foundation models support structured perception,
symbolic world-model construction, symbolic reasoning, and planning and
control, but do not directly control the CPS. The resulting world models,
specifications, interfaces, and system structure expose explicit artefacts for
downstream assurance.

Testing and Validation focuses on empirical evidence.
Conformance-based testing, structured scenario generation, DSL-guided test
synthesis, specification mining, and behavioural coverage and adequacy analysis
discover failures and generate validation evidence. Testing also provides
counterexamples and constraint-validation results to verification.

Verification and Assurance Mechanisms focuses on
formal guarantees and assurance artefact synthesis. Contract
verification, interface verification, and transformation verification establish
properties over tractable system abstractions and interfaces, while runtime
monitor synthesis and safety constraint synthesis translate verified properties
into monitors and enforceable constraints for operational use by the runtime
assurance layer. Verification and testing interact bidirectionally: formal
constraints guide testing, while empirical counterexamples refine verification
artefacts.

Across these pillars, neuro-symbolic integration provides shared
assurance artefacts through symbolic world models, DSLs and structured
representations, contract specifications, and neural–symbolic interfaces.
These artefacts bridge stochastic learning components and explicit reasoning
and provide common objects for system construction, testing, and verification.

Distinct from the three assurance pillars, the Runtime Assurance Layer
operationalises their outputs during system execution through a
Simplex architecture (Sha, 2001). It integrates system structure and
interfaces from the architectural pillar, failure modes and threshold
calibration from testing and validation, and monitors and safety constraints
from verification and runtime assurance. A high-performance learning-enabled
controller operates under a runtime monitor, while a verified safe controller
and shielding or switching mechanisms intervene when unsafe behaviour or
constraint violations are detected. Thus, Pillar 3 develops the verified
properties and enforcement mechanisms needed for runtime assurance, whereas
the bottom layer instantiates and executes these mechanisms to maintain
operational safety under uncertainty.

1. Foundation Models as Assistive Components focuses on
system construction. Foundation models support structured perception,
symbolic world-model construction, symbolic reasoning, and planning and
control, but do not directly control the CPS. The resulting world models,

2. Testing and Validation focuses on empirical evidence.

title: From Reasoning to Action: Consequence-Grounded Alignment for Vision-Language-Action Models
authors: Yixue Zhang,Wenke Xia,Kun Wu,Wenbo Yu,Pei Ren,Junnan Nie,Di Hu,Zhengping Che,Chang Liu
abstract:
Reasoning informs decision-making by connecting intended actions with their expected consequences. Building on this principle, recent vision-language-action models incorporate embodied chains of thought (ECoTs) as an intermediate stage in action generation. However, such guidance remains implicit, as actions are conditioned on the generated ECoTs rather than explicitly optimized to align with them.
To bridge this gap, we introduce the Consequence-grounded Reasoning-to-Action alignment method called CoRAct, an offline training framework that explicitly aligns reasoning and action through reward-guided optimization in action noise space.
Specifically, CoRAct formulates two physically grounded ECoT components as verifiable signals: movement specifies the intended motion, whereas waypoints encode the expected spatial consequence of execution. By jointly modeling ECoT reasoning, action generation, and action-conditioned future prediction, a unified Mixture-of-Transformers explicitly couples each action with its articulated intent and predicted consequence. For action candidates generated from sampled noise, CoRAct computes alignment rewards based on motion consistency with the described movement and agreement between predicted outcomes and the specified waypoints. These rewards drive group-relative optimization of the initial noise distribution, steering action generation toward consistency with the articulated intent and expected consequence.
Extensive experiments across RoboCasa, VLABench, and real-world manipulation tasks demonstrate consistent gains in task success and generalization over strong ECoT-based VLA baselines. Further analyses reveal improved reasoning–execution alignment and show that our method can ground externally provided ECoTs in executable behavior, supporting zero-shot adaptation to novel scenarios by leveraging knowledge from powerful VLMs.
Our project page and dataset are publicly available at
https://onlyxingxingzyx.github.io/CoRAct/.
introduction:
Human decision-making often involves prospective reasoning that connects intended actions with their expected consequences. Such reasoning mediates between task intent and concrete behavior by relating action formulation to anticipated outcomes.
Inspired by this capability, recent vision-language-action (VLA) models increasingly integrate intermediate reasoning into action generation in the form of embodied chains of thought (ECoTs) [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]. By structuring action generation around textual plans, visual subgoals, spatial targets, and action-level intentions, ECoTs provide an intermediate interface between task understanding and physical execution [6, 7]. As the paradigm evolves, embodied reasoning is increasingly integrated into the perception–action pipeline, extending beyond purely textual deliberation toward representations more closely tied to physical control.

Prior efforts have improved VLA generalization
through diversity-driven task generation
[8], visual data augmentation
[9], and unified vision-motion
representation learning [10].
While these approaches enhance generalization
across diverse tasks, objects, and visual conditions,
adapting to unseen semantic constraints and novel
task compositions requires reasoning beyond
learned action patterns.
Embodied reasoning offers a complementary path
toward such out-of-distribution generalization
by connecting task intent with anticipated
physical consequences.
However, its potential remains limited if
the generated actions fail to faithfully
realize the articulated reasoning. Existing VLA models typically use ECoTs as conditioning context for action generation, leaving this correspondence to be learned implicitly from demonstrations rather than enforced through an explicit optimization objective [4, 5, 11, 12]. In embodied control, this gap has concrete consequences: a model may articulate an appropriate motion yet generate an action that deviates from it, or anticipate a plausible spatial outcome that execution fails to realize. These discrepancies reveal a missing link between coherent intermediate reasoning and physical behavior that faithfully reflects both the stated intent and the expected outcome.

To bridge this gap, we introduce CoRAct, an offline training framework for consequence-grounded reasoning-to-action alignment. CoRAct explicitly optimizes the consistency between embodied reasoning and generated actions through reward-based learning in the action noise space. The key idea is to treat the motion intent and spatial expectations expressed in embodied reasoning as verifiable constraints for action generation. These signals provide concrete criteria for evaluating whether generated actions follow the articulated reasoning and whether their predicted consequences agree with the expected outcomes. By translating these consistency evaluations into alignment rewards, CoRAct establishes a direct connection between embodied reasoning and action optimization, enabling reasoning-aware improvement of robotic policies.

Specifically, CoRAct extracts two physically grounded signals from ECoT reasoning: movement for describing the intended motion and waypoints for representing the expected spatial consequence.
To connect these reasoning signals to action generation and future consequences, we build a unified Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT) architecture that jointly models ECoT reasoning, action generation, and action-conditioned future prediction. This joint formulation associates each generated action with both its articulated intent and predicted consequence, allowing the same action candidate to be evaluated against the reasoning that motivates it and the future outcome it is expected to produce. CoRAct therefore measures whether a generated action follows the described movement and whether its predicted consequence agrees with the specified waypoint, and converts these two forms of consistency into alignment rewards.
Building on these alignment signals, CoRAct optimizes action generation in the noise space. For each reasoning context, multiple action candidates are generated from sampled noise and evaluated for motion and consequence consistency. The resulting rewards drive group-relative optimization of a conditional noise predictor, guiding it toward noise samples that induce actions better aligned with both the intended motion and expected consequence. This improves the fidelity between ECoT reasoning and generated actions, strengthening reasoning-to-action alignment.

We evaluate CoRAct across RoboCasa, VLABench, and real-world manipulation tasks, demonstrating consistent improvements in task success and generalization over strong ECoT-based VLA baselines. Further analyses show stronger alignment between reasoning and execution, with the benefits extending beyond reasoning generated by the policy itself. In particular, CoRAct can ground ECoTs provided by powerful VLMs in executable actions, allowing their knowledge and decision-making capabilities to guide manipulation in novel scenarios. This capability enables zero-shot adaptation through external reasoning without additional policy training, extending ECoTs from an intermediate reasoning representation to a general interface for guiding physical behavior.

Overall, our main contributions are as follows:

We introduce CoRAct, a consequence-grounded alignment framework that explicitly makes consistency between embodied reasoning and physical execution.

Building on joint training, we derive alignment rewards from motion consistency with movement descriptions and agreement between predicted outcomes and waypoints. title: PRIME W0: Physical Priors from World Models for Embodied Manipulation
authors: Huabin Peng,Fagang Jin,Yancong Wei,Tengfei Ma,Chuhang Liu,Chao Yu,Liqing Chen
abstract: 未获取到摘要
introduction:
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models [5, 16, 4] have emerged as a
dominant paradigm for generalist robot policies, casting manipulation as
conditional generation over visual and language tokens. By pretraining on
large-scale internet data and fine-tuning on robot demonstrations, VLAs achieve
impressive breadth across tasks and embodiments. Recent flow- and
diffusion-based VLAs further improve action expressiveness by replacing
autoregressive decoders with continuous generative processes, enabling
multi-modal action distributions and smoother trajectories [4].

Despite these advances, most VLA policies remain feed-forward: at each
control step they condition action generation only on the current observation
and instruction, without an explicit model of how the scene will evolve.
This creates two coupled limitations. First, temporal myopia: long-horizon
tasks with occlusion, contact ambiguity, or multi-phase manipulation require
tracking motion trends and anticipating near-future scene layout, yet repeating
the full VLM on every historical frame is prohibitively expensive. Second,
semantic compression: many architectures route action decoding through a
single compressed VLM representation, discarding the hierarchical
semantic–spatial structure accumulated across intermediate layers that is
critical for fine-grained motor control.

Flow-matching action decoders exacerbate both issues. During denoising, early
steps benefit from high-level task semantics while late steps require precise
perceptual grounding and kinematically consistent trajectories. A policy that
conditions only on the present frame and a collapsed VLM summary cannot

title: Ask to Evolve: A Unified Harness for Lifelong Embodied Navigation with Hybrid Action Space and Persistent Memory
authors: Kai Sheng,Liuyi Wang,Jinlong Li,Haojie Dai,Chengju Liu,Qijun Chen
abstract:
Giving embodied agents the freedom to act autonomously, initiate interactions, and understand their surroundings through experience is a step toward bringing them to life in the physical world. Realizing this vision requires action, interaction, and memory to work together, so that each encounter can inform current decisions and contribute experience for future tasks. We present EvoLife, a unified navigation harness that enables a multimodal embodied agent to choose how to move, when to ask, and what experience to carry forward. Its hybrid action space supports waypoint navigation, local discrete adjustments, pixel-based navigation, and object-directed navigation. Active interaction allows the agent to seek clarification or assistance when it encounters ambiguity or difficulty, while persistent spatial memory binds observations and dialogue to places, retaining useful experience to guide subsequent visits. We evaluate eight benchmarks across four task families: vision-language navigation, object navigation, interactive instance navigation, and continuous multi-task navigation.
With an average of only 1.87 active interactions per episode, our method achieves a first-visit success rate (SR) of 100% across four 100-episode sets spanning vision-language navigation and object navigation.
Complete-sequence SR reaches 98% on 50 LHPR-VLN sequences and 94% on 50 GOAT-Bench sequences. In the R2R revisit setting, success weighted by path length (SPL) increases from 82.23% to 93.31% with retained experience. Multi-day physical navigation further demonstrates exploration, proactive help-seeking, and revisiting remembered places. Together, these results advance the vision of bringing embodied agents to life through autonomous action, proactive interaction, and the accumulation and reuse of experience.
introduction:
Lifelong embodied navigation calls for agents that can take initiative in how they act, interact, and accumulate experience. An agent should be able to choose how to pursue a goal according to its environment and task requirements, ask questions when it encounters ambiguity, seek assistance when progress becomes difficult, and carry what it learns into future tasks. These capabilities give concrete meaning to the vision of bringing embodied agents to life in the physical world. Through sustained engagement with their surroundings, agents can connect what they perceive with what they do, use interaction to develop their understanding, and build experience that remains useful beyond a single encounter.

People navigating unfamiliar environments naturally ask for clarification, request directions, and seek help when needed. Embodied agents need the freedom to take the same initiative. A question can clarify an instruction, identify a useful continuation, or obtain assistance with a physical obstacle. The value of that interaction can also extend beyond the immediate task: an answer about a place, together with the observations and actions that follow, can become experience for a later visit. This motivates the central idea of Ask to Evolve: an agent actively asks to improve its understanding, acts on the resulting information, and retains useful experience to guide future behavior.

Embodied navigation provides concrete settings for studying this process. Vision-language navigation connects linguistic instructions with visual observations and navigation decisions, including movement through continuous environments [3, 27, 26, 12]. Interactive navigation introduces dialogue as a source of clarification and assistance [49, 38, 13], while iterative and lifelong navigation make earlier encounters relevant to subsequent tasks [25, 24]. Systematic real-world evaluations have documented a substantial gap between simulated and physical navigation performance [54, 55]. This gap highlights the importance of coordinating perception, decision-making, and execution, together with the ability to obtain assistance and reuse experience in real environments.

Existing methods offer useful foundations. Topological planners connect visual waypoints with continuous control [1], and language-model navigators integrate observations, reasoning, and actions through execution interfaces [82, 83]. Memory-based systems retain observations and behavior, while navigation harnesses preserve maps and task records across sessions [63, 80, 7]. These advances motivate a unified systems question: how can an embodied agent keep multiple ways of moving, actively requested assistance, and remembered experience available within the same decision loop? The connection matters because an interaction may change the next movement, revise the interpretation of a place, and contribute knowledge that is useful during a subsequent task.

We introduce EvoLife, a unified harness for lifelong embodied navigation with a hybrid action space, active interaction, and persistent spatial memory. Its action space supports four complementary modes: waypoint navigation toward a selected spatial location, local discrete adjustments for fine control, pixel-based navigation toward a selected image location, and object-directed navigation toward an identified target. These modes give the agent flexibility in expressing its movement intention. It can select a spatial waypoint, make a short adjustment, indicate a visible location, or approach an object, according to the task and available observations. Execution returns the actual outcome, allowing the agent to inspect its progress and choose its next action. Fig. 2 presents the overall framework.

Active interaction is part of this ongoing decision process. The agent chooses when to ask and formulates its question using the current task, observations, and relevant memory. It can request clarification when an instruction is ambiguous, ask for guidance when the continuation is uncertain, or seek practical assistance when the environment prevents progress. After receiving a response, the agent decides how to act and uses subsequent observations and execution feedback to assess the outcome. Interaction therefore gives the agent an active means of obtaining information and assistance while remaining connected to movement and the experience generated through execution.

Persistent spatial memory allows these experiences to accumulate across tasks. Place records bind locations to descriptions, observations, historical images, and dialogue. Information acquired through an interaction can update a place description, support a later navigation decision, or help interpret a familiar environment under changed conditions. New observations can, in turn, prompt revisions to existing records.
This continuous accumulation and refinement of spatial knowledge allows the agent’s experience to evolve across successive tasks. By creating, retrieving, updating, and reusing historical memories, the agent can not only acquire new knowledge from current encounters but also leverage evolving experience to guide future decisions.

We evaluate EvoLife on eight navigation benchmarks across four task families: vision-language navigation [3, 27, 26], object navigation [42, 65, 69], interactive instance navigation [21, 48], and continuous multi-task navigation [47, 24]. The main study includes six sets of 100 single-task episodes and two sets of 50 continuous sequences.
With an average of only 1.87 active interactions per episode, our method achieves a success rate (SR) of 100% across four 100-episode sets spanning vision-language navigation and object navigation.
Complete-sequence SR reaches 98% on LHPR-VLN and 94% on GOAT-Bench. In the R2R revisit setting, success weighted by path length (SPL) increases from 82.23% to 93.31% with retained experience. Ablation analyses further examine interaction and experience reuse, while multi-day physical experiments demonstrate exploration, proactive help-seeking, and revisiting remembered places.

Our contributions are threefold:

Hybrid action space.
We propose EvoLife, which enables an embodied agent to select among four navigation modes and adapt subsequent decisions based on execution feedback.

Active interaction.
We integrate proactive interaction into the navigation loop, allowing the agent to autonomously decide when to ask, generate clarification or assistance requests, and incorporate responses into navigation decisions.

Persistent memory.
We develop a dynamic long-term memory mechanism that associates observations, descriptions, and dialogue with spatial locations, enabling explicit memory updates and continuous experience accumulation across tasks.

Together, extensive benchmark evaluations and multi-day physical experiments advance the vision of bringing embodied agents to life through autonomous action, proactive interaction, and accumulated experience that guides future encounters.

title: ScheduleGen: Demonstration Generation via Skill Scheduling for Multi-Arm Imitation Learning
authors: Neel Jawale,Stephan Pleines,Soha Pouya,Yuke Zhu,Ajay Mandlekar,Caelan Garrett
comment: . Project website and videos:this https URL
abstract:
Multi-arm robot platforms, including bimanual and humanoid robots, have the capability to complete tasks
with lower cycle times than single-arm systems, but they are more difficult to safely control due to the presence of multi-arm constraints.
The paradigm of training generalist robot policies from massive datasets is a promising approach to address general-purpose multi-arm manipulation, but the acquisition of large multi-arm manipulation datasets remains a bottleneck.
Automated demonstration generation can alleviate this burden by synthesizing new demonstrations from a handful of source demonstrations, but existing algorithms ignore multi-arm constraints and as a result often induce unsafe and unsuccessful behaviors.
We address this limitation by introducing ScheduleGen, an integrated planning & scheduling algorithm for multi-arm demonstration generation.
We evaluate ScheduleGen on 28 simulation task variants, including seven externally authored RoboDojo tasks and settings inaccessible to prior systems; it achieves 79.6% mean data-generation success and trains policies with 65.5% mean success.
ScheduleGen policies outperform those trained on a state-of-the-art data generation baseline, and achieve 50–80% success across eight real-world variants through zero-shot sim-to-real and real-to-sim-to-real transfer.
Videos and more at: schedulegen.github.io.
introduction:
Generalist robot policies [1, 24] hold the promise of seamlessly solving a wide range of manipulation tasks across diverse robot embodiments. There is substantial interest in applying this paradigm to multi-arm embodiments, especially bimanual and humanoid robots, due to their ability to address a wider range of tasks compared to single-arm embodiments. Such embodiments make it possible to address tasks requiring multi-arm coordination and larger manipulation workspaces, and also have the potential to carry out tasks more efficiently due to simultaneous operation.

However, the predominant method for training generalist robot policies requires large-scale data collection, usually obtained through months of human teleoperation effort [8, 16]. Collecting such datasets is already painful and costly for single-arm embodiments, but these problems are exacerbated in the multi-arm setting, due to the need for special teleoperation interfaces [29, 32, 5], and the resulting increase in operator burden. It can furthermore be difficult to capture desirable multi-arm coordination characteristics due to the limitations of the teleoperation interface [15].

Synthetic data generation in simulation is a compelling method to address this need. Prior methods allow for the generation of large-scale datasets with minimal human effort [21, 6] but fail to address some key challenges of generating data for multi-arm scenarios.
Some works use planning-based approaches [22, 4, 6], but contact-rich tasks remain difficult for such methods, and generating data for diverse multi-arm coordination characteristics remains challenging. DexMimicGen [15] is able to handle different contact-rich tasks, but the coordination behaviors that it can generate are entirely dictated by the human demonstrations used to seed the process, limiting data diversity. Furthermore, the absence of planning means that it cannot handle situations where arm-arm or arm-object collisions are prevalent, such as wide object distributions or cluttered workspaces.

To address these shortcomings, we present ScheduleGen, a multi-arm manipulation data generation method that can encompass diverse multi-arm coordination strategies, long-horizon and contact-rich manipulation, and a wide range of workspaces and embodiments, including challenging object initializations and cluttered scenes. Given a small set of annotated demonstrations, ScheduleGen preserves object-relative contact skills, replans collision-free transitions, and jointly schedules the arms under task and collision constraints.

The contributions of this paper are:

ScheduleGen, a new automated demonstration generation algorithm for multi-arm systems that integrates planning, scheduling, and demonstration adaptation.

ScheduleGen utilizes a novel planning formulation that first plans single-robot behavior to adapt object-centric skill demonstrations and then safely coordinates the robots by framing scheduling as a Mixed Integer Linear Program (MILP) with constraints evaluated using GPU-accelerated collision checking.

We demonstrate ScheduleGen’s applicability to long-horizon contact-rich tasks, challenging resets, cluttered workspaces, and configurable coordination strategies across bimanual, four-arm, and humanoid systems. We evaluate ScheduleGen on 28 task variants across 3 simulation frameworks. On comparable tasks, ScheduleGen-trained policies outperform prior work DexMimicGen [15]. In zero-shot sim-to-real and real-to-sim-to-real evaluation, the learned policies achieve 50–80% success across eight real-world variants.

3. We evaluate ScheduleGen on 28 task variants across 3 simulation frameworks. On comparable tasks, ScheduleGen-trained policies outperform prior work DexMimicGen [15]. title: Decoding Geometry, Not Tokens: Efficient VLMs for Robot Affordance and Trajectory Prediction
authors: Akila Ayanthi,Darshana Priyasad,Tharindu Fernando,Dimity Miller,Sridha Sridharan,Clinton Fookes,Peyman Moghadam
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
comment: IEEE/CVF Winter Conference on Applications of Computer Vision (WACV 2027)
abstract: Predicting where to grasp and how to move is fundamentally a geometry problem. Vision-language models treat it as language generation instead. They tokenize spatial coordinates into text and decode them autoregressively. This mechanism ignores spatial structure and truncates continuous precision. Errors compound across coordinate tokens during decoding. In this paper, we show that compact off-the-shelf VLMs with 0.5–2B parameters already encode rich spatial information in their intermediate hidden states. Autoregressive decoding is the dominant bottleneck for trajectory prediction, while affordance prediction depends additionally on feature depth and decoder architecture. We expose the latent spatial information with a lightweight, geometry-compatible prediction head that attaches to a frozen backbone. It reads features from an intermediate hidden layer, conditions a learned query on the task instruction and refines it via cross-attention over the visual tokens to regress affordance boxes and trajectory waypoints directly as continuous values, without modifying the backbone. We evaluate on ShareRobot-Bench and AGD20K. Our 2B variant reduces trajectory error by over 60% and improves ShareRobot-Bench affordance mAP by 85% relative to the autoregressive baseline. It approaches RoboBrain on trajectory prediction (0.251 vs 0.191 DFD) at 3.8×\times higher throughput. These results demonstrate a favorable accuracy–efficiency trade-off for instruction-conditioned 2D geometric prediction.
introduction:
Vision-language models (VLMs) are powerful tools for general-purpose reasoning, demonstrating strong performance across visual question answering [6, 20], image captioning [21, 38], and scene understanding [10, 31].

However, using VLMs efficiently for robotic manipulation remains challenging, particularly for instruction-conditioned geometric prediction prior to physical execution. Manipulation requires spatially precise outputs describing where to interact with the scene (i.e., affordance prediction) and how to move there (i.e., trajectory prediction), whereas standard VLMs are designed primarily for tokenized language generation. Practical robotic systems also operate under constrained compute budgets [11, 44], while modern VLMs can contain billions of parameters [1, 2]. We therefore ask: can compact VLMs provide accurate geometric predictions for robotic affordance and trajectory prediction, while retaining efficient inference?

Existing approaches typically use VLMs for robotic manipulation by producing tokenized integers that are decoded autoregressively [28, 40, 16]. This effectively treats geometric prediction as a language generation problem. Although this allows direct utilization of pre-trained VLMs and their existing architectures, it introduces a structural mismatch between the prediction mechanism and the task objective: Token-level cross-entropy learning objectives do not penalize geometric distance, finite token vocabularies do not allow for continuous spatial outputs and introduce quantization error, and autoregressive generation compounds errors across coordinate tokens. While larger VLM capacity, particularly when paired with large-scale training on robotics data [16, 9, 13] can yield performance gains for robotics manipulation in spite of this mismatch, this is at the cost of substantially lower inference speeds and higher compute requirements.

In this paper, we investigate how compact, off-the-shelf VLMs can be repurposed for geometric prediction. We replace token-based coordinate generation with a lightweight geometry-compatible decoder that directly regresses affordance boxes and trajectory waypoints from a frozen VLM. Our systematic ablations show that direct continuous prediction is the primary source of improvement for trajectory prediction, while affordance prediction depends more strongly on the interaction between prediction interface, representation depth, and decoder architecture. Layer-wise analysis further reveals that useful spatial information is already present across the VLM representation hierarchy, although its accessibility varies with task and depth. Our contribution is therefore not the DETR architecture itself, but identifying the decoding-interface mismatch and showing how existing geometric representations can be exploited efficiently.

Overall, we make three empirically validated claims:

A geometry-compatible prediction interface substantially improves affordance and trajectory prediction while preserving the efficiency of compact VLMs (Sec. 4.2).

Direct continuous prediction is the primary source of improvement for trajectory prediction, while affordance prediction depends on the interaction between prediction interface, representation depth, and decoder architecture (Sec. 4.3).

Compact VLMs already encode useful spatial information across their representation hierarchy, with its accessibility varying across tasks and model depth (Sec. 4.4).

1. A geometry-compatible prediction interface substantially improves affordance and trajectory prediction while preserving the efficiency of compact VLMs (Sec. 4.2).

2. Direct continuous prediction is the primary source of improvement for trajectory prediction, while affordance prediction depends on the interaction between prediction interface, representation depth, and decoder architecture (Sec. 4.3).

3. Compact VLMs already encode useful spatial information across their representation hierarchy, with its accessibility varying across tasks and model depth (Sec. 4.4).

title: UMI-Live for In-The-Wild Bimanual Robotics Data Collection
authors: Govind Velamoor,Adrian Lin,Sam Jung,Spencer Mateega,Brandon Y. Yang,Amish Sethi
abstract: Universal Manipulation Interface (UMI) devices allow human experts to demonstrate tasks for robot learning without teleoperating physical robots. Using these demonstrations as training data still requires a consistent hardware setup, calibration, and data processing. We present UMI-Live, a full-stack open-source bimanual UMI system for in-the-wild data collection. We design our custom UMI-Live hardware to integrate camera and LiDAR–inertial sensing, onboard compute, and power, without external tracking equipment or calibration within the collection environment. We implement a simple user interface for recording data while an asynchronous pipeline performs parallel SLAM reconstruction and publishes training-ready datasets. We also release software that supports dual-YAM teleoperation and VLA policy training and inference. We validate UMI-Live data quality by fine-tuning π0.5\pi_{0.5} and MolmoAct2, achieving success rates of 10/10 and 8/10, respectively on a bimanual pick-and-place task. Furthermore, we release 40 hours of UMI-Live data across three tasks, and complete hardware designs, software, and reproduction guides at our project website.
introduction:
Much of the recent progress in robot manipulation has come from imitation learning, in which policies learn manipulation behaviors from human demonstrations, increasingly drawn from large and diverse datasets. Diffusion policies [6] and vision-language-action (VLA) models such as RT-2, OpenVLA, π0\pi_{0}, π0.5\pi_{0.5}, and GR00T N1 [4, 14, 3, 2, 18] are all trained this way. More recently, world-action models (WAMs) jointly predict future visual observations and robot actions [29, 13, 24], which allows them to build on large-scale video pretraining. Video alone, however, carries no robot action labels, so WAMs still learn to act from action-labeled demonstrations. These methods allow robots to perform tasks ranging from pick-and-place to dexterous manipulation, including towel and shirt folding [3]. Learning these skills in new environments still depends on expert demonstrations covering the relevant objects and interactions. Collecting high-quality demonstrations across diverse environments therefore continues to be a key challenge in robot learning.

Action-labeled demonstrations are commonly collected by teleoperating physical robots. Large collection efforts such as DROID and ABC-130K show the value of collecting demonstrations across operators, tasks, and environments [12, 1]. Because each collection site must host the robot along with its control, perception, and safety infrastructure, expanding to new environments requires transporting this equipment or maintaining additional robot stations. The Universal Manipulation Interface (UMI) removes this requirement by letting experts demonstrate tasks with handheld grippers instead of robots [7]. UMI showed that policies trained on wrist observations and reconstructed gripper trajectories from in-the-wild demonstrations can perform challenging tasks, including bimanual ones.

Subsequent UMI systems have explored different sensing, tracking, and gripper designs. However, reproducing these systems requires clear instructions for building and calibrating the hardware, together with software for processing the recordings. Some UMI configurations use stationary tracking rigs or backpack-mounted computers, which add equipment to set up or carry [19, 25]. Bulky gripper designs can also make dexterous manipulation of small objects difficult [19]. Furthermore, each recording must be reconstructed and converted into a training-ready dataset. Manually managing these steps becomes tedious, and we believe that operators should be able to start the next demonstration while the software prepares completed recordings for training and physical robot evaluation.

We present UMI-Live, a complete hardware and software system for in-the-wild bimanual collection and robot learning. Each UMI-Live gripper integrates camera and LiDAR–inertial sensing, onboard compute and storage, and removable power. An operator can continue recording data with the press of a single button, while an asynchronous pipeline transfers completed recordings and performs parallel reconstruction, gripper position and jaw opening estimation, validation, and dataset preparation. We also provide software for dual-YAM teleoperation, policy training, and inference. We release approximately 40 hours of demonstrations across three tasks and evaluate policies fine-tuned on mixtures containing mostly UMI demonstrations. The handheld demonstrations are collected at a different location and under different lighting conditions from those used for robot evaluation, while the smaller teleoperation component provides demonstrations from the target robot and scene.

We make the following contributions.

Reproducible bimanual hardware for in-the-wild collection. We present self-contained handheld grippers with integrated sensing, compute, storage, power, and operator controls, together with hardware designs and construction and calibration guides for reproducing the system.

Complete software integration from recording to robot deployment. We provide software for coordinated recording, asynchronous transfer, parallel and batched processing, LeRobot dataset preparation, dual-YAM teleoperation, and policy training and inference. Operators can continue collecting while completed demonstrations are processed.

A public bimanual dataset and physical robot validation. We release approximately 40 hours of demonstrations across three manipulation tasks and evaluate two VLA policies through physical rollouts. Following mixed-data fine-tuning, π0.5\pi_{0.5} succeeds in up to 10/10 trials and MolmoAct2 succeeds in 8/10 trials compared with 0/10 for its released checkpoint.

title: Information-Driven Collaborative Autonomy for Heterogeneous UAV/UGV Teams
authors: Joshua Yuriv Pilipovsky
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Systems and Control (eess.SY); Optimization and Control (math.OC)
abstract:
This paper considers the problem of coordinating a heterogeneous team of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) and unmanned ground vehicles (UGVs), where the ground vehicles must traverse a domain containing an unknown number of potentially hazardous targets.
The UAVs provide aerial sensing using onboard optical cameras, and their trajectories must adapt to both the ground routes and the information collected about the targets.
We formulate the aerial search problem using ergodic control, which distributes sensing effort according to a spatial information density to balance exploration and target localization.
The formulation incorporates dynamic camera field-of-view sensor footprints and probabilistic detection models that depend on vehicle position and attitude.
Angles-only measurements are processed through Bayesian inference and marginalization over data-association hypotheses to obtain a Poisson multi-Bernoulli (PMB) approximation of the target posterior, representing both detected and undetected targets.
This belief directs aerial sensing toward unexplored regions along the ground routes and viewpoints that improve target localization.
Ground planning combines chance-constrained target avoidance, enforced through confidence sets, with a void-probability objective that favors routes unlikely to contain threats.
We solve each team’s optimization problem in a fully decentralized manner using a nested SCvx*–C-ADMM scheme, with outer sequential convex programming iterations and inner distributed consensus optimization, accounting for nonlinearities, nonseparable objectives, and continuous-time inter-agent separation constraints.
A closed-loop scheme updates both fleets’ trajectories as information becomes available and permits ground motion when the remaining route risk falls below a prescribed threshold.
Numerical case studies examine the effects of sensing geometry and target uncertainty, compare decentralized and centralized solvers, and demonstrate full closed-loop collaboration between multiple UAVs and UGVs.
introduction:
Collaborative autonomy deals with the problem of coordinating multiple autonomous vehicles to accomplish a common objective.
In a homogeneous team, the vehicles typically share similar motion and sensing capabilities, allowing coordination to be formulated around a common vehicle and sensor model.
Heterogeneous teams introduce an additional level of coupling, since the capabilities of one vehicle class may be needed for another to complete its task.
For example, unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) can observe regions that are inaccessible to unmanned ground vehicles (UGVs), while the ground vehicles can carry the payloads needed to execute a mission.
This complementary use of aerial and ground platforms has been studied in coordinated exploration and mapping (Dewan et al., 2013), collaborative localization (Butzke et al., 2016), and persistent sensing with mobile recharging (Naveed et al., 2025).

In this work, we consider a UAV/UGV team in which the ground vehicles must traverse a bounded domain containing an unknown number of potentially hazardous targets.
The UAVs provide aerial overwatch, using onboard optical cameras to discover, localize, and track these targets before the UGVs encounter them.
The difficulty is that neither fleet can plan effectively in isolation.
The value of a UAV observation depends on its relevance to the ground routes, while the admissibility of those routes depends on what the UAVs have observed.
Moreover, failing to detect a target does not imply that a region is empty, since the camera has a limited field of view and a non-unit probability of detection.
The planning problem must therefore account for both uncertainty in detected targets and the possibility of targets that have not yet been observed.

A natural approach to the aerial search problem is ergodic control, which seeks trajectories whose time-averaged spatial statistics match a prescribed distribution over the search domain.
Regions assigned greater probability mass receive proportionally more sensing effort, allowing a single objective to express both broad exploration and concentrated information gathering.
The work of Mathew and Mezić (2011) introduced multiscale metrics for measuring deviations from ergodicity and designing multi-agent coverage dynamics.
Subsequent works formulated continuous-time ergodic trajectory optimization (Miller and Murphey, 2013) and used expected information densities to guide active sensing with nonlinear measurement models (Miller et al., 2016).
The commonly used spectral metric compares weighted Fourier coefficients of the trajectory occupation measure with those of the desired spatial distribution.
Alternatively, Hughes et al. (2025) formulate ergodic trajectory optimization using maximum mean discrepancy between kernel mean embeddings in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space, allowing coverage objectives to be specified from samples on more general domains.

For a fleet of UAVs, the ergodic objective depends on the aggregate coverage of all agents and thus couples their trajectories through the team Fourier coefficients.
Abraham and Murphey (2018) address this coupling through consensus on the coverage statistics, obtaining decentralized ergodic control for agents with nonlinear dynamics.
The sensing model introduces a second difficulty: the point occupation measure of a vehicle does not describe the ground area observed by a camera whose footprint changes with altitude and attitude.
Finite sensor footprints and obstacle constraints have been incorporated into ergodic coverage by Ayvali et al. (2017).
Here, we derive the elliptical ground footprint from the position and attitude of the camera and construct a smooth, normalized sensing kernel from this geometry.
Integrating this kernel along a trajectory gives an occupation measure that describes the spatial distribution of camera coverage and depends on both the translational and rotational motion of the UAV.
Its spectral coefficients enter the fleet ergodic objective, so that the trajectories are optimized with respect to the area observed by the cameras.
The same camera geometry also enters a spatially varying detection probability and an angles-only measurement model with pose-dependent covariance.
This connects the coverage model used in trajectory planning with the missed detections and measurement uncertainty accounted for in Bayesian inference.

The search distribution must, in turn, reflect the information collected by the UAVs.
Random finite set (RFS) theory provides a natural Bayesian description of this information, since both the number of targets and their states are uncertain (Mahler, 2007).
The measurements are also a finite set, containing an unknown combination of target detections and clutter, with some targets producing no measurement.
Poisson multi-Bernoulli mixture (PMBM) filtering represents undetected targets by a Poisson point process and detected targets by Bernoulli components conditioned on global data-association hypotheses (García-Fernández et al., 2018).
Marginalizing the association uncertainty provides tractable multi-Bernoulli approximations (Williams, 2015).
These ideas have also been used for multi-agent planning that balances the discovery of new objects with the tracking of existing ones (Nguyen et al., 2020).
Here, we specialize the measurement update to camera-based, angles-only observations with pose-dependent detection and measurement quality, and maintain a Poisson multi-Bernoulli (PMB) approximation of the target posterior.
This distinction between detected and undetected targets is particularly useful for ground planning, since avoiding known tracks alone does not account for threats in regions that have not been sufficiently explored.

Planning around the estimated target positions alone neglects this uncertainty.
Chance-constrained trajectory optimization instead limits the probability of violating a safety requirement (Blackmore et al., 2011), and confidence sets provide a geometric means of accounting for uncertain target locations.
For a multi-object belief, the corresponding question is whether an entire region contains any targets.
The RFS void probability, namely, the probability that a set contains no objects, has been used to impose safety constraints in sensor control (Beard et al., 2017); more recently, Han et al. (2026) have developed belief control barrier functions from a Poisson representation of multi-object uncertainty.
We use the PMB void probability over the corridor swept by a candidate UGV route, which accounts for both the residual undetected-target intensity and the existence and location uncertainty of detected tracks.
Its negative logarithm supplies a route-risk cost, while a separate threshold on the remaining fleet corridor determines when the UGVs may proceed under the current belief.
As sensing reduces uncertainty or reveals a threat, the ground routes and the aerial search distribution are updated accordingly.

Solving the resulting fleet trajectory problems at a centralized ground station requires aggregating all vehicle decision variables and constraints.
A decentralized formulation instead allows each vehicle to solve a local problem and exchange the quantities needed to coordinate with its neighbors.
Consensus alternating direction method of multipliers (C-ADMM) provides an established framework for this purpose when the local problems are convex (Boyd et al., 2011).
For trajectory planning, Rey et al. (2018) combine decentralized ADMM with adaptive linearization of collision constraints for agents with linear dynamics.
For nonlinear model predictive control, Stomberg et al. (2026) develop a closely related nested scheme in which decentralized sequential quadratic programming uses ADMM to solve the coupled quadratic subproblems.
In our setting, nonlinear vehicle dynamics, camera footprints, and collision constraints likewise require an outer approximation method before the fleet problem can be distributed into convex local solves.

To this end, we use successive convexification (SCvx), which replaces the nonlinear optimal control problem by a sequence of convex subproblems, with virtual controls and trust regions to handle infeasible linearizations and control the approximation error (Mao et al., 2016).
The SCvx* extension embeds these iterations in an augmented Lagrangian framework to address feasibility of the original nonlinear problem (Oguri, 2023).
We also adopt the continuous-time constraint formulation of Elango et al. (2024), in which integrated constraint violations are represented by auxiliary dynamics, to account for inter-agent separation between discretization nodes.
Within each SCvx* iteration, local copies and graph flows separate the shared collision constraints and the global ergodic coefficient sum, allowing the convex subproblem to be solved using neighbor-to-neighbor C-ADMM updates.

The main contributions of this work are as follows:

We formulate multi-UAV ergodic trajectory optimization with optical sensor footprints that depend on the full camera pose.
Starting from a conic field of view, we derive the position, orientation, and extent of the ground footprint and construct a smooth footprint kernel that defines the team occupation measure and its Fourier coefficients.
The resulting ergodic objective measures coverage of the ground area observed by the cameras throughout their motion.

We connect Bayesian inference from UAV angles-only measurements to both aerial and ground planning through a shared PMB target belief.
The resulting formulations direct aerial sensing toward unexplored regions along the ground routes and informative views of detected targets.
The same belief accounts for detected and undetected threats in ground planning through confidence-set avoidance and a route-risk cost based on the PMB void probability.

We develop a novel decentralized method for non-convex fleet trajectory optimization problems by combining outer SCvx iterations with inner C-ADMM solves.
The method accommodates nonlinear dynamics, continuous-time inter-agent collision avoidance, and nonseparable team objectives.
For the UAV problem, we additionally introduce a new graph-flow formulation of C-ADMM that replaces the global coefficient-sum constraint with local balance equations and neighbor agreement.
We establish its equivalence at consensus to the centralized convex subproblem, enabling decentralized optimization of the coupled ergodic objective without a central coefficient aggregator.

We construct a closed-loop coordination scheme that updates aerial sensing plans as the target belief evolves, replans ground routes when newly confirmed threats affect them, and authorizes ground motion according to the remaining route risk.
Numerical case studies assess UAV search through spatial coverage and ergodic mismatch, and UGV planning through route risk, control effort, and progress toward the goals.
We also evaluate solver convergence, computational scaling, and solution quality relative to centralized optimization.

The paper is organized as follows.
Sections 2 and 3 introduce the notation and mathematical preliminaries.
Section 4 formulates the UAV sensing and trajectory optimization problem and its decentralized solution.
Section 5 derives the RFS measurement update and PMB posterior approximation.
Section 6 presents the UGV risk-aware trajectory optimization problem.
Section 7 describes the feedback between the two fleets, followed by numerical case studies in Section 8 and concluding remarks in Section 9.

title: Utility-WAM: Correcting Future-Induced Action Changes
authors: Feihong Zhang,Xi Lin,Yulong Shi,Zuxing Lu,Yanghong Mei,Zhaopeng Gu,Tingyu Yuan,Zihao Liang,Yinuo Wang,Zhaowen Li
abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) can condition robot actions on generated visual futures, but this additional context is neither cost-free nor uniformly beneficial. We examine what a predicted future actually changes: the action delta Δ​a\Delta a between the future-conditioned and future-free execution paths of the same model. Under a shared WAM checkpoint, this delta barely shifts average benchmark success (+0.8+0.8 points on LIBERO, −0.8-0.8 on RoboTwin 2.0), while generating visual futures increases inference latency by 1.7–1.9×\times. These aggregate metrics conceal a concentrated failure mode that we term future-induced negative transfer: while predictive deltas benefit long-horizon tasks (+2.4+2.4 points on LIBERO-Long) and remain negligible on most routine manipulations, they induce severe degradation on precision tasks—with Press Stapler and Place Can Basket losing 54.0 and 34.0 points, recurring as top failure modes across independently trained WAM variants. We introduce Utility-WAM for in-place correction of future-conditioned control. Its primary learning component is a residual adapter that repairs future-induced velocity deltas under a frozen shared WAM by aligning them with ground-truth dynamic guidance and penalizing excess error beyond the future-free baseline. The adapter selectively eliminates the majority of severe task drops (reducing losses to 6.0 and 14.0 points) while preserving long-horizon foresight. To eliminate superfluous video computation, a lightweight pre-generation gate reuses counterfactual action outcomes to selectively bypass video generation on 75.5% of RoboTwin queries, cutting latency by 38% while improving average success to 93.3% on RoboTwin 2.0 and 98.9% on LIBERO. On physical bimanual manipulation across three real-world tasks, Utility-WAM succeeds in 53 of 60 trials, compared to 43 for FAST-WAM.
introduction:
World Action Models (WAMs) couple robot control with future visual prediction, but their deployment choices differ. DreamZero (Ye et al., 2026b), Vidar (Feng et al., 2025), and LingBot-VA (Li et al., 2026b) generate visual futures for action prediction; FAST-WAM (Yuan et al., 2026) omits future video at deployment; and AdaWAM (Tang et al., 2026) routes visual reasoning by execution phase. These approaches mainly ask whether or when to spend computation on visual prediction. We instead ask what a predicted future changes: the action delta Δ​a\Delta a it induces relative to a matched future-free path. This delta may help, hurt, or be negligible, while its video-generation cost is always paid.

FAST-WAM already suggests this tension: its separately trained future-generating variants improve LIBERO but degrade RoboTwin 2.0 relative to future-free inference (Yuan et al., 2026). Our controlled comparison under one shared Stage-1 checkpoint reproduces this small sign reversal (Table 2), but the averages hide where the harm lies. Following the standard definition of negative transfer as deterioration caused by an additional information source (Wang et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2023), we call deterioration relative to the future-free path future-induced negative transfer (Section 2) and find it to be a concentrated failure mode rather than a uniform effect.

We therefore treat the action delta Δ​a\Delta a as the central object of study.
Empirically, this delta provides meaningful guidance on long-horizon tasks,
remains negligible on most standard manipulations (26 of 50 RoboTwin tasks change
by at most one point), but induces severe failure on precision tasks such as
Press Stapler and Place Can Basket (hereafter the two severe tasks),
which also recur as the most degraded tasks across FAST-WAM variants (Appendix C.2).
Because pure routing cannot rectify a corrupted action vector once future conditioning is invoked,
the foundational challenge is to repair future-induced action changes while preserving
the predictive foresight where it genuinely helps.

To address this, we introduce Utility-WAM, which decouples test-time imagination into targeted action correction and selective compute allocation. Rather than discarding future generation or distilling it into a current-only policy—which compromises long-horizon performance—Utility-WAM retains the future-conditioned path while attaching a lightweight residual adapter to a frozen shared WAM. The adapter directly repairs harmful action shifts by aligning predicted velocity deltas with beneficial corrections supported by ground-truth futures. Furthermore, because physical imagination remains computationally expensive and unneeded on routine decisions, a pre-generation gate reuses the adapter’s counterfactual action outcomes to selectively bypass video generation entirely when no action benefit is expected.

Our contributions are as follows:

Characterizing Future-Induced Negative Transfer: We formalize test-time imagination via the action delta Δ​a\Delta a relative to a matched future-free reference. We demonstrate that small benchmark-average effects mask severe, reproducible performance collapse on precision tasks across diverse WAM configurations.

Targeted Action Correction: We propose a residual adapter that repairs future-induced velocity deltas via ground-truth future alignment and an excess-error penalty. On RoboTwin 2.0, the adapter recovers 89% and 59% of the losses on the two severe tasks (accounting for 80% of its overall 1.7-point gain) while preserving gains on the remaining 48 tasks and long-horizon suites.

Adaptive Deployment and Physical Validation: By deriving a pre-generation utility gate from paired adapter outcomes, Utility-WAM invokes video prediction on only 24.5% of RoboTwin queries (cutting latency by 38%) and achieves reported averages of 98.9% on LIBERO and 93.3% on RoboTwin 2.0. On real-world bimanual hardware, it improves success from 71.7% to 88.3% (+16.7 pp).

We demonstrate that small benchmark-average effects mask severe, reproducible performance collapse on precision tasks across diverse WAM configurations.

2. Targeted Action Correction: We propose a residual adapter that repairs future-induced velocity deltas via ground-truth future alignment and an excess-error penalty. On RoboTwin 2.0, the adapter recovers 89% and 59% of the losses on the two severe tasks (accounting for 80% of its overall 1.7-point gain) while preserving gains on the remaining 48 tasks and long-horizon suites.

title: SONIC-K1: Porting a Universal Humanoid Motion Tracker to a Small Humanoid on a Single GPU
authors: Kyrylo Kolesnichenko,Jong-Hoon Kim
abstract:
We present SONIC-K1, to our knowledge the first open-weights whole-body motion tracker for the Booster K1 humanoid,
obtained by adapting the SONIC framework to this smaller robot. The policy is trained from scratch on a single shared
GPU with a small fraction of the compute reported for SONIC. In MuJoCo simulation, it tracks nearly all held-out
motion clips and performs well on external benchmarks under SONIC’s success criterion. On the real K1, it tracks
upper-body and slow motions, while stepping and turning remain less reliable, and simulation experiments show a
sensitivity to action latency. These results show broad motion-tracking capability on a modest training budget and
point to quantitative hardware evaluation as the main next step. Code, policy weights and evaluation tools are
publicly available.
introduction:
A general motion tracker is a single policy that takes a reference trajectory and outputs joint commands. Once a robot has
one, motion capture, pose estimation from video and teleoperation can all drive the same
controller. SONIC [1] pushed
this approach to 700 h of motion data and 128 GPUs. The code is open, but it is built for the Unitree G1, and most labs
cannot afford to train it at that scale.

Our lab works with the Booster K1 [2], a 22-DoF humanoid that is noticeably smaller than the G1, and we
wanted a SONIC-style tracker for it on the hardware we have. We kept SONIC’s architecture, PPO settings and rewards,
retargeted 9,991 Bones-SEED clips [3] to the K1 with UMR [4], and trained from scratch for 50,000
iterations on a single H100 that was shared with other users. The resulting model, SONIC-K1, is to our knowledge the
first general motion tracker for the K1 with public weights. It tracks 97.4% of 1,985 held-out clips in MuJoCo [5] under SONIC’s success rule. We have also run it on the real robot. It
works for many motions, though not all of them, and we go through where it fails.

This report makes three contributions:

title: ProLoop: Progress-Aware Closed-Loop Framework via Structured State Relations for Long-Horizon Robotic Task Planning
authors: Runxin Zou,Qingmiao Liang,Jiatao Zhang,Xinyan Lv,Liangyu Qie,Meiyi Bu,Wei Song,Shiqiang Zhu
abstract:
Long-horizon robotic tasks are commonly decomposed into semantic subgoals
to simplify planning. However, subgoal progress in LLM-based planning is
typically inferred implicitly from interaction histories. Inaccurate estimates
can misguide execution and allow local errors to propagate.
To address this, we propose ProLoop, a Progress-Aware Closed-Loop
framework that derives explicit subgoal progress from structured relations between
desired and execution states. A learned State-Relation Monitor assesses these
relations, which are then aggregated into subgoal progress as
ongoing, deviated, or completed. The resulting progress guides execution
adaptation, enabling reliable progress-aware control throughout execution.
Experiments on AgentBoard ALFWorld and a real-world robotic platform show that
ProLoop improves success rate by 12.94% overall and by
15.46% on Hard tasks, while reducing environment interactions
by 32.3%.
introduction:
Recent advances in robot task planning increasingly leverage large language models (LLMs) to
generate coherent multi-step plans
[1, 2].
Despite strong performance on complex tasks, LLM-based planning remains susceptible to hallucinations
and logical inconsistencies
[3, 4].
To manage long-horizon planning complexity, hierarchical methods
decompose tasks into semantic subgoals, allowing each stage to focus on a simpler intermediate objective
[5, 6, 7].
However, during subgoal execution, subgoal progress is still commonly inferred implicitly by the LLM
from accumulated interaction trajectories and multi-source information
[8].
Inaccurate progress estimates can therefore misguide execution, allowing local errors to accumulate
and propagate across subsequent subgoals.

Building on these observations, recent studies
[9, 8]
address this problem by introducing explicit checks at selected checkpoints to
assess the current execution state and then support replanning
(see Fig. 1).
These checks form a feedback loop that reduces reliance on implicit progress inference by the LLM.
However, such checkpoint-based feedback cannot timely respond to changes in subgoal progress,
since reassessment occurs only at the next checkpoint.
During robotic execution, this delay can allow erroneous actions
to alter the environment state,
making recovery costly or even infeasible
[10, 11].
We therefore ask:
How can robots maintain reliable progress awareness throughout subgoal execution
to enable timely closed-loop adaptation?

A useful intuition comes from how people perform everyday tasks. People assess progress by relating
the current state to the intended outcome before deciding what to do next. Following this intuition,
we define robotic subgoal progress by aggregating structured relations between desired subgoal
conditions and the evolving execution state into ongoing, deviated, or completed.

This formulation raises two key challenges.
Constructing comparable desired and execution states.
A semantic subgoal specifies its desired outcome in natural language, whereas the execution state
must be reconstructed from evolving actions, observations, perception, and contextual information.
Making the two states comparable is difficult,
but essential for accurate subgoal progress assessment.
Using progress to guide execution without sacrificing LLM flexibility.
Even with reliable progress assessment, different progress states call for different responses.
Excessive intervention during ongoing execution may disrupt useful LLM reasoning and action generation,
whereas insufficient intervention after deviation may allow errors to persist.
Moreover, completion should be leveraged beyond stage termination, as its associated outcomes must be selectively transferred to support subsequent planning.

To address these challenges, we propose ProLoop, a
Progress-Aware Closed-Loop framework for long-horizon robotic task planning.
For each active subgoal generated by the LLM-Based Subgoal Planner,
Structured State Construction first converts the subgoal’s desired outcome
and evolving execution information into comparable desired and execution states
under a shared task-state schema.
A learned State-Relation Monitor then assesses these condition-level relations
and derives the active subgoal progress as ongoing, deviated, or completed.
The resulting progress drives Progress-Guided Adaptation:
ongoing execution preserves the underlying LLM’s reasoning process,
deviation triggers targeted correction, and completion permits transition to the next subgoal.
Additionally, upon completion, Completion-Gated Memory Update
uses planner-generated retention cues to selectively summarize task-relevant
execution information for subsequent planning.

To assess the effectiveness of ProLoop, we conduct experiments on the AgentBoard
[12] ALFWorld household
planning benchmark, which contains six task categories with easy and hard difficulty levels.
Empirical results demonstrate improved overall performance, with especially substantial gains on
hard tasks. We further validate ProLoop on a physical robot.
Our contributions are threefold:

We propose ProLoop, a unified progress-aware closed-loop framework for robotic task planning
that integrates structured state construction, state-relation monitoring, and progress-guided adaptation.

We define explicit subgoal progress through structured relations between desired and
execution states, distinguishing ongoing, deviated, and completed progress.

We demonstrate that ProLoop improves task success rate and progress rate on ALFWorld while
requiring fewer environment interactions. We further validate its feasibility on a physical robot.
