title: OpenFlyV2: An onboard vision-language-action model for aerial perception and navigation
authors: Junli Liu,Zhongrui You,Chenhui Li,Zhen Li,Yuyang Tian,Qizhen Chen,Delin Qu,Haoming Song,Dong Wang,Xuelong Li,Zhigang Wang,Bin Zhao
abstract:
Human cognition flexibly draws on a shared perceptual foundation to understand environments, attend to referenced entities, reason about spatial relationships, and act. Endowing aerial robots with an analogous functional organization remains challenging, as existing systems are often specialized for individual capabilities, dependent on offboard computation, or unable to sustain closed-loop operation on resource-constrained platforms. We present OpenFlyV2, a unified onboard vision-language-action architecture that uses a shared vision-language representation to support semantic understanding, language-grounded perception, spatial reasoning, and continuous aerial control within a single model. A compact action expert converts the shared multimodal context into short-horizon flight waypoints, while motion-aware temporal memory and action priors reduce the computational cost of closed-loop execution. We construct OpenFlyV2-130K, a simulation-based dataset comprising approximately 70,000 navigation trajectories and 60,000 vision-language instruction–response pairs. OpenFlyV2 generates action chunks, each comprising 12 waypoints, entirely onboard at 10 Hz using an NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX. It transfers zero-shot from simulation to physical quadrotor flight, achieving a 48% navigation success rate across four real-world environments without real-world aerial training data. Extensive results demonstrate that broad vision-language competence and continuous closed-loop flight can coexist within a single model on a resource-constrained aerial platform.
Code will be made publicly available at https://github.com/Ideal-ljl/AeroBrain.
introduction:
Human intelligence is characterized by the ability to flexibly coordinate perception, reasoning, and action according to changing goals [30]. Rather than treating each capability as an isolated task, different functions can be invoked as needed and coordinated within a common cognitive system [41, 46]. This functional flexibility suggests an important goal for embodied intelligence: enabling a single system to support diverse capabilities and engage them according to task demands.

For aerial robots, this functional flexibility requires more than translating language instructions into flight trajectories. Vision-language navigation (VLN) provides a natural setting for connecting linguistic goals with visual observations and action, from instruction-following benchmarks to multilingual and continuous-environment settings [3, 32, 31], but an aerial system may also need to interpret scene semantics, ground language-referenced entities, and reason about spatial relationships according to task demands. Visual question answering (VQA) and embodied referring-expression benchmarks examine complementary aspects of understanding and language grounding [1, 43]. In the aerial domain, datasets and platforms address landmark-directed navigation [33, 57, 20], while recent models investigate hierarchical planning and direct language-conditioned control [16, 59]. A central challenge is therefore to bring these capabilities together in a system that can also sustain closed-loop navigation entirely onboard. Offboard inference can alleviate local computational constraints, but makes the navigation loop dependent on communication availability and latency. Onboard execution instead requires multimodal understanding, temporal context processing, and waypoint generation to operate within limited computational resources while responding to new observations during flight. These demands are compounded by long-range observations, rapid viewpoint changes, partial observability, and three-dimensional motion in aerial environments [38]. Together, these requirements motivate a unified aerial vision-language-action model that combines broad understanding and language-conditioned flight behavior with the computational efficiency needed for onboard closed-loop operation.

Building such a system poses three coupled challenges in capability integration, supervision, and onboard execution. First, a single model must support diverse vision-language capabilities while also connecting the same perceptual and linguistic context to continuous flight behavior when action is required. Second, training requires large-scale aerial supervision that links scene semantics and spatial relationships to language-conditioned flight behavior across changing viewpoints and diverse three-dimensional environments. Third, the model must process visual history and generate continuous flight commands while meeting the latency constraints of onboard hardware. This constraint is especially important for aerial navigation: although an unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) can slow down or hover while waiting for the next prediction, frequent interruptions reduce average flight speed and overall mission efficiency, limiting the UAV’s ability to exploit its inherent agility. These challenges make capability integration, scalable supervision, and computational efficiency inseparable considerations in the design of an onboard aerial vision-language-action system.

Multimodal pretraining and visual instruction tuning provide reusable representations for image understanding and language-conditioned interaction [2, 34, 36]. PaLM-E connects such representations to embodied reasoning [15], while RT-1, RT-2, OpenVLA, and Octo demonstrate increasingly general robot policies trained across tasks [7, 64, 29, 22]. These developments motivate adapting shared vision-language representations to the perception and control demands of aerial robots.

To address these challenges, we developed OpenFlyV2, an onboard vision-language-action model that integrates vision-language understanding and flight control within a single architecture. A shared vision-language backbone processes the current observation, language input, and historical context, and supports semantic understanding, visual grounding, and spatial reasoning. When physical action is required, a compact action expert operates on the same multimodal context to generate short-horizon continuous flight commands. The individual capabilities can be accessed according to task demands.

Temporal context is important for language-conditioned navigation, allowing past observations and executed movements to inform instruction interpretation and subsequent decisions [24, 11]. Previous methods represent this context through topological maps or video histories [12, 61]. However, processing dense visual histories increases computational cost, creating a trade-off between retaining useful context and sustaining efficient onboard inference. To address this trade-off, we introduce Motion-Adaptive Memory (MAM), which compresses flight history into a bounded set of event-level tokens by combining motion segments with their associated visual anchors. This representation retains motion-conditioned visual context while limiting the historical input to the vision-language backbone. For waypoint generation, we exploit the observation that short-horizon UAV trajectories are concentrated around a small set of recurring motion patterns. We encode this structure in a Motion-Structured Prior (MSP), which constructs a context-conditioned source distribution around a selected and adjusted motion prototype for flow-based generation. This motion-informed initialization enables the action expert to generate waypoint sequences with fewer denoising steps, reducing the computational cost of onboard action generation. Together, MAM and MSP reduce the costs of processing visual history and generating waypoint sequences, enabling efficient closed-loop navigation on resource-constrained onboard hardware.

Training OpenFlyV2 required supervision spanning both vision-language understanding and aerial navigation. We therefore constructed a scalable data-generation pipeline drawing on AirSim environments [50], Unreal Engine (UE) scenes, and real-world scenes reconstructed by our team using 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) [28]. This pipeline generated approximately 70,000 language-conditioned navigation trajectories and 60,000 aerial perception-and-reasoning instruction–response pairs across 13 environments. A subset of the navigation trajectories provides supervision for waypoint prediction, whereas the instruction–response pairs cover semantic understanding, visual grounding, and spatial reasoning, enabling these capabilities to be learned jointly with navigation. Language annotations were generated automatically and subsequently verified by human annotators. All task-specific training samples were generated through simulation or rendering, without using real-world flight demonstrations for policy training.

We evaluated OpenFlyV2 across vision-language capabilities, simulated navigation, onboard inference, and physical flight. A single 1-billion-parameter checkpoint achieves performance competitive with or superior to that of general-purpose vision-language models and existing vision-language navigation methods across semantic understanding, visual grounding, spatial reasoning, and language-conditioned navigation. Ablation studies quantify the contributions of MAM and MSP to navigation performance and computational efficiency. On an NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX, OpenFlyV2 generates action chunks at 10 Hz, supporting closed-loop navigation entirely onboard. We further deployed the same checkpoint on a physical quadrotor across four real-world environments, where it achieved a navigation success rate of 48% without real-world training data. These results show that broad aerial vision-language capabilities and closed-loop flight can be integrated within a single model operating on a resource-constrained aerial platform.

title: Cross-Controller Transfer via In-Context Behavior Adaptation
authors: Jonathan Yang,Chelsea Finn,Dorsa Sadigh
abstract: Generalist robot policies increasingly learn from data collected across diverse tasks and embodiments, yet typically assume a single controller for each robot. This assumption limits transfer because different controllers can assign different physical meanings to the same action and may require different strategies to complete a task. We study how to transfer robot data across both embodiments and controllers without allowing conflicting action interpretations to interfere with learning. Our setting spans six controller types as well as variations in controller gains and compliance. We propose a framework that encodes behavioral interaction under a controller through examples of commanded actions and the resulting robot motions. A transformer context encoder summarizes these interactions, allowing a single policy to adapt in context. Across real-world experiments, our method improves average success by 33 percentage points over naive data pooling, achieves 50% success on unseen controller modes and 52% on unseen controller gains, and transfers to tasks with limited controller-specific data. On contact-rich tasks such as USB insertion and surface wiping, behavioral interaction context enables the policy to adapt not only its actions but also its strategy. Our results provide a path toward generalist robot policies that can leverage data collected across diverse action interpretations. For more information, visit https://controller-transfer.github.io.
introduction:
Deploying a policy on a new robot raises a deceptively simple question: how will its actions actually move the robot? Scaling robot datasets has produced increasingly general policies that operate across diverse scenes, tasks, and embodiments. Yet most policies assume that large portions of their data share the same controller per robot and that the controller used at deployment is known a priori. This assumption is limiting: in reality, data contains significant variability across control spaces (e.g., joint vs. Cartesian), control targets (e.g., position vs. velocity), and control parameters (e.g., varying stiffness or gains). For example, data collected through VR teleoperation might encode compliant Cartesian commands, while data collected through puppeteering might encode stiff joint targets, causing the exact same action vector 𝐚\mathbf{a} to have substantially different physical interpretations. Moreover, even on the same embodiment, different tasks may benefit from different controllers. In this paper, we study the question: how can we learn from data collected across this wide range of controller configurations?

Two lines of prior work inform controller transfer, but address different parts of the problem. Cross-embodiment research has shown that data can transfer across robots with different morphologies, sensors, and action spaces, but typically assumes a single, fixed controller for each robot setup. For example, in large-scale multi-robot policies like RT-X[1], a specific robot and its associated controller are uniquely tied to a distinct physical lab or background. Consequently, the policy can easily infer the controller setup purely from the visual scene, sidestepping the challenge of conflicting action interpretations. Meanwhile, research on compliant control shows that controller choice directly impacts task performance[2]. For example, data collected with a controller that feels natural to a human teleoperator may not produce the data most beneficial for policy learning [3]. However, this line of work typically studies how to select or tune a controller for a particular robot and task, rather than how to learn from data collected under many controllers. Our work bridges these two directions: we study how a generalist policy can pool demonstration data with conflicting action interpretations and adapt its behavior when the active controller cannot be inferred from the visual scene.

At first glance, one might treat controller transfer as a dynamics problem: identify the active controller and analytically remap actions to match nominal forces or kinematics. However, dynamics remapping only preserves how an existing motion is realized under new dynamics, not how an expert would choose to act. Consider USB insertion: under a compliant controller, a human demonstrator deliberately presses against the port and searches laterally for alignment. Under a stiff controller, that same contact-seeking trajectory causes the connector to jam, requiring a cautious, alignment-first approach that avoids contact altogether. While system identification or torque matching can predict how a controller will respond to an action, it cannot invent the strategy an expert would adopt. Cross-controller transfer is therefore not a matter of remapping dynamics, but of inferring the appropriate behavioral strategy and determining the actions that will realize that strategy.

Learning controller-dependent strategies from controller parameters and the current observation alone would require dense demonstration coverage across task–controller combinations, which is costly to collect on physical robots. Instead, we condition the policy on interaction trajectories collected under the deployment controller, even when those trajectories come from other tasks. A transformer context encoder inspired by Perceiver [4] compresses these interactions into a fixed set of tokens that condition a single vision-language-action (VLA) policy. By learning across source tasks, the policy can reuse this behavioral interaction context to select an appropriate strategy for a target task with little or no target-task data under that controller. Finally, since physical demonstrations inevitably have limited controller coverage, we also introduce a synthetic data augmentation scheme that analytically remaps actions across controllers; the behavioral context disambiguates the resulting multimodal action modes, enabling safe scaling across diverse controllers.

We make three contributions. First, we formulate cross-controller transfer as behavioral adaptation under conflicting action interpretations, distinguishing the problem from system identification and action remapping. Second, we develop a context-conditioned VLA policy that combines synthetic controller relabeling with a Perceiver encoder, which compresses commanded–achieved interaction histories into fixed-length tokens for adaptation without test-time training. Third, we evaluate the approach across five real-world manipulation tasks, six controller types, and continuous gain variations. When tasks are demonstrated under only a single controller type, our method improves zero-shot success by 2323 percentage points over task-neutral dynamics context, improves success by 3535 percentage points over synthetic relabeling alone on unseen controller modes, and transfers behavioral context across contact-rich tasks while retaining 78%78\% of in-domain performance.

title: CuBot-STT: Simultaneously Transport and Tighten for Lattice-type Modular Reconfiguration Robot
authors: Chongxi Meng,Da Zhao,Yanmin Zhou,Runjie Shen,Zhipeng Wang,Bin He
comment: . Submitted to IEEE/ASME Transactions on Mechatronics
abstract:
Lattice-type modular reconfigurable robots rearrange standardized modules across tasks.
Dedicated transport robots reduce module weight and cost by eliminating module level reconfiguration actuators.
But existing systems use low capacity connections or internal fastening robots that occupy space for functional components.
This paper presents CuBot-STT, which integrates module transport, interface locking, and release in one external robot.
Cubic modules provide structural support and 24​V24\,\mathrm{V} power distribution.
On each face, a gear transmission converts one external input into motion of four helical locking points, preserving internal space.
The robot uses alternating foot support, a gripper for module handling, and a tightening head for interface actuation.
The controller coordinates two-foot support and module locking through continuous constraint transfers.
The planner decomposes relocation costs into an analytical lower bound and a residual learned through expert-guided, goal conditioned Q-learning.
Contact face A∗A^{*} search expands relocation sequences into robot primitives satisfying connectivity, asymmetric manipulation, and foot stance constraints.
Experiments demonstrate normal and tangential interface capacities of 300​N300\,\mathrm{N} and 490​N490\,\mathrm{N}, electrical continuity across six modules, and autonomous reconfiguration of an 11-module lattice.
Planning benchmarks show superior search efficiency over analytical guidance and bidirectional heuristic search, with generalization beyond training lattice sizes without fine-tuning.
introduction:
Modular reconfigurable robots (MRRs) adapt their morphology to different environments and tasks by rearranging standardized units. This capability supports locomotion, manipulation, and structural construction [1]. Conventional self-reconfigurable robots typically integrate locomotion actuators, active docking mechanisms, a power supply, and a controller into each module [2, 3, 4]. As the number of modules or the required structural load increases, this architecture incurs substantial self-weight and hardware cost, reducing load-bearing efficiency. External assembly architectures [5, 6, 7] address these limitations by assigning module rearrangement to dedicated robots that move over a lattice of reversibly connected modules [8]. The structural units can then provide lightweight support and electrical power distribution. Integrating joints, wheeled drives, and sensing units further enables large-scale multifunctional robotic systems [9, 10]. The central challenge is to combine module transport with rigid electromechanical interface locking and release in a single external robot. This must be achieved while preserving internal space for functional components.

Existing material–robot systems exploit the relationship between robot motion and module geometry to reduce dependence on global localization. Their interfaces, however, rarely combine high load capacity, electrical continuity, and robotic release. Passive magnetic connections enable inchworm robots to traverse a lattice and transport units but provide limited load capacity [6]. Electropermanent magnetic docking within a module provides approximately 88.4​N88.4\,\mathrm{N} of normal holding force, with limited shear capacity [11]. Snap fits facilitate robotic insertion of new units [12]. Together with separate connectors or reversible thermal soldering, they also allow PCB lattice units to integrate structural, power, and signal functions [13, 9]. However, snap-fit release still requires manual unfastening [12]. These connection approaches also involve trade-offs in load capacity, repeated assembly and disassembly, and energy consumption relative to mechanical fastening. A comparative study of architectural lattice systems likewise shows that the practical benefits of robotic assembly depend on the connection type and system implementation [14]. An interface that is physically reversible is not necessarily one that a robot can both lock and release. Reconfiguration therefore requires a complete sequence of tool engagement, locking, active release, and module extraction. Functional lattices subject to frequent reconfiguration and substantial loads consequently require rigid electromechanical interfaces that support high-current conduction and robotic locking and release.

Transferring fastening actuators from modules to mobile robots simplifies module design but creates a conflict between fastening access and functional integration. External bipedal inchworm robots can transport and place units on a lattice [15], whereas miniature robots operating inside the lattice actuate captive fasteners [16]. Combining these roles, Gregg et al. [7] demonstrated construction and reconfiguration of a 256-unit structure using internal robots for fastening and external robots for transport. This division of labor is effective for hollow structural trusses. Functional modules, however, may contain drive motors, batteries, control boards, or specialized payloads, leaving insufficient space for an internal robot and its tools. A single external transport robot (TR) must therefore perform module transport, interface locking, and active release while preserving the module interior for functional payloads.

Combining these functions in one robot introduces coupled execution and planning constraints. During each relocation, physical constraints transfer among the two feet, gripper, tightening tool, and module interfaces. The mechanism must provide external access to the interfaces, and the controller must coordinate module positioning, tool engagement, and locking. At the task level, the relocation sequence [5, 17] must preserve structural connectivity while satisfying two-foot stance, asymmetric pickup and placement adjacency, and approach-direction constraints [18, 10]. Weighted single-robot scheduling under connectivity constraints has been shown to be NP-hard [19], making large configuration spaces challenging for conventional heuristic search. Moreover, each discrete relocation must be expanded into a collision-free contact-face path and continuous joint trajectories.

To address these challenges, this paper presents CuBot-STT, an externally driven lattice system comprising cubic module units (CMUs) and a bipedal alternating-support TR (Fig. 1). A hierarchical planning and control framework coordinates reconfiguration and execution. The main contributions are as follows:

Externally operated interface–transport robot co-design: An electromechanical interface and transport robot are co-designed to integrate rigid locking, power transfer, and reversible module unit transport while preserving internal module unit space for functional payloads.

Value-guided hierarchical reconfiguration planning: A hierarchical planner combines expert-guided residual value learning with contact-face motion planning to generate executable relocation sequences under connectivity, asymmetric manipulation, and two-foot support constraints.

Prototype and large-scale validation: A physical prototype and large-scale benchmarks validate interface strength, electrical continuity, autonomous reconfiguration, and planning scalability, demonstrating the feasibility of externally driven assembly of functional modular lattices.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section II introduces the module units, transport robot mechanical design, and operation sequence. Section III describes the hierarchical control architecture, contact-constrained kinematics, expert-guided value-learning configuration search, and contact-face atomic action expansion. Section IV reports interface mechanical and electrical tests, physical transport demonstrations, and planning algorithm evaluations. Section V concludes the paper and discusses future work.

title: RAIBO-Wagon: Real-Time Navigation System for a Legged Robot Towing a Wagon
authors: Insung Yang,Eunchae Kim,Jungwoo Hur,Seunghun Jeon,Donghyuk Choi,Jemin Hwangbo
abstract: Legged robots have demonstrated advanced capabilities across a wide range of real-world tasks, yet much of this progress concerns the robot controlling only itself. Once the robot is coupled to an external object—particularly an underactuated one—the dynamics of the combined assembly become more complex. Towing a wagon is a common practical scenario, where coupled dynamics make reliable navigation challenging. This difficulty is amplified in confined spaces, where collision-free navigation requires finding a narrow set of feasible paths under strict real-time constraints. To address this, we propose a navigation framework that combines Conditional Flow Matching (CFM) with Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) control over a learned Forward Dynamics Model (FDM). The CFM model mitigates the initialization problem of MPPI and accelerates its convergence, while MPPI with the FDM recovers feasible solutions beyond the CFM model’s training distribution by iterative refinement. We integrate the framework into a full-stack navigation system for RAIBO-Wagon, a quadruped towing a custom wagon, and validate it in real-world outdoor experiments on 15 m-long courses through confined spaces, with all sensing and computation performed fully onboard. The system achieves an 85% success rate across 40 trials, towing a total load of up to 40 kg—nearly 100% of RAIBO’s body weight.
introduction:
Quadrupedal robots have demonstrated advanced locomotion capabilities over challenging terrain [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]. Recently, they have been applied to tasks beyond locomotion, such as loco-manipulation [7, 8, 9], whole-body manipulation [10, 11], and pedipulation [12, 13]. Payload transport can further extend their practical utility, but the load a quadruped can carry on its own body is limited. Towing a wagon overcomes this limitation, combining the load capacity of a wheeled carrier with the terrain traversability of legged locomotion.

However, coupling the quadruped and the wagon yields an underactuated system with an enlarged footprint, and the wagon’s wheels further restrict its motion to its heading. These properties make it difficult to maneuver the wagon through constrained environments such as narrow corridors and doorways. To address this issue, prior work has relied on model-based trajectory optimization using explicit quadruped-wagon dynamics modeling, which incurs high computational costs [14]. As a consequence, this approach has been demonstrated only in short-horizon settings or with preplanned trajectories, precluding its application to real-time adaptive execution. These limitations motivate the objective of this work: a navigation framework for a quadruped towing a wagon that generates dynamically feasible commands under real-time constraints in confined spaces.

This objective calls for an approach that is both dynamics-aware and computationally lightweight. One promising direction combines learning-based dynamics modeling with sampling-based optimization. In particular, Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) control has proven effective on wheeled robots [15, 16]: it rolls out candidate trajectories through a learned forward dynamics model (FDM) and optimizes actions without gradient computation. Unlike policies based purely on imitation learning or reinforcement learning (RL), this formulation reasons over the dynamics at inference time, yet avoids the computational cost of full model-based trajectory optimization. Recent work has extended this approach to quadrupedal navigation, demonstrating its effectiveness on legged platforms [17, 18]. In our setting, however, standard warm-starting in MPPI, such as time-shifting the previous action sequence, struggles to find valid trajectories within a real-time budget. Coupling the quadruped and the wagon confines feasible trajectories to a narrow region of the command space, which random perturbations around the shifted sequence rarely reach.

To this end, we introduce a navigation framework in which MPPI is warm-started by a Conditional Flow Matching (CFM) model [19]. CFM models are well suited for real-time warm-starting, as they generate promising sample candidates in only a few integration steps. To train the CFM model on high-quality demonstrations, we construct an offline expert pipeline free from real-time constraints: it first plans a path using a learned collision-risk predictor that evaluates the full quadruped-wagon configuration, and then tracks this path with MPPI. Distilling the resulting commands into the CFM model embeds this costly wagon-aware planning into a single generative model, which supplies MPPI with feasible candidates at runtime. Deployed online, the CFM model and MPPI are complementary: the CFM model mitigates MPPI’s initialization problem by concentrating samples in high-reward regions. In addition, the online MPPI recovers feasible solutions beyond the CFM model’s learned distribution by re-optimizing the samples. Together, these properties enable real-time navigation of a quadruped towing a wagon in confined spaces.

We validate our framework through experiments in both simulation and the real world. In simulation, our CFM-based warm-start outperforms vanilla MPPI, more than doubling the success rate in the most constrained settings. The CFM warm-start also outperforms alternative generative architectures, and the full framework surpasses alternative ways of combining the CFM model with the FDM. For real-world deployment, we use RAIBO2, a quadrupedal robot [6], which pulls a custom wagon that is attached to the robot through a 3-DOF passive joint with an encoder measuring the relative yaw angle. By relying solely on onboard LiDAR for mapping and localization with no external infrastructure, it navigates a 15 m outdoor course as shown in Fig. 1. Across 40 trials on eight different terrains with both static obstacles and pedestrians, it achieves an 85% success rate. Throughout these trials, it tows a total load of up to 40 kg including the wagon, nearly equal to its own body weight.

In summary, the main contributions of this work are as follows:

We present a full-stack quadrupedal wagon-towing system, integrating a wagon-aware locomotion controller with a navigation framework that operates purely on onboard sensing and computation without preplanned trajectories.

We achieve real-time sampling-based navigation under coupled quadruped-wagon dynamics by warm-starting MPPI with an offline-distilled CFM model and rolling out candidates through a learned forward dynamics model.

We demonstrate towing a total load of up to 40 kg, nearly equal to the robot’s own body weight, and validate the navigation system through extensive real-world experiments.

title: Event2Reward: Learning Robotic Rewards from Progress Relations
authors: Junnan Nie,Zitian Fan,Jiachen Zhang,Junyi Lao,Likui Zhang,Chenghao Liu,Xiaoyang Lu,Yunbo Wang,Yixue Zhang,Linbo Zhai,Jiayi Li,Mengzhe Wang,Xichang Wu,Bin Wang,Chang Liu,Tianle Zhang,Songfang Huang
abstract:
Learning task progress from robot demonstrations provides a practical way to
construct dense shaping rewards for robotic reinforcement learning. A common
approach uses normalized demonstration time as progress labels, implicitly
assuming monotonically increasing task progress. During policy exploration,
however, actual task progress can stall or even regress. Such models may
mistake regressions for progress, assigning positive shaping rewards to
actions that cause progress loss. Real suboptimal and failed executions
offer corrective experience, but assigning absolute progress values to their
states is difficult. Our key observation is that stalls, regressions, and
recoveries establish local relative progress relations even when absolute
progress is unknown. We introduce Event2Reward, which uses normalized
temporal labels to anchor the progress scale and these within-trajectory
relations to constrain local changes, combining absolute and relative
progress supervision. Its progress predictions serve as potentials for
reward shaping. We curate an event-annotated dataset from approximately 100K
raw real-robot execution records, covering successful, suboptimal, and
failed executions, without requiring framewise absolute progress labels.
Under the same training budgets, Event2Reward improves average policy
success by 18.16 percentage points over a baseline using only sparse task
rewards across 40 tasks in four LIBERO suites. On real robots, average
success after 30 minutes of wall-clock training reaches 60.0% on three
precise insertion tasks and 90.0% on three object manipulation tasks,
exceeding the sparse-reward baseline under the same budget by 36.7 and 23.3
percentage points, respectively. Ablation studies further show that absolute
progress supervision and relative progress relations are complementary, with
joint supervision yielding better downstream policy learning.
introduction:
Reinforcement learning (RL) enables robots to improve manipulation
skills through trial and error [17].
However, learning on real robots
often requires extensive and costly interaction. Reward shaping
offers a way to accelerate policy learning by improving
credit assignment with dense rewards.
A common approach learns task progress from successful demonstrations,
using normalized elapsed time as a
proxy [14, 30].
This temporal supervision encodes
monotonically increasing task progress. Progress estimates can serve
as potentials for reward shaping, with the shaping term computed from
discounted differences between successive predictions [21].
During policy exploration,
however, robots routinely produce suboptimal and failed executions,
in which progress can stall or even regress. The reward model may
still predict rising progress during such non-ideal behavior,
assigning positive shaping rewards even when progress
stalls or regresses. Instead of
improving credit assignment, such rewards credit the actions
that caused the loss, hindering rather than accelerating policy
improvement.

A natural remedy is to train the reward model directly on
suboptimal and failed executions. However, normalized time
continues to assign increasing progress values during stalls
and regressions, so it cannot provide valid absolute progress
supervision for these executions. A common workaround repeats
or reverses demonstration frames to synthesize stalls and
regressions with labels known by
construction [14, 30], but these
edits cannot introduce failure states absent from the original
demonstrations. Another workaround uses outcome labels or
trajectory-level preferences, which do enable reward learning
from real suboptimal and failed
executions [13, 14]. These
signals describe overall execution quality, whereas progress-based
shaping rewards depend on progress changes between adjacent
observations. Such overall judgments therefore leave the timing
and direction of these changes underdetermined: a failed execution
can retain partial progress, while a successful one can include
regressions and recoveries. How, then, can we obtain local progress
supervision from real executions without assigning an absolute
progress value to every state?

Our key observation is that task events in real executions can
establish local progress relations even when absolute progress
values are unknown. For example, consider a robot moving a cup
from a table onto a shelf. If the cup slips from the gripper and
falls back onto the table, how much progress remains is difficult
to quantify, yet this state clearly holds less task progress than
the state just before the drop. We directly supervise the progress
predictions used for reward shaping with these within-trajectory
progress relations, which encode the direction of change between
temporally anchored states. We combine these relations with
normalized temporal labels from successful demonstrations to
train our reward model, Event2Reward (Figure 1).
The temporal labels anchor the numerical scale of predicted
progress, while the relations constrain the direction of local
progress changes in real suboptimal and failed executions.

We also contribute an event-annotated dataset curated from
approximately 100K raw real-robot execution records across multiple
sources, spanning successful, suboptimal, and failed executions.
The annotations identify where task progress stalls, regresses,
or recovers, and link these events to temporal regions and
reference states. They turn observed execution events into local
progress comparisons beyond terminal outcomes, without requiring
framewise completion percentages. We combine two-pass VLM annotation
with independent human annotation and review
(Appendix A.3).
We will release the structured annotations, data splits, and tools
for constructing progress comparisons, providing a reusable resource
for reward learning and execution analysis.
We train Event2Reward through pretraining and rollout joint training,
then adapt it using a small set of target-task executions.

We evaluate whether Event2Reward improves policy learning on 40
LIBERO [15] tasks and six real-world tasks on Franka
robots. The real-world experiments cover three precise insertion tasks
trained with SERL [16, 17] and three manipulation
tasks trained with DSRL [28] using a
π0\pi_{0} [4] base policy. Across the four LIBERO suites,
Event2Reward improves average policy success by 9.96–13.76 percentage
points over the strongest baseline in each suite under matched
interaction budgets. In real-world experiments with a matched 30-minute
training budget, Event2Reward increases average success from 37.8% to
60.0% on precise insertion tasks and from 81.7% to 90.0% on manipulation
tasks, compared with Robometer, the strongest learned reward baseline
in each setting. Our ablations show that combining
temporal labels with within-trajectory progress relations yields
larger gains in downstream policy learning than combining them
with trajectory-level preferences. Combining temporal and relational
supervision outperforms either alone in downstream policy learning.

title: EgoContact: Evaluating Physical Intelligence with Egocentric Video
authors: Adam Deryło,Alexey Gavryushin,Daniel Cremers,Marc Pollefeys,Xi Wang
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
abstract:
Egocentric video has emerged as one of the most scalable sources of data for learning generalizable manipulation priors. Yet, despite its growing use in pretraining robotic policies, it has been underutilized as a validation tool for physical intelligence, a key component of which is understanding where to make contact with an object to achieve an intended interaction.
We present EgoContact, a large-scale egocentric dataset for evaluating the generalizability and precision of learned manipulation priors through future contact-point prediction. EgoContact contains 22.5K manually verified interaction events, each with a pre-contact observation, semantic intent, and pixel-precise contact locations. We find that current methods often struggle to predict precise interaction contacts and sometimes fail to localize the target object in diverse, in-the-wild scenes, even when allowed multiple predictions. Furthermore, we demonstrate the usefulness of EgoContact’s annotated interactions for robotic manipulation: simply using EgoContact as the memory bank of an existing affordance-transfer policy improves grasp success from 14.2% to 31.2% in simulation and from 16% to 58% on a real robot.
introduction:
Robotic manipulation has advanced rapidly in controlled settings, yet reliable generalization to diverse, in-the-wild scenarios remains elusive. Such generalization calls for more than just passive semantic understanding of objects and available actions, requiring a model capable of translating high-level intent into concrete physical interactions in novel environments. Yet acquiring such physical grounding directly from robot experience is fundamentally difficult to scale, as real-world robot data remains costly and confined to narrow domains.
By contrast, egocentric video offers a compelling source of scalable supervision. Everyday human activity captures a wide range of objects manipulated for diverse purposes in natural environments [1, 2]. Recent work therefore extracts pseudo-labeled interactions from egocentric video to pretrain dexterous and generalizable robotic policies [3, 4, 5]. While pseudo-labeled egocentric data has enabled scaling policy training, it offers no direct way to evaluate the physical knowledge these models actually acquire.

Evaluating such physical intelligence at scale, however, remains a fundamental challenge. Robot rollouts provide direct evidence, but are expensive, difficult to reproduce, and entangle physical understanding with perception, planning, embodiment, and control. Simulation is repeatable, but restricts the diversity of objects, interactions, and physical conditions and introduces a sim-to-real gap. Existing egocentric benchmarks retain real-world diversity, but primarily model the observed human through actions, narrations, objects, or motion [2, 1, 6, 7]. We instead ask whether human behavior can serve as a reproducible probe of the physical knowledge that makes that behavior possible.

Each observed interaction ties a semantic intent to a concrete realization on an object surface. Knowing that a bottle is graspable, for example, does not specify where the fingers should make contact; recognizing that a drawer will be opened does not identify the handle through which opening can be realized. We therefore focus on a specific component of physical intelligence: the ability to ground an intended action in the object locations that physically support it. Predicting these locations before contact isolates an action-relevant decision without prescribing an embodiment-specific hand pose, trajectory, or controller. This leads to our central question: can current models robustly infer precise, action-conditioned contacts before interaction? Unfortunately, existing benchmarks cannot resolve this question, constrained either by limited spatial precision in their annotations [1] or by insufficient scale and diversity [8, 7, 9].

To close this gap, we introduce EgoContact, a large-scale validation benchmark designed to answer this question. EgoContact contains 22.5K interaction events sampled from unconstrained egocentric video. Each event includes a manually verified contact time, pre-contact observations, semantic intent, object localization, and two pixel-precise contact locations representing the thumb and an opposing finger. These annotations formulate future contact-point prediction: given a pre-contact observation and its action context, a model predicts where the subsequent interaction will occur. The task combines the diversity of human video with fixed, manually verified ground truth, enabling repeatable evaluation without requiring robot execution.

Using EgoContact, we evaluate current methods for affordance grounding, affordance transfer, and vision-language reasoning. We find that these methods often struggle to predict precise interaction contacts and sometimes fail to localize the target object, even when allowed multiple predictions. We then examine whether the understanding measured by EgoContact is relevant to robotic manipulation. To investigate this, we replace the memory bank of RAM [10], an existing affordance-transfer policy, with EgoContact while keeping the rest of the policy fixed. This simple change improves grasp success in both simulation and real-world experiments, demonstrating that contact grounding matters for robotic manipulation.

In summary, we make three contributions:

We introduce EgoContact, a validation dataset that uses human interaction as a scalable probe of precise, action-conditioned physical grounding.

We benchmark a wide range of methods, finding that all struggle to predict precise contact points.

We show that contact grounding matters for manipulation: an EgoContact memory bank improves grasp success in simulation and on a real robot.

1. We introduce EgoContact, a validation dataset that uses human interaction as a scalable probe of precise, action-conditioned physical grounding.

2. We benchmark a wide range of methods, finding that all struggle to predict precise contact points.

3. We show that contact grounding matters for manipulation: an EgoContact memory bank improves grasp success in simulation and on a real robot.

abstract: In sampled cascade linear active disturbance rejection control (LADRC) of quadrotors, the extended-state observer typically receives the instantaneous command, although the delayed measurement reflects an earlier, rotor-filtered acceleration. This paper proposes actuator-aware (AA) observer inputs: altitude and attitude observers use limited virtual inputs filtered by an assumed rotor model and aligned with the measurement delay, and horizontal observers use acceleration reconstructed from measured attitude. Fixed gains are selected on the discrete-time model under sensitivity and step-response requirements and stationary covariance ceilings on each channel’s control variance and increment and on the noise-induced inner-loop increment of the full cascade. In paired set-point trials, PID-Budget, AA-Budget and AA-HalfGain reach mean RMSEs of 65.5, 19.2 and 16.9 mm; under a stricter common cascade ceiling, the AA designs reach 29.9 and 26.4 mm versus 72.3 mm for a PID that uses roughly double their rotor-command increment. PX4 software-in-the-loop runs reproduce these results. Behind EKF2, a noise model fitted to the estimation errors predicts the roll/pitch and yaw increments within 5% on held-out and out-of-sample runs and the total rotor-command increment within 14%. Redesigned for this stack under the same sensitivity and response specification and estimator-aware ceilings, AA-Budget-E reduces the set-point RMSE from 59.1 mm (PID-E) to 44.0 mm with a lower rotor-command increment in every paired set-point and lemniscate run (mean S6 rotor-command-increment reductions relative to PID-E: 45% before and 15% after output quantization); AA-HalfGain-E beats PID-E only on the lemniscate. The evidence is simulation-based, and the ceilings are nominal tuning constraints.
introduction:
Quadrotor trajectory control couples disturbance rejection, sensor-noise sensitivity, actuator dynamics, and measurement timing [1]. Active disturbance rejection control (ADRC) estimates a lumped disturbance using an extended-state observer (ESO) and compensates for it in the control law [2, 3]. In a sampled cascade, however, the instantaneous commanded input may differ from the acceleration associated with a delayed measurement: rotor dynamics filter the command, and the measurement refers to an earlier plant state. Increasing observer bandwidth can then amplify both measurement noise and the residual caused by this input inconsistency.

This work addresses that implementation problem with two distinct observer-input paths (Fig. 1). For altitude and attitude, the controller reconstructs normalized inputs from the limited thrust and torque before rotor allocation, propagates them through a first-order actuator model, and aligns the result with the measurement time. For horizontal motion, the observer uses near-hover acceleration reconstructed from measured attitude rather than the instantaneous tilt command. The nominal model uses unity normalized input gain and separates the actual plant lag and delay from the internal observer assumptions. These choices do not reconstruct post-allocation rotor clipping or adapt the assumed delay during variable-latency tests.

Observer-input consistency is combined with fixed-gain activity-aware tuning. The sampled linear covariance model includes the closed attitude loop, its observer, actuator lag, and measurement buffers. It predicts tracking error, noise-induced virtual-control variance, and sample-to-sample increments. During horizontal gain selection, an additional inner-control increment ceiling includes the propagation of position and velocity noise through tilt commands. Sensitivity, overshoot and settling-time requirements constrain the same candidate search; the design target is Ms≤1.98M_{s}\leq 1.98, followed by a separate final audit against Ms≤2M_{s}\leq 2.

Actuator models in observers, delay alignment and half-gain tuning each have precedents; the contribution lies in two design concepts. First, observer-input consistency in a sampled cascade with rotor lag and measurement delay: a commanded observer input adds the structural residual (18) to the disturbance estimate, which raises the sensitivity peak with observer bandwidth at fixed controller bandwidth (Section V-B) and, in the redesigned ablation, allows the response and sensitivity requirements to be met, within the stated finite search, only at the lowest observer/controller ratios, where the best commanded-input design found for ωo/ωc≥1\omega_{o}/\omega_{c}\geq 1 has 9.2 times the mean RMSE of AA-Budget (Section V-D). Second, the outer-to-inner noise path becomes an explicit design constraint: the cascade-level increment σΔ​ui,cas\sigma_{\Delta u_{i},\mathrm{cas}} is predicted on the full cascade model, agrees with nonlinear hover measurements, and enables a comparison under a common strict cascade-increment ceiling (Section V-C); with a shaping filter for the estimation error, the same constraint is computed for estimator-fed loops (Section IV-G).

The main contributions are:

Two actuator-aware observer-input paths for sampled cascade LADRC, delay-aligned actuator-model inputs (altitude/attitude) and measured-attitude inputs (horizontal), with ablations of both input paths.

A fixed-gain covariance design whose channel-level and cascade-level activity ceilings are computed for white or estimator-coloured measurement noise, validated on code-generated controllers inside PX4.

A paired nonlinear simulation assessment including a comparison under a common strict cascade-increment ceiling, noise and latency stress, and fixed-gain rotor-lag mismatch, repeated in PX4 software-in-the-loop with the controllers code-generated into the autopilot, including a redesign for the estimator-fed loop under the same sensitivity and response specification and estimator-aware increment ceilings.

title: Tracking Task Progress Through Errors and Recovery:A Benchmark and Recurrent Distributional Model
authors: Chen Wang,Xinze Niu,Zihao Zhu,Keru Zhou,Yicheng Xu,Shihao Jin,Wenhao Wang,Bowen Jiang,Chang Zhou,Li Liu,Maoqing Yao
abstract:
Operational strategies for long-horizon robotic tasks require reliable evaluation
to determine whether execution is progressing, stalling, regressing, or recovering
from errors. Yet real-world robot datasets that capture error recovery and provide
frame-level error annotations remain scarce. To address this gap, we introduce
and open-source ReSTEP, a dataset of 3,156 episodes across two manipulation tasks
with semantic stage labels and frame-level error annotations. ReSTEP supports
training and benchmarking progress monitors through successful execution,
mistakes, and recovery. Existing progress estimators can struggle to distinguish
visually similar task stages and maintain temporally consistent predictions while
responding to genuine setbacks. We therefore propose REMORA, an online progress
estimator that combines recurrent visual memory, distributional prediction, and
causal peak selection. Memory retains execution history to help resolve visual
ambiguity, while distributional prediction represents alternative progress
hypotheses and causal peak selection tracks a supported hypothesis over time.
Together, these components enable consistent progress tracking that remains
responsive to errors and recovery. Experiments on both ReSTEP tasks demonstrate
that REMORA outperforms the state-of-the-art SARM baseline in progress accuracy
and temporal consistency.
introduction:
Recent advances in vision-language-action (VLA) models have enabled
language-conditioned robots to perform increasingly diverse manipulation tasks
and generalize to unfamiliar objects and
environments [1, 2, 3, 4].
However, strong action-generation capabilities do not by themselves provide
reliable self-assessment: a policy may produce plausible motions while stalling
or undoing earlier work. This limitation becomes especially consequential in long-horizon tasks. A complementary task-progress estimator can provide
monitoring, changes in estimated task progress can be used to construct dense
rewards for reinforcement learning [5, 6] and to reweight
demonstration samples in imitation
learning [7, 8, 9]. Progress feedback could also help address
the substantial data demands of VLA training by identifying stalled or regressing
executions that warrant expert corrections during DAgger-style data
collection [10, 11]. These applications
require progress estimates that remain temporally consistent under partial
observability while remaining sensitive to genuine setbacks.

Existing work on visual progress and reward estimation broadly follows two scoring designs. One derives scores from VLM embedding similarities [12, 13] or judgments generated by pretrained or fine-tuned VLMs [7, 5, 6, 14, 15, 16]. The other trains dedicated prediction heads or networks for progress, relative progress, or task completion, including heads built on pretrained VLM or VLA representations [17, 8, 18, 9, 19]. These approaches demonstrate the utility of visual progress signals, with several reporting improvements in downstream robot learning. Nevertheless, limitations in spatial and temporal reasoning can make VLM-derived scores unreliable for subtle changes in task state [13, 14]. Coarse scoring scales can obscure small improvements [15, 16], while time-derived supervision can conflate elapsed time with actual task advancement [18, 8, 16, 14]. Moreover, some methods rely on full-trajectory context or retrospective progress reconstruction, limiting their applicability to online progress monitoring [7, 9].

Beyond these challenges, progress estimation requires modeling temporal dependencies in both visual observations and progress predictions. On the input side, successive images reveal motion, state changes, and event order that may be ambiguous or unobservable in an isolated frame. Integrating this information helps distinguish visually similar observations associated with different task stages [17]. However, short or sparsely sampled observation histories can omit earlier events needed to interpret the current state, while processing more frames increases computational cost [8, 19]. On the output side, successive progress estimates should describe a coherent task evolution. Many methods ultimately produce a scalar estimate through direct regression or by taking the expectation of a predicted distribution [18, 8, 19]. When the available visual history leaves multiple task stages plausible, the conditional progress distribution can remain multimodal. Squared-error regression or an expectation-based readout can then average distinct hypotheses into an intermediate value that corresponds to neither stage.

Learning from unsuccessful executions presents a further challenge because dataset with error frame annotation are difficult to obtain. Methods such as ReWiND and SARM therefore augment demonstrations with temporally reversed segments to provide supervision for decreasing progress [18, 8]. Although useful, time reversal can produce physically implausible sequences and does not necessarily capture the dynamics of real mistakes and subsequent recovery [18]. Restricting supervision to successful demonstrations and synthetic reversals can consequently leave informative failure and recovery behavior underused.

We introduce REMORA, a framework for online task-progress estimation that
combines temporal visual context with distributional prediction and causal peak
selection (Fig. 2). We develop and study this framework on two
real-world logistics tasks using demonstrations that include successful
executions, mistakes, and recoveries. Comparison with SARM on parcel handling shows
that REMORA achieves lower mean absolute error and higher Spearman rank
correlation, indicating more accurate progress estimates and better preservation
of the relative progress ordering across observations.

Our contributions are threefold:

ReSTEP: An error-annotated dataset for progress estimation.
We release more than 15 hours of robot demonstrations across 3,156 episodes
covering parcel handling and medicine-bottle scanning and storage. Semantic
stage annotations and frame-level error labels capture successful executions,
mistakes, and recoveries, supporting both model training and benchmarking.

A recurrent distributional progress model.
We augment a pretrained VLA backbone with categorical value heads and a
recurrent visual memory to represent ambiguous progress states in their
temporal context. Stage and error annotations supervise both advancing and
decreasing progress, retaining observations of mistakes and recoveries
during training.

Causal peak selection for temporal consistency.
We introduce a decoder that selects a supported peak from the current progress
distribution based on the previous estimate. This rule favors continuity
across successive predictions while allowing decreases supported by the
distribution, providing a causal readout of potentially multimodal progress.

title: CAPTURER: A Dexterous Aerial Manipulator for Dynamic and Precise Grasping across Diverse Environments
authors: Meng Wang,Jindou Jia,Sicheng Zhou,Zeshuai Chen,Kexin Guo,Xiang Yu,Lei Guo
abstract: As a representative form of embodied robotic interaction, aerial grasping requires close coordination between the aerial platform and manipulator. Most existing systems perform aerial grasping with static or slowly moving targets under fixed scenarios. Dynamic and precise grasping across different conditions introduces additional challenges, including target motion, localization drift, dynamic coupling, and external disturbances. In this work, we present CAPTURER, a dexterous aerial manipulator for centimeter-level grasping across diverse environments. To achieve the challenging goal, we first develop an onboard perception system for state estimation and target detection. Drift correction and global pose transformation are introduced to improve target localization during flight. A cooperative motion planner is proposed to coordinate the mobility of the aerial platform with the dexterity of the manipulator according to the relative target state. To maintain grasping accuracy under disturbances, we design a disturbance-rejection controller to compensate for dynamic coupling, model uncertainty, and external disturbances. The capability of CAPTURER is validated through indoor and outdoor experiments with both static and moving targets. The results demonstrate that CAPTURER achieves centimeter-level grasping accuracy for a marker pen measuring only 1.5 cm in diameter at flight speeds exceeding 1.5 m/s.
introduction:
Aerial robots have evolved from laboratory prototypes into increasingly capable platforms for autonomous operation in complex environments (Aucone and Mintchev, 2025). Their high mobility has enabled applications such as autonomous drone racing (Song et al., 2023), navigation through dense forests (Zhou et al., 2022), and resilient flight under adverse weather conditions (O’Connell et al., 2022). Despite these advances, most aerial robots still primarily serve as sensing and observation platforms. Performing physical interaction remains considerably more challenging, particularly when the task requires both fast motion and precise contact with the external environment.

Aerial manipulators combine the large-range mobility of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) with the local operability of manipulators, enabling physical interactions in difficult-to-access and hazardous environments (Kaya et al., 2025; Khamseh et al., 2018; Ollero et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2022; Cao et al., 2025b). Early studies have demonstrated aerial interaction using grippers mounted on multirotor platforms (Lindsey et al., 2011; Thomas et al., 2014). Soft and compliant grippers are subsequently developed to enlarge the effective contact region and increase grasp tolerance for different target geometries (Appius et al., 2022; Ubellacker et al., 2024). Specialized systems have also achieved millimeter-level accuracy in aerial insertion tasks (Wang et al., 2024b). In addition, coordinated multi-robot systems have demonstrated aerial construction and manipulation over extended workspaces (Zhang et al., 2022).

However, most existing aerial systems operate under quasi-static or near-hovering conditions. Moreover, the grasping motion is often predefined or generated offline. The operating mode does not fully exploit the mobility and agility of the aerial platform during physical interaction. Many systems also rely on external localization infrastructure to maintain accurate positioning. Vision-based approaches reduce this dependence, but they commonly assume that the target is always visible within the camera’s field-of-view (FoV) during operation (Seo et al., 2017; Lai et al., 2022b; Hu et al., 2023). These assumptions are restrictive when the target moves or when the robot operates across different environments.

Other approaches use deformable or morphing aerial platforms for grasping and interaction (Zhao et al., 2018; Shi et al., 2020; Xu et al., 2024). These systems exploit the vehicle body itself as part of the manipulation mechanism. However, the achievable interaction workspace and local adjustment capability are constrained by the airframe structure. Specialized mechanisms, such as permanent-magnet grippers (Luo et al., 2023) and delta-type manipulators (Cao et al., 2024), have also demonstrated dynamic grasping. In Ubellacker et al. (2024), dynamic grasping of a large box is achieved using onboard cameras, while a soft gripper is employed to enlarge the effective contact area and improve grasp tolerance. However, many of these studies rely on task-specific mechanisms, relatively large targets, or predefined motion trajectories. The ability to adapt online to target motion, localization uncertainty, dynamic coupling, and environmental disturbances remains limited.

Dynamic and precise aerial grasping therefore requires more than increasing the speed of an existing aerial manipulation system. During a grasping maneuver, the target state may change continuously, while the aerial platform and manipulator move simultaneously. The robot must estimate the target state onboard, determine how motion should be distributed between the platform and manipulator, and accurately execute the resulting motion under internal and external disturbances. These requirements are strongly coupled, which become more demanding as the interaction speed increases.

In this study, our objective is to enable an aerial manipulator to autonomously perform precise grasping of static and moving targets across different operating environments. Autonomous operation is achieved without relying on external localization. The aerial platform provides large-range mobility for target approach, while the manipulator supplies local dexterity for precise adjustment. Meanwhile, the control framework maintains grasping accuracy in the presence of composite disturbances.

Dynamic and precise aerial grasping introduces three closely coupled technical problems.

The first problem is perception. Precise grasping requires consistent estimation of both the aerial manipulator state and the target state. Unlike conventional aerial navigation, the manipulator moves relative to the floating base during operation. This motion changes the system configuration and induces additional disturbances to the aerial platform. Meanwhile, onboard localization is subject to accumulated drift. The problem becomes more difficult for a moving target because the perception system must continuously update its position while the robot itself is moving (Khamseh et al., 2018; Ollero et al., 2022). When the target leaves the FoV, measurement updates become unavailable and prediction uncertainty increases. Moreover, dynamic grasping requires a consistent target representation that remains usable by the motion planner during platform and manipulator motion.

The second problem is planning. The aerial platform provides large-range mobility, whereas the manipulator provides more precise local adjustment (Ollero et al., 2022; Lee et al., 2026). Different combinations of platform and manipulator motions can satisfy the same end-effector requirement, while resulting in different remaining workspaces for subsequent adjustment. The cooperative planner must allocate motion according to their respective characteristics and the relative target state. Moreover, the attitude information of the aerial platform should be incorporated into the planning process because it directly affects the end-effector state.

The third problem is control. The manipulator motion causes coupling effects that act on both the moving platform and manipulator dynamics (Shabana, 2020; Ollero et al., 2022). Moreover, the coupling effects become more pronounced during dynamic operation and can significantly degrade tracking accuracy. In addition, model uncertainty and external disturbances would deteriorate the flight performance of the aerial manipulator, ultimately reducing grasping accuracy (Zhang et al., 2022; Cao et al., 2025b).

Notice that the aforementioned problems are not independent. Perception provides the relative target state required for motion coordination. The cooperative planner generates the desired trajectory for both the aerial platform and manipulator. The resulting manipulator motion subsequently changes the coupling disturbance acting on the aerial platform and affects grasping accuracy. Each component must be specifically addressed to meet the requirements of dynamic and precise grasping, while the interactions must be considered at the system level.

To address these coupled issues, we present CAPTURER, an autonomous aerial manipulator for precise grasping across diverse environments. CAPTURER is composed of a coaxial quadrotor and a rigid-link serial manipulator. Each component is specifically developed to address the requirements of dynamic and precise aerial grasping. Fig. 1 summarizes the framework and the information exchanged between its components.

We first develop an onboard perception framework for dynamic aerial grasping. The framework combines state estimation and onboard target detection. A drift correction mechanism is developed to reduce accumulated localization error. Moreover, a global pose transformation further transfers target observations into a reference frame. This allows target information acquired from different robot states to be used consistently during the grasping process. With respect to moving targets, the target state is continuously updated to provide the relative information required by the cooperative planner. An active yaw search strategy is further introduced to detect targets outside the initial camera’s FoV.

Next, we propose an optimization-based cooperative motion planning method for the aerial platform and manipulator. The planner jointly optimizes their motions according to dynamic characteristics and the relative target motion. In comparison with the strict constraint that the flight attitude is fixed (Luo et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2023), the platform attitude is explicitly included in the optimization to improve coordination during grasping. By optimizing both motions within a unified formulation, the planner coordinates the mobility of the quadrotor with the local dexterity of the serial manipulator. The presented algorithm can continuously adapt motion allocation as the target state changes.

Finally, we present a robust anti-disturbance controller for dynamic manipulation. A full-state dynamic model is exploited to construct the coupling forces and torques induced by manipulator motion. A robust differentiator is used to provide the high-order signals required by the coupling model. The estimated coupling effects are compensated through a feedforward channel. Moreover, two observers are developed to compensate for residuals arising from model uncertainty and external disturbances. This design enables accurate tracking of the references generated by the cooperative planner during dynamic grasping.

The proposed scheme is verified through extensive experiments. We first assess the onboard perception system through state estimation and target detection experiments. The presented robust controller is compared with baseline methods under composite disturbances. Finally, the ability of CAPTURER is validated through real aerial grasping experiments with stationary and moving targets under both indoor and outdoor conditions. CAPTURER achieves centimeter-level grasping accuracy and successfully grasps a marker pen only 1.5 cm in diameter at speeds exceeding 1.5 m/s.

To recap, our contributions are summarized as follows:

We develop CAPTURER, a dexterous aerial manipulation system for dynamic and precise grasping. An onboard perception framework is developed to integrate state estimation, target detection, drift correction, global pose transformation, and active target search. The resulting perception pipeline provides consistent robot and target states during flight and reduces the dependence on external localization and initial target visibility (Ubellacker et al., 2024; Zhong et al., 2020).

We develop CAPTURER, a dexterous aerial manipulation system for dynamic and precise grasping. An onboard perception framework is developed to integrate state estimation, target detection, drift correction, global pose transformation, and active target search. The resulting perception pipeline provides consistent robot and target states during flight and reduces the dependence on external localization and initial target visibility (Ubellacker et al., 2024; Zhong et al., 2020).

An optimization-based cooperative motion planning method is proposed to jointly optimize the states of the aerial platform and the manipulator according to their dynamic characteristics and the relative target motion. The platform attitude information is explicitly incorporated into the end-effector prediction model, allowing large-range aerial mobility and local manipulator dexterity to be coordinated. Unlike pre-programmed motions (Appius et al., 2022; Chen et al., 2022) and one-shot offline solutions (Thomas et al., 2014; Ubellacker et al., 2024; Luo et al., 2023), the proposed planner supports online replanning at a rate exceeding 25 Hz.

Unlike existing methods that compensate only first-order coupling terms (Cao et al., 2024; Kim et al., 2018), a full-state disturbance rejection controller is proposed for dynamic aerial manipulation. The nonlinear coupling effects are compensated through a feedforward channel, while a robust differentiator is employed to estimate the required high-order signals. Moreover, residual observers are incorporated to estimate the remaining disturbances caused by model mismatch and external disturbances, thereby improving tracking accuracy during manipulation.

abstract: Collecting naturalistic human manipulation demonstrations with accurate contact force and hand pose is essential for robot dexterous manipulation policy and foundational world model learning—yet no existing wearable platform provides both calibrated fingertip force sensing and occlusion-resilient hand tracking in a form factor that preserves natural manipulation behavior. We present Tactus, a textile-integrated sensing glove that co-optimizes three design pillars: (1) a thin, conformal 3D-knit form factor (1.5 mm1.5\text{\,}\mathrm{mm} fingertip stackup) designed to minimize interference with natural manipulation, (2) strategically placed capacitive tactile sensors at manipulation-relevant regions informed by empirical contact studies, and (3) IMU-fused pose tracking that maintains accuracy through the hand-object occlusions where manipulation data is most valuable. Tactus includes a documented calibration pipeline for cross-glove consistency and per-session calibration for subject-dependent correction. To enable objective comparison, we introduce standardized benchmarking protocols for tactile force regression and hand pose estimation, and apply them to Tactus and two commercially available tactile gloves — to our knowledge the first quantitative cross-platform evaluation of this kind. Tactus resolves a minimum detectable force of 0.59 N0.59\text{\,}\mathrm{N} at 95% confidence, 1.6–2.7× lower than the commercial baselines, and with 0.87 cross-participant consistency, while our pose tracking sustains 11.0 mm11.0\text{\,}\mathrm{mm} fingertip keypoint relative error during manipulation, when occlusion is heaviest. We show that these combined signals support object property estimation, slip detection, and representative recording of hand-object interaction — yielding demonstration data with the fidelity required for contact-aware manipulation policies and world models.
introduction:
Learning dexterous manipulation from human demonstrations is a promising path toward general-purpose robot skills, and the quality of that demonstration data has been shown to directly impact downstream policy performance [1]. There are three major options for capturing human manipulation sequences: egocentric-Computer-Vision (ego-CV) only; CV with an exoskeleton-based solution; and CV with a sensing-glove-based solution.

The ego-CV-only approach is the least intrusive of the three and obtains the most natural manipulation data, but CV cannot recover high-fidelity hand pose under occlusion, which becomes more severe exactly when hand-object interaction happens. Paliwal et al. reported that in ego-CV recorded manipulation tasks, << 10% of the raw data eventually are usable for training purposes [2]. Besides limitation in measuring hand pose, vision-based methods cannot directly measure the contact forces that are important for fine dexterity tasks. Exoskeleton-based systems like MILE [3] provide high-fidelity kinesthetic data but constrain finger motion and alter grasp strategies; recent systems such as WHED [4] and DexEXO [5] achieved some progress, but still made great trade-off of naturalism with data quality. Sensing gloves promise both naturalism and direct force measurement, yet as we detail in the following section, no existing platform jointly provides calibrated force sensing, occlusion-resilient pose tracking, and a form factor validated to preserve natural grasp behavior.

We present Tactus, a textile-integrated tactile and pose sensing glove designed from the ground up for naturalistic manipulation data collection, as shown in Fig. 1. It is a 3D-knit textile glove, built in left- and right-hand variants, carrying 47 capacitive textile force sensing locations spanning fingertip to palm and 16 6-DoF IMUs; Sec. III-C details the sensing and electronics. Besides the glove design, our major contributions are the following:

Minimal interference with natural grasp behavior, validated with human manipulation studies (Sec V-A). A thin, conformal 3D-knit base glove (1.5 mm1.5\text{\,}\mathrm{mm} fingertip stackup) with low-profile, stretchable embedded sensors minimizes encumbrance while preserving the fidelity of natural manipulation.

Minimal interference with natural grasp behavior, validated with human manipulation studies (Sec V-A). A thin, conformal 3D-knit base glove (1.5 mm1.5\text{\,}\mathrm{mm} fingertip stackup) with low-profile, stretchable embedded sensors minimizes encumbrance while preserving the fidelity of natural manipulation.

Data-driven tactile sensor placement (Sec. III-A) and efficient calibrated force sensing at every contact location (Sec. IV-A). Placement is optimized by ink studies and a sensor-compliance threshold that maintains 65% fingertip coverage across a broad anthropometric range in a single glove size. Calibrated forces are recovered in two stages: a scalable pneumatic-pressure factory calibration and a per-session online procedure.

Standardized benchmarks. We introduce Protocol-Tactile (normal contact force Sec. V-B) and Protocol-Pose (hand pose tracking Sec. V-C) and apply to both Tactus and commercially available gloves, yielding the first reproducible quantitative cross-platform comparison.

Application validation (Sec. VI). Tactus tactile and pose data enables force-dependent robotic perception and manipulation tasks—object material classification, slip detection, and multi-sensory hand object manipulation.
