title: Controlling Continuum Robot Shape in Enclosed Space with Embedded Sensing using IMU and Actuator Feedback
authors: Jiahe Wang,Sultan Haidar Ali,Eric Weissman,Jiefeng Sun
abstract:
Controlling continuum robots’ shape to operate in confined, enclosed environments is challenging, since it cannot rely on external observation. Existing embedded shape sensing methods, although they can provide shape reconstruction, are insufficient to enable real-time shape control due to limitations in reconstruction accuracy, computational speed, and compatibility with shape-state representation.
In this work, we present an embedded shape-sensing framework that uses readily available IMU and actuator feedback to reconstruct the continuum-robot shape with a neural network, providing accurate shape feedback at 400​Hz400~\mathrm{Hz} for physical closed-loop control. We systematically investigate four key reconstruction design choices: shape-state representation, network architecture, training objective, and sensing inputs, through more than 5,0005{,}000 trained models on one- and three-segment continuum robots. The selected framework achieves global shape errors of 0.9%​L0.9\%L and 1.7%​L1.7\%L (of the robot length) for the one- and three-segment systems, respectively. In closed-loop control, one-segment tip tracking achieves a 6.1%​L6.1\%L error and three-segment shape control achieves a 2.3%​L2.3\%L global shape error, whereas IMU–PCC reconstruction using the same uncompensated measurements fails. Enclosed-space experiments further demonstrate operation without external observation. These results provide a practical framework for translating readily available embedded sensing into high-rate feedback for continuum robot closed-loop control.
introduction:
Continuum robots achieve compliant motion through distributed deformation, adapting their bodies to unstructured environments and operating in enclosed spaces [1]. However, existing continuum-robot operation in enclosed or visually occluded environments remains challenging [2, 3]. The major limitation is that the shape state of continuum robots’ feedback often relies on external observation, such as motion capture, which requires an instrumented workspace and continuous line of sight [4]. Embedded shape sensing, reconstructing the shape state from measurements available on the robot itself, is the most promising option.

Existing embedded shape sensing has primarily focused on improving reconstruction accuracy, with comparatively limited consideration of downstream closed-loop control, as summarized in Tab. I. First, achieving low reconstruction error and a high update rate for real-time closed-loop control is challenging. Distributed IMUs [5, 6, 7], magnetic sensors [8], and strain sensors [9, 10, 11] provide local orientation or deformation measurements that can be combined with continuum kinematics to recover the robot shape. Accurate reconstruction requires sensor-specific calibration and processing, while piecewise-constant-curvature (PCC) assumptions may not hold under nonuniform bending. Optical-fiber-based sensing can provide accurate distributed deformation measurements, but often requires dedicated interrogation hardware, complex fabrication, and limited sensing lengths [12, 13, 14]. Actuator feedback, such as motor encoder and torque measurements, provides a more readily available sensing source [15, 16], but only indirectly reflects the robot configuration. Recovering the shape from these measurements through physical models introduces additional iterative estimation and computational requirements [17].

Second, even when relatively low reconstruction error and a high update rate can be achieved, a gap remains between the reconstructed state and the closed-loop control state. Learning-based approaches directly map embedded measurements to a selected representation of the reconstructed state, for example, by combining actuator feedback with machine learning [18, 19, 20] or by combining optical sensing with deep learning [13, 21]. However, the choice of reconstructed shape state affects both the accuracy of the estimation and the geometric information available for control. Including orientation retains richer geometric information but introduces higher-dimensional and constrained variables that are more difficult to reconstruct accurately. Simpler position-based representations may omit segment-local deformation information relevant to full-body shape control [22]. Beyond the shape-state representation, network architecture, training objective, and sensing inputs can further affect reconstruction accuracy, temporal consistency, and computational cost. The key challenge is therefore not only to reconstruct the continuum-robot shape state accurately and efficiently, but to systematically design a control-oriented reconstruction framework.

Consequently, as summarized in Tab. I, a gap remains between embedded shape reconstruction and its systematic validation on closed-loop control for continuum robots. This challenge arises because these requirements (real-time computation, reconstruction accuracy, and representation compatibility) depend on multiple reconstruction design choices, including shape-state representation, sensing inputs, network architecture, and training objective. For example, increasing model complexity or temporal history may improve reconstruction accuracy but increase computation and reduce the achievable feedback rate. Despite these considerations, existing studies have primarily evaluated embedded shape sensing through reconstruction metrics, with comparatively limited task-level control validation [18, 20, 25, 23].

In this work, we develop a practical embedded shape-sensing and control framework that enables accurate and robust shape control of a continuum robot in an enclosed environment.
The framework reconstructs the robot shape from readily available IMU, motor encoder, and torque measurements without requiring a dedicated sensor-specific filtering or drift-compensation pipeline, simplifying the implementation of embedded shape sensing. We then systematically investigate four key reconstruction design choices: shape-state representation, network architecture, training objective, and sensing inputs for neural network (NN) training. The resulting framework operates at 400​Hz400~\mathrm{Hz}, with the reconstructed shape state used directly for Koopman identification and model predictive control (MPC) [26, 22, 27]. The framework is experimentally validated through one-segment tip tracking, three-segment shape control, and enclosed-space operation without external observation. The main contributions are as follows:

An embedded shape sensing and control framework for continuum-robot closed-loop control using readily available IMUs and actuator feedback, without dedicated sensor-specific filtering or drift compensation;

A systematic investigation of the key factors influencing shape reconstruction performance, including network architecture, shape-state representation, training objective, and sensing inputs, through more than 5,0005{,}000 trained models on one- and three-segment continuum robots;

Task-level control validation beyond modeling accuracy, demonstrating that the reconstructed state can serve directly as high-rate feedback for physical closed-loop control, including one-segment tip tracking, three-segment shape control, and enclosed-space operation without external observation.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Sec. II formulates the embedded shape-sensing and control framework. Sec. III presents the physical implementation, model training, and reconstruction design study. Sec. IV evaluates shape reconstruction and closed-loop control, including enclosed-space demonstrations. Sec. V concludes the paper.

title: Robotic Data Inoculation
authors: Qiyang Li,Zhiyuan Zhou,Charles Xu,Sergey Levine
abstract:
Modern robot learning systems feed on high-quality demonstration data, and their performance hinges on coverage. Without good coverage, small errors compound and the policy can quickly go into out-of-distribution states from which it cannot recover.
Yet there is no principled way of collecting high-coverage data, and data collection often relies on heuristic instructions to human operators. Purely online reinforcement learning (RL) explores at the cost of safety and sample efficiency, while DAgger-style interventions require the policy to fail by chance before a human can correct it.
In this paper, we ask instead whether we can modify how the robot behaves during data collection to collect more useful data.
We propose Data Inoculation (DI), a shared-control framework in which a human provide closed-loop teleoperation commands while a residual policy perturbs these commands. The residual policy is trained online, on the growing dataset, with the same reward-maximizing objective later used for policy extraction, so its perturbations steer data collection toward the deviations a policy trained on the data would make.
These perturbations expose the robot to a wider range of states, while the human’s continuous corrections provide recovery demonstrations, “inoculating” the dataset against the learner’s future mistakes while the human remains in control. On three challenging real-world robotic tasks, DI consistently improves or matches the success rate of policies trained with both behavioral cloning and offline RL, showing DI as an effective data collection strategy for improving downstream policy performance.
introduction:
Modern robot learning systems have shown promise in acquiring complex manipulation skills (e.g., shirt-folding [7], tea/juice-making [28]) from demonstration data.
While there has been extensive recent research on the design of these models, the quality of the data the models are trained on is every bit as critical. Good data should have high coverage: it should contain a wide range of states to maximize the chance that the policy generalizes to the states that it actually visits at test time. In practice, coverage is determined by the scenes where data is collected and the behaviors of the teleoperators, which must strike a balance between consistency and variety. Improving data quality and coverage through task design and operator instruction is largely heuristic and ad hoc. Can we instead directly modify how the robot behaves during data collection to provide for more useful data?

Existing solutions largely sit at the two extremes of how the robot is being controlled. Aside from the human-driven teleoperation which exhibits obvious drawbacks above, a learned policy may control the robot autonomously and collect data. While this allows us to run RL online which improves the policy upon its own experience overtime, real-world exploration can be sample inefficient and unsafe. DAgger-style methods partially address this by using learned policy to drive the robot until it makes a mistake, where a human intervenes and corrects it, often through teleoperation. This is reactive: each intervention requires a failure to occur naturally, and rare failure modes may take many rollouts to appear, and for many tasks (e.g., that require working with delicate objects that may break) failures cannot be corrected once they occur.

In this paper, we argue that autonomous policy rollout and human control should not be mutually exclusive, and a shared-control framework in which a learned agent and the human drive the robot together allows for better data collection. Our framework is simple: the human retains closed-loop teleoperation of the robot that supplies the demonstration signal as usual in the form of control commands, but these commands are perturbed by a residual policy, which is trained online on the growing dataset, in a way that mimics the mistakes a policy trained on the current data might make. We call this residual policy an inoculative policy because it exposes data collection to controlled, human-corrected “doses” of the learner’s expected mistakes, so that the policy learned from the collected data is already robust to them. The human can therefore correct policy-like deviations continuously throughout every data collection episode rather than only after a visible failure while ensuring safety because they are always in control of the robot. The resulting data collection strategy, which we call Data Inoculation (DI) (Figure 1), produce data that are favourable for downstream policy extraction—it contains near-failure states paired with actions that allow recovery from these states, which is exactly the good coverage data that would help behavior cloning (BC) to learn the recovery behavior directly but also help offline RL to learn better value functions.

Our main contribution is the new data collection strategy (DI). We evaluate DI on three challenging real-world robotic tasks and show that DI consistently improves or matches the success rate of the policies extracted from both behavior cloning (BC) and offline RL. These results demonstrate the benefits of proactively inoculating data collection so that the policies become more robust at deployment time.

title: Catch It All!: Generalizable Dynamic Catching with a Dexterous Hand
authors: Arth Shukla,Kehlani Fay,Huaze Liu,Darin Djapri,Alexiy Buynitsky,Nicklas Hansen
abstract: Catching arbitrary objects requires generalization to novel projectiles and real-time adaptation to unpredictable contact dynamics under noisy visual observations. This paper presents Catch It All!, a sim-to-real catching framework for humanoid robots that generalizes and adapts to unseen objects with variable physical properties for underhand and overhand catches, using only one egocentric camera. We learn policies which generalize to unseen objects with varying geometry, deformability, elasticity, and physical properties. Effective grasps which adapt real-time to object poses and shapes are learned through careful grasp reward design. We provide safety-aware curricula which enable safe, high-frequency action execution near hardware limits, including wrist torque limits as low as 5 N⋅m5\text{\,}\mathrm{N}\text{${\cdot}$}\mathrm{m}. We validate our system by deploying zero-shot on a Unitree G1. With only one egocentric camera, Catch It All! successfully performs underhand and overhand catches on 9 unseen objects not seen during training, including low-rebound plushes, semi-deformable toys and chip bags, and rigid-elastic objects with high rebound on contact.
introduction:
Dexterous catching is a fundamental dynamic manipulation problem, requiring precise synergy between vision and control under tight timing constraints  [1, 2]. For a successful catch, robots must achieve low-latency, adaptable, and generalizable visuomotor reflexes, as thrown objects vary widely in their contact and grasp dynamics. On humanoid platforms, this problem is compounded. Unlike industrial manipulators, humanoid arms typically operate under significantly lower torque limits and control bandwidth, making it easy to exceed hardware limits and damage a robot. Humanoids rely on lighter actuators to ensure safety and work within mobile power constraints. Catching requires learning high-frequency, reactive behaviors without exceeding these hardware limits. Prior systems demonstrate high-speed interception on quadrupeds and industrial manipulators [1, 3, 4, 5]; unlike these platforms, with wrist torque limits as low as 5 N⋅m5\text{\,}\mathrm{N}\text{${\cdot}$}\mathrm{m}, humanoids are more susceptible to hardware limits during high-frequency action execution.

Generalizable catching across diverse objects with a wide range of physical properties is a challenge. Prior sim-to-real works rely on simplified projectiles with low elasticity such as sandbags [5, 6] which are more forgiving to imprecise timing or weak grasps. In simulation, prior work has achieved catching diverse projectiles [7]; however, zero-shot transfer to general unseen objects in the real world remains an open problem. To overcome these limitations, our framework leverages careful reward and curriculum design, achieving zero-shot real world transfer with generalization to unseen objects while executing safely within hardware limits.

We present Catch It All!, a generalizable dexterous catching framework for underhand and overhand catching that operates on a single egocentric camera without motion capture or human demonstrations. Our contributions are: (1) generalizing to novel objects in both underhand and overhand catches through grasp reward design and a toss curriculum, (2) safe action execution near hardware limits via curricula on torque clipping and reward penalties, and (3) zero-shot sim-to-real transfer, capable of catching objects unseen in simulation both underhand and overhand.

title: Self-Supervised Doppler-Guided RF Odometry
authors: Kunzhe Song,Jialuo Du,Jingkai Lin,Huacheng Zeng
abstract: Radio-frequency (RF) sensing enables robot ego-motion estimation in darkness, smoke, and fog, yet RF odometry remains challenging because multipath and moving reflectors make cross-frame matching highly ambiguous. Existing methods often rely on auxiliary inertial sensors or ground-truth pose supervision. We present RFWalk, a self-supervised, RF-only odometry framework that models dense correspondences across range-azimuth frames as random walks on a space-time graph and learns them from unlabeled sequences through temporal cycle consistency. To rule out correspondences that are cycle-consistent but physically implausible, we introduce a Doppler consistency loss that constrains correspondence-induced motion using radial velocity measured by the RF sensor itself. Ego-motion is then recovered through robust SE⁡(2)\mathrm{SE}(2) registration that suppresses uncertain correspondences and those arising from independently moving objects. Without pose labels or auxiliary sensors, RFWalk remains competitive with supervised baselines in static scenes and reduces absolute trajectory error by 58% in dynamic scenes with moving pedestrians.
introduction:
Reliable ego-motion estimation is a fundamental capability for autonomous robots, underpinning localization, mapping, and navigation.
Cameras and LiDAR have become the dominant sensing modalities for odometry [6, 12, 37], yet their performance can degrade substantially in darkness, smoke, fog, and dust.
Radio-frequency (RF) sensing, particularly millimeter-wave (mmWave) radar, provides a complementary sensing modality that is robust to illumination changes and airborne obscurants while remaining compact and inexpensive enough for mobile robots [14, 25, 1, 38].
These properties have motivated growing interest in RF-based odometry and simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM) [26, 32, 22].

Despite these advantages, estimating ego-motion from RF observations alone remains challenging.
The core difficulty lies in establishing reliable correspondences between consecutive RF frames.
Compared with optical images or LiDAR point clouds, range-azimuth (RA) heatmaps have coarse angular resolution and are heavily affected by multipath propagation and specular reflections, producing unstable or spurious structures that may vanish or shift across frames.
In feature-poor or repetitive environments, multiple candidate matches can be geometrically indistinguishable.
Moving reflectors such as pedestrians further complicate the problem, since correspondences on independently moving objects do not follow the rigid ego-motion shared by the static scene.

Existing RF odometry methods follow several strategies to address these challenges, but each leaves part of the problem unresolved.
Scan-matching approaches [2, 28] align consecutive RF observations geometrically, yet remain vulnerable to multipath, coarse angular resolution, and geometric degeneracy.
Radar-inertial systems [20, 8, 26, 39] improve motion observability by incorporating an IMU, at the cost of additional sensing, calibration, and synchronization.
Doppler-based approaches [19, 32] exploit radar-measured radial velocity as a direct motion cue, but typically assume that most reflectors are static.
Moreover, learning-based components in these pipelines [28, 32] require ground-truth trajectories or co-located LiDAR supervision, both of which are costly to collect at scale.
As a result, accurate RF-only odometry without pose supervision remains an open problem, particularly in dynamic environments.

In this work, we introduce RFWalk, a self-supervised odometry framework that relies solely on RF observations and formulates ego-motion estimation as physics-informed cross-frame correspondence learning (Fig. 1).
Rather than regressing poses directly, RFWalk models dense correspondences between RA frames as random walks on a space-time graph [16, 30], learns these correspondences from unlabeled RF sequences, and recovers ego-motion from the resulting correspondence field.
Neither ground-truth poses nor auxiliary sensors are required during training or inference.

The key idea is to combine two complementary sources of self-supervision intrinsic to the RF signal.
Temporal cycle consistency encourages correspondences that persist across time, while Doppler measurements provide an independent physical constraint on the radial displacement implied by each correspondence.
Unlike prior Doppler-based methods, we do not use Doppler to estimate ego-velocity directly; instead, we use it to determine whether each local cross-frame association is physically plausible.
This constraint applies to both static and moving reflectors and penalizes incorrect matches that remain cycle-consistent in repetitive or geometrically ambiguous scenes.
We further enforce consistency between composed multi-step correspondences and their direct counterparts to reduce drift, and recover motion through robust SE⁡(2)\mathrm{SE}(2) registration that suppresses uncertain or independently moving correspondences.
Together, these components turn ambiguous RF matching into physically grounded, self-supervised motion estimation.

We evaluate RFWalk on the public Radarize benchmark [32] and on the RFWalk dataset, which we collect using a 60 GHz mmWave ISAC platform in indoor scenes with moving pedestrians.
Without pose supervision or auxiliary sensing, RFWalk remains competitive with supervised baselines in static scenes and reduces absolute trajectory error by 58% relative to the strongest baseline in dynamic scenes.
Its advantage becomes more pronounced as scene dynamics increase.
From the least to the most dynamic scenes, its error grows by less than 1 m, compared with 2.3–8.2 m for the supervised baselines.
These results suggest that physics-informed correspondence learning offers a promising path toward scalable RF odometry from unlabeled sequences.

We summarize our main contributions as follows.

We formulate RF odometry as physics-informed, self-supervised correspondence learning, enabling dense cross-frame associations to be learned from unlabeled RF sequences without ground-truth poses or auxiliary sensors.

We introduce Doppler consistency supervision, which converts per-cell radial velocity into a local physical constraint on correspondence-induced displacement. This constraint applies to both static and moving reflectors and suppresses physically incompatible matches that cycle consistency alone cannot rule out.

We enforce compositional consistency across multi-step correspondences and recover motion through confidence-aware robust SE⁡(2)\mathrm{SE}(2) registration, improving long-horizon stability and robustness to dynamic clutter.

1. We formulate RF odometry as physics-informed, self-supervised correspondence learning, enabling dense cross-frame associations to be learned from unlabeled RF sequences without ground-truth poses or auxiliary sensors.

2. We introduce Doppler consistency supervision, which converts per-cell radial velocity into a local physical constraint on correspondence-induced displacement. This constraint applies to both static and moving reflectors and suppresses physically incompatible matches that cycle consistency alone cannot rule out.

3. We enforce compositional consistency across multi-step correspondences and recover motion through confidence-aware robust SE⁡(2)\mathrm{SE}(2) registration, improving long-horizon stability and robustness to dynamic clutter.

title: Open-World Object Motion Anticipation via Meta-Learned Semantic Adaptation
authors: Mason Peterson,Gage MacLin,Camilla Tabasso,Jonathan P. How,Joshua Migdal,Tye Brady,Taskin Padir
abstract:
Anticipating the motion of nearby objects is critical for safe and efficient robot navigation.
Without a proper understanding of what may move, a robot may plan overly conservative, inefficient trajectories to guarantee safety, or it may be overly risky, resulting in unacceptable collisions.
While tracking and predicting the motion of known objects has seen significant progress,
little research addresses how a robot should adapt online to novel objects, including anticipating how one object may move another (e.g., a person operating a forklift to move a pallet).
To enable this capability, we propose a meta-learned graph neural network that leverages a semantic, geometric, and relational history of objects to accurately predict, from a few online observations, when objects will begin to move in new environments.
We demonstrate that our method, which is trained only in simulation, accurately anticipates the motion of objects unseen at training time, transfers to hardware without any fine-tuning, and outperforms a vision-language model and a class-frequency baseline in both simulation and hardware experiments.
Our method’s accurate prediction enables collision-free traversals in a closed-loop navigation simulation, while remaining within four seconds of the fastest, collision-prone planner.
introduction:
Operating in complex, busy environments requires autonomous robots to reason not only about the locations of nearby obstacles, but also about whether they will move.
Incorrectly predicting object motion is problematic in both the overly risky and the overly conservative case: a robot that assumes objects will remain static may collide when objects move unexpectedly [1], while a robot that treats every object as potentially dynamic may take inefficient paths or even freeze up entirely in busy scenes [2].
Detecting currently moving objects is a mature field of research [3]; however, only detecting an object once it is in motion is not enough to guarantee safe navigation.
To guarantee safety, a robot must act with increased caution around objects that are likely to begin moving, which requires anticipating motion onset with calibrated probabilities.
Anticipating object motion onset, however, is challenging.
Generalizable motion anticipation must be able to adapt to objects unseen during training and represent how object motion is conditioned on relationships with other objects in a scene.

In complex, previously unseen environments,
obvious approaches for anticipating object motion onset are insufficient.
A pre-trained neural network can only learn a fixed prior over which appearances tend to move; it cannot account for objects or environments absent from its training data.
Alternatively, a look-up table defining motion probabilities for all objects would lack important relational information that governs many objects’ motion.
Additionally, since relationships can be multi-hop and combinatorial (e.g., a person driving a forklift moving a pallet of boxes), a hand-crafted relational table would not scale either.
Furthermore, while vision-language models have demonstrated impressive capabilities, they cannot easily retain the context of a scene over time, and they run too slowly for online use.
These failures motivate our approach: a learned graph neural network (GNN) capable of online adaptation to novel objects.

The key insight we offer is that predicting when an object is likely to move requires semantic information, spatial information, and accumulated per-scene evidence.
An object’s semantic identity carries a strong prior on how it moves and can be inferred from appearance similarity without class labels.
For instance, when a previously unobserved robot is seen moving, its appearance can be used to predict that a similar object is likely to move as well.
Combining semantic appearance information with spatial relationships enables correctly predicting object motion in complex scenarios, such as a novel mobile manipulator moving carts.
Finally, to enable spatial and semantic understanding in novel environments, a robot should be able to learn from new observations of object behavior to predict future motion onset.

We leverage these insights by constructing a GNN with nodes encoding appearance features and edges encoding spatial relationships.
Rather than learning a fixed mapping from appearance to motion, our network is trained across many simulated episodes to meta-learn how to accumulate motion and interaction evidence within a scene, so that it can adapt to novel objects and environments from a few test-time observations without any weight updates.
To prevent overfitting to semantics seen during training, we apply a scene-consistent training augmentation to the DINO embedding [4] associated with each object.
We show that this, combined with our meta-learning strategy, enables our network to adapt to novel object classes at test time while still exploiting semantic information within a single scene, as shown in Figure 1.
Our proposed method outputs calibrated probabilities that correspond accurately to true motion onset, enabling their use as input to a mobile robot motion planner for collision-free navigation.

In summary, the contributions of this paper include:

The novel problem of open-world object motion anticipation: predicting which currently static objects will begin moving within a given time horizon. We formulate this as estimating a calibrated per-object motion onset probability, conditioned on the history of scene observations.

A recurrent GNN model trained with semantic embedding augmentation that meta-learns from past relational interactions to anticipate object motion, generalizing on the fly to novel objects.

A series of simulation and hardware experiments demonstrating that our method accurately predicts the motion onset of objects unseen at training time, and that its calibrated predictions enable collision-free closed-loop navigation.

1. The novel problem of open-world object motion anticipation: predicting which currently static objects will begin moving within a given time horizon. We formulate this as estimating a calibrated per-object motion onset probability, conditioned on the history of scene observations.

2. A recurrent GNN model trained with semantic embedding augmentation that meta-learns from past relational interactions to anticipate object motion, generalizing on the fly to novel objects.

3. A series of simulation and hardware experiments demonstrating that our method accurately predicts the motion onset of objects unseen at training time, and that its calibrated predictions enable collision-free closed-loop navigation.

title: Learning Event-based Obstacle Avoidance via Differentiable Simulation
authors: Chenlu Shou,Yunfan Ren,Jiaxu Xing,Davide Scaramuzza
abstract:
Reliable obstacle avoidance is essential for safe quadrotor flight in unknown environments, yet conventional frame-based cameras remain challenged by motion blur, limited dynamic range, and latency under fast motion.
Event cameras, with sub-millisecond latency, high dynamic range, and negligible motion blur, offer a promising alternative, but leveraging them for closed-loop control remains difficult.
Existing approaches either adopt cascaded architectures that first estimate depth and then map it to control commands, introducing error propagation, or achieve end-to-end control through costly offline pretraining before online fine-tuning can even begin.
We address these challenges with a CUDA-based event simulator that exploits GPU parallelism to render events efficiently within the training loop, integrated into a differentiable simulation pipeline that enables direct gradient backpropagation through the differentiable physics model, improving sample efficiency.
This allows us to train an end-to-end policy that maps event frames directly to control commands, without intermediate depth estimation.
We validate our approach through zero-shot real-world deployment on a quadrotor, achieving robust obstacle avoidance in both odometry-assisted and odometry-free settings, including under low-light conditions where conventional cameras typically fail.
introduction:
Quadrotors have been widely adopted in autonomous robotics for applications such as industrial inspection, package delivery, and search-and-rescue, where reliable obstacle avoidance is essential for safe operation in unknown environments [1].
However, achieving robust vision-based obstacle avoidance remains challenging, particularly during high-speed flight, because conventional frame-based cameras are susceptible to motion blur, limited dynamic range, and sensing latency.
Unlike traditional cameras that capture image frames at a fixed rate, event cameras [2], modeled after the biological retina, operate asynchronously.
Each pixel functions independently, and an event is triggered only when the change in log-intensity at pixel coordinates exceeds a predefined threshold, with polarity indicating an increase or decrease in brightness.
This bio-inspired sensing mechanism inherently minimizes motion blur and provides sub-millisecond latency and a much higher dynamic range, making event cameras highly suitable for agile applications [3, 4, 5].
Most notably, Sony AI’s Ace [3], the first real-world table tennis AI agent competitive with human athletes, uses event-based spin estimation to return high-speed shots.

In this work, we leverage these advantages to address vision-based obstacle avoidance in quadrotor flight.
A closely related method [6] adopts a cascaded architecture, in which a perception network first predicts depth from the input event stream, and a separate velocity predictor maps this estimated depth to control commands.
This architecture makes control performance dependent on the accuracy of an intermediate depth estimate: errors in depth prediction can propagate to the control commands and compromise obstacle avoidance.
This dependence motivates learning a direct mapping from event data to control commands, allowing the visual representation to be optimized jointly with the control policy for the obstacle-avoidance task.

An end-to-end policy that maps event data directly to control commands would avoid this issue, but training such a policy at scale requires an event simulator that can generate large volumes of event data efficiently.
Existing event generation tools remain computationally expensive, making them a major bottleneck for policy training.

Furthermore, using model-free reinforcement learning (RL), such as proximal policy optimization (PPO) [7], to train such a policy is notoriously sample-inefficient, particularly when learning directly from high-dimensional visual inputs such as event data, which require large numbers of interactions to extract useful features.
Differentiable simulation offers a promising alternative.
By computing gradients through the simulated dynamics analytically, policies can be optimized via backpropagation, improving sample efficiency. Recent works have demonstrated the effectiveness of differentiable simulation across various learning scenarios [8, 9, 10].
In this work, we present an end-to-end control framework for event-based obstacle avoidance that maps event frames directly to control commands.
We investigate both odometry-assisted and odometry-free settings to examine the policy’s dependence on external velocity estimates.
In the latter, the policy uses only onboard attitude information as state input and learns to infer velocity-related information from the event history.

To summarize, the key contributions of this work are:

We develop a CUDA-based event simulator that exploits GPU parallelism to generate event observations efficiently within the policy training loop.
At a resolution of 64×4864\times 48 with 128 parallel environments, our simulator achieves 60,248 environment steps per second, approximately 14×14\times the throughput of the state-of-the-art [11].
We further assess the transfer of the simulated event representation through offline velocity estimation on real-world event data.

We integrate this simulator into a differentiable simulation pipeline that optimizes the control policy by backpropagating gradients through the simulated dynamics.
This framework enables policy convergence in approximately 3 hours on a laptop equipped with an NVIDIA RTX 5060 GPU, without a separate offline event-data generation and representation-pretraining stage.

We demonstrate zero-shot deployment on a real-world quadrotor, achieving obstacle avoidance in both odometry-assisted and odometry-free settings.
We further demonstrate successful flight under low-light conditions with illuminance as low as 5.8 lux.

1. We develop a CUDA-based event simulator that exploits GPU parallelism to generate event observations efficiently within the policy training loop.
At a resolution of 64×4864\times 48 with 128 parallel environments, our simulator achieves 60,248 environment steps per second, approximately 14×14\times the throughput of the state-of-the-art [11].
We further assess the transfer of the simulated event representation through offline velocity estimation on real-world event data.

2. We integrate this simulator into a differentiable simulation pipeline that optimizes the control policy by backpropagating gradients through the simulated dynamics.
This framework enables policy convergence in approximately 3 hours on a laptop equipped with an NVIDIA RTX 5060 GPU, without a separate offline event-data generation and representation-pretraining stage.

3. We demonstrate zero-shot deployment on a real-world quadrotor, achieving obstacle avoidance in both odometry-assisted and odometry-free settings.
We further demonstrate successful flight under low-light conditions with illuminance as low as 5.8 lux.

title: Selective Sliding Mode Control Enhances Robustness of Aerial Robots Under Disturbances
authors: Anoop Kiran,Thales C. Silva,Nora Ayanian
abstract:
Quadrotor control under disturbances such as wind gusts and payload variations remains challenging. First-order sliding mode control (SMC) and matched/unmatched uncertainty distinction are classical approaches; however, neither tells a practitioner which loops in a cascaded controller should be made robust to sustain disturbances, how to tune those loops, nor what the additional costs are on an embedded processor. Applying robust control uniformly across all axes addresses disturbances indiscriminately, adding tuning effort on axes where no disturbance acts. On inherently underactuated vehicles, disturbances along some axes cannot be opposed directly at all.
We propose a principled methodology for deciding where robust control belongs in a cascaded architecture, with all control running onboard the vehicle. We recover the acting disturbance from PID hover flights under disturbance by inverting the equations of motion, use the recovered signal to identify and quantify the excited axes, and deploy robust control where it counts. Experiments on a Crazyflie 2.1 quadrotor under slung-payload and oblique-wind disturbances show tracking improvements concentrated on the axes the rule selects, and gain sweeps confirm that the switching gain reduces error on matched axes but has no effect on an excited unmatched axis, as the analysis predicts.
introduction:
Quadrotors are increasingly deployed for infrastructure inspection, search and rescue, and monitoring, where external disturbances routinely degrade tracking performance and transient stability [1, 2, 3]. Counteracting these disturbances is complicated by underactuation: four control inputs must govern six degrees of freedom, and quadrotors produce no lateral force directly and must tilt to move sideways. This same structure, however, offers an opportunity. The distinction between disturbances that actuators can directly oppose (matched) and those they cannot (unmatched) [4, 5, 6] offers a natural criterion for where robust control is worth deploying. Yet this structure is rarely exploited, with robust switching laws applied uniformly across all axes rather than only where a disturbance can be opposed [7, 8, 9].

Cascaded PID remains the practical default for its low computational overhead and intuitive tuning [10]. However, its disturbance rejection is limited by the bandwidth-noise tradeoff of fixed-gain linear feedback [11]. Integral action removes constant steady-state error asymptotically, so mid-flight payload addition or a sudden crosswind induces a transient excursion before the integrator converges. Raising PID gains for faster rejection amplifies measurement noise and shrinks the stability margin, trading one limit for another.

To overcome these linear limits, alternative robust control schemes exist, but each carries requirements on onboard resources, sensing fidelity, or modeling that can be difficult to meet on lightweight quadrotors. Estimate-and-cancel schemes, such as Incremental Nonlinear Dynamic Inversion (INDI) [12], rely on high-rate angular acceleration feedback and precise control-effectiveness models, both of which are degraded onboard, where differentiated gyro signals are noisy and models only approximate. In disturbance and extended-state observers (DOBs/ESOs) [13, 14, 15], high observer gains amplify high-frequency IMU measurement noise and introduce phase lag through the low-pass filtering they typically require, while lower gains track fast transient disturbances more slowly. Adaptive schemes [16, 9] require persistent excitation to guarantee parameter convergence; step disturbances at hover, such as an attached payload, provide little excitation, which can leave adaptation slow or prone to drift. Learning-based methods have shown promise in handling unmodeled dynamics [17, 18, 6], but typically lack deterministic error bounds unless coupled with model predictive architectures [4, 19], whose real-time optimization remains considerably more expensive than a fixed control law.

Bound-based robust schemes are far less demanding to implement onboard: sliding mode control (SMC) requires only the tracking error, its derivative, and a disturbance bound, reducing online evaluation to a few algebraic operations per axis per cycle [20]. Yet standard quadrotor SMC adds switching terms to every axis, including the lateral ones the vehicle cannot directly actuate, where a switching term does not improve rejection, adds parameters to tune, and can degrade tracking when switching terms in the position and attitude loops act on the same lateral force [7, 8, 9]. Moreover, such work is largely evaluated in continuous-time simulation under ideal state feedback [21, 8], leaving the discretization, chattering, and compute trade-offs of real hardware untested. Existing quadrotor SMC work does not use flight data to decide which axes need a switching term, which parameter to tune on each, or what it costs onboard.

Observer- and inversion-based methods estimate the disturbance online to cancel it on every axis. We instead measure the disturbance once, from PID hover flight logs, and our selective approach places a switching term only where a disturbance is both present and actuator-reachable (Fig. 1). In a nutshell, the key intuition is that robustness is useful only when the controller has the authority to act.

Contributions: This work turns the matched and unmatched distinction into a practical procedure for deploying robust control. Specifically, the contributions are:

A per-axis deployment rule that identifies from PID hover flights where robust control belongs and which parameter to tune on each axis, built on actuation geometry and the gain response of boundary-layer SMC (Sec. IV).

Hardware validation under a slung payload and an oblique wind, showing that the switching gain reduces error only on matched axes while the surface slope governs unmatched ones, and that tracking improves on exactly the axes the rule selects (Secs. V-A–V-B).

An evaluation under fully onboard state estimation showing that selective SMC retains its advantage over INDI, at no added computational cost over the built-in PID (Secs. V-C–V-D).

title: Inertial Steering and Motion Prediction of Tracked Vehicles on Low-Adherence Surfaces
authors: Mathis Turgeon-Roy,Mohamed Ounally,Veronica Vannini,Olivier Roy,François Pomerleau
abstract:
Tracked vehicles are widely used in off-road applications, but their conventional motion models often rely on no-slip assumptions that become inaccurate on low-adherence surfaces.
Rather than treating inertial effects arising from slip as a disturbance to be minimized, this work investigates how inertial effects arising from a moving mass can be deliberately exploited for steering on low-friction surfaces.
A dynamic model for an articulated tracked vehicle with a passive trailer is developed, allowing inertial effects from trailer motion to be captured.
The approach is experimentally evaluated on ice, where our dynamic model outperforms the kinematic baseline.
We also propose a mixed dynamic-kinematic model to adapt predictions to both surface and situation by exploiting predictions from both methods.
Finally, we demonstrate inertial steering on a mono-track vehicle without a conventional steering mechanism, showing that controlled movements of an internal mass can generate turning motion on ice.
The resulting behavior can be predicted using the proposed dynamic model by representing the internal mass as a frictionless trailer, revealing the analogous dynamics between the two configurations.
These results demonstrate the feasibility of inertial steering as an alternative steering mechanism for tracked vehicles operating in low-adherence environments.
introduction:
Tracked vehicles are a well-established design for off-road heavy-duty tasks in variable ground conditions due to their augmented surface of contact [30].
Their popularity makes motion modeling of tracked vehicles an important concern for autonomous systems acting in domains such as agriculture [7], mining [32], and defense [36].
While skid steer remains the most common track configuration, tracked vehicle designs have diversified [3], and articulated vehicles that steer by reorienting a passive trailer relative to the towing body are one example, as pictured in Fig. 1 a).
Traditionally, motion models for tracked vehicles assume perfect adherence to the ground at a point of the track and determine the  ICR (ICR) accordingly through simple kinematic models [13].
Nonetheless, on low-adherence surfaces such as ice, the ability to generate lateral forces diminishes, and the accuracy of simple kinematic models is severely hindered [2].

In the past, slip has been mainly treated as an unknown disturbance to be estimated, compensated, or minimized, rather than as a locomotion mechanism to be deliberately exploited [8].
One estimation approach augments classical kinematic models with slip parameters identified either online or from prior terrain characterization [33, 10].
In control publications, these models are commonly integrated into  MPC (MPC) to regulate slip as ground adherence changes [29].
The resulting behavior is safe but conservative, as the vehicle slows down precisely where friction saturates, limiting potential mobility.
Yet for certain robots, losing ground adherence also opens the opportunity for an alternative steering mechanism, with articulated vehicles serving as a representative example.
As illustrated in Fig. 1 b), when reorienting its trailer, an articulated vehicle also moves a mass mm relative to its towing body, which generates an inertial steering wrench.
On ice, as the kinematic model loses fidelity, the trailer can accelerate and move faster, increasing its inertial contribution to steering.
Inertial steering then appears as a complementary mechanism to maintain or even increase mobility on low-friction surfaces.

In this paper, we investigate the mixed use of kinematic and dynamic motion models for an articulated tracked vehicle with a passive trailer to reduce prediction error in adverse traction conditions.
Moreover, we pushed the concept of dynamic modeling further by predicting the motion of a vehicle without classical steering.
As depicted in Fig. 1 c), we implemented a mass-shifting system on a stand-alone track that we will refer to as a mono-track configuration in this text.

More specifically, the contributions of this paper are:

An adaptation of a modular contact friction model for articulated track and mono-track vehicles on ice;

A derivation and an experimental validation of a mixed inertial and friction steering model for an articulated vehicle; and

An experimental validation of a mono-track vehicle steered exclusively through intentional inertial variation.

title: AtomTree: A Hierarchical Framework for State-Aware Embodied Instruction Following with LLMs
authors: Haotian Zhai,Tianming Sha,Junnan Li
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computation and Language (cs.CL)
abstract: Embodied instruction following in interactive environments requires agents to interpret natural language commands and complete long-horizon tasks. Existing planners either rely on large labeled trajectories, or use few-shot and zero-shot LLM prompting that produces a whole plan in a single serial reasoning process. These approaches depend on linguistic common sense, commit to a plan from the initial instruction, and only update after failures, which weakens robustness and state awareness. We present AtomTree, a hierarchical framework for state-aware task planning with LLMs. AtomTree incrementally builds a tree of subgoals and actions, where the LLM decides at each step, from the current symbolic state, whether to further decompose or to output a grounded low-level action. A lightweight memory module summarizes past outcomes for reuse in later decisions. When a low-level action stalls, AtomTree triggers hierarchical backtracking replanning to return to the parent node and regenerate the subtree plan from the latest state, preventing continued drift along an incorrect trajectory. In zero-shot evaluation on the ALFRED benchmark, AtomTree outperforms prior LLM-based planners. Project page: https://zhaihaotian.github.io/atomtree-website/.
introduction:
“Planning is the art and practice of thinking before acting.”
— Patrik Haslum

Building embodied agents that can execute diverse household tasks from natural language instructions and rapidly acquire new skills is a core goal in robotics and embodied AI[1, 2, 3]. Embodied Instruction Following (EIF) requires an agent to jointly perform visual perception, subgoal planning, navigation, and object interaction in interactive 3D environments to complete long-horizon tasks such as “clean a mug and place it into the coffee machine.”[1] In benchmarks such as ALFRED[1], this requires not only language understanding but also continuous instruction decomposition and execution under partial observability. Therefore, how to achieve EIF that is both generalizable and capable of long-horizon planning under limited supervision remains an open problem[4].

A straightforward approach is to train policy networks with large-scale pairs of natural-language instructions and expert action sequences[5, 6, 7, 8, 9]. However, both instruction annotation and expert demonstration collection are expensive and time-consuming, and collecting sufficient data in complex environments is often impractical. To reduce annotation cost, several recent studies manually design action sequences for specific task types, but such predefined procedures do not scale well across heterogeneous tasks[10, 11]. Another line of work leverages prior knowledge from large language models (LLMs) for task planning. LLM-Planner[12] uses few-shot in-context learning to generate high-level subgoal sequences, which are then executed by low-level controllers. FLARE[4] further introduces visual information during planning. Socratic Planner[13] decomposes instructions via self-questioning and performs Socratic-style replanning with visual feedback after failures.

Despite these advances, most LLM-based methods remain unstable on complex long-horizon tasks. On ALFRED Valid Seen, we perform an error analysis of state-of-the-art few-shot planning methods[4] and categorize failures into four groups in Fig. 1: planning errors, navigation failures, perception failures, and interaction failures . When task horizon is measured by ground-truth PDDL plan length, planning errors account for approximately 38.9%38.9\% when the length is no greater than 77, close to interaction failures at 35.2%35.2\%. When the length exceeds 77, planning errors increase to 68.7%68.7\% and become the dominant failure mode. We further group tasks by the PDDL length threshold kk. As kk increases from 55 to 1515, the proportion of planning errors among all failures rises monotonically from around 50%50\% to nearly 100%100\%, showing a strong linear relationship with task length (Pearson r=0.8892r=0.8892, p≈2.1×10−5p\approx 2.1\times 10^{-5}). This finding indicates that, in long-horizon embodied instruction following, the primary bottleneck has shifted from low-level navigation, perception, and interaction to high-level task planning itself.

The key limitation of existing LLM-based planners on long-horizon tasks is that decision making is still centered on a single unidirectional sequential plan[1, 12, 10, 11, 13]. After receiving an instruction, the model typically generates a full high-level plan in one pass based mainly on linguistic commonsense, and replanning is triggered passively only after repeated subgoal failures, rather than through closed-loop decisions at every step conditioned on the current environment state. Consider the ALFRED instruction “Put a washed potato slice on the white table.” The environment ontology does not contain a category named “white table,” and only exposes a limited set of semantic classes such as “Dining Table.” The agent must infer during execution that “white table” is aligned with the observed dining table instance, revealing the gap between human language and environment ontology. By analogy to travel planning, humans rarely commit all details at the outset. Instead, they first decide high-level steps such as “go to Paris” and “book flights and hotels,” and then refine details based on actual conditions.

Motivated by this observation, we model EIF as a state-conditioned sequential decision process[14] in which, at each decision node, the agent determines whether to further decompose the current objective or directly execute an atomic action based on the current state and subgoal, resulting in an AtomTree composed of decomposition and execution nodes. This state-driven hierarchical reasoning can mitigate error accumulation caused by one-pass sequential planning in long-horizon settings.

Building on this formulation, we propose AtomTree, which explicitly organizes planning as a tree of decomposition nodes and execution nodes. At each node, the policy conditions only on the current environment state, the current instruction segment, and internal memory to decide whether to decompose into finer subgoals or output an atomic action. For example, for the instruction “slice a tomato with a knife,” if the agent is already holding a knife in front of the tomato, AtomTree directly selects the slice action. From an initial state, the system instead decomposes the objective top-down into subgoals such as “find a knife,” “pick up the knife,” and “move to the tomato,” followed by progressive refinement and execution. To realize true state awareness, we maintain memory in each node state to summarize historical observations, enabling consistent context for downstream decisions. When a low-level action stalls for an extended period, we do not perform only local replanning for that action. Instead, we trigger a Hierarchical Backtracking Replanning mechanism that returns to the corresponding parent node and regenerates the subtree plan conditioned on the latest environment state. This enables structured top-down adjustment after local failures, rather than accumulating deviation along an incorrect sequential trajectory.

We conduct a systematic evaluation of AtomTree on the ALFRED benchmark. The results show that, under a fully zero-shot setting, AtomTree surpasses state-of-the-art few-shot LLM-based planners on multiple primary metrics, and even achieves better performance than some few-shot and supervised methods, with especially strong gains on long-horizon tasks and complex instructions. Based on these results, our main contributions are as follows:

We propose AtomTree, a hierarchical tree-structured planning framework for EIF, which explicitly models “decompose / execute” decisions as a state-aware Markov process.

We propose AtomTree, a hierarchical tree-structured planning framework for EIF, which explicitly models “decompose / execute” decisions as a state-aware Markov process.

We design a memory mechanism to enable the planning process to remain continuously aligned with the current environment state during execution, rather than relying on a one-shot sequential plan.

We validate the effectiveness of the framework through zero-shot experiments on ALFRED. Compared with representative few-shot, zero-shot, and supervised baselines, AtomTree achieves stronger overall performance.

1. We propose AtomTree, a hierarchical tree-structured planning framework for EIF, which explicitly models “decompose / execute” decisions as a state-aware Markov process.

2. We design a memory mechanism to enable the planning process to remain continuously aligned with the current environment state during execution, rather than relying on a one-shot sequential plan.

3. We validate the effectiveness of the framework through zero-shot experiments on ALFRED. Compared with representative few-shot, zero-shot, and supervised baselines, AtomTree achieves stronger overall performance.

title: Value Function-Guided MPPI for Hierarchical Planning and Control in Off-Road Autonomous Navigation
authors: Anoushka Alavilli,Raymond Song,Guanya Shi,Jeff Schneider
abstract: Autonomous navigation in off-road terrain is commonly achieved using hierarchical control and planning architectures that rely on explicit cost maps and one-way information flow from a high-level planner to a low-level controller, decoupling planning from the true execution cost experienced during control. We propose a hierarchical planning and control framework in which information flows bidirectionally, allowing the low-level controller to guide trajectory selection at the planning level. The highest level of the hierarchy is a Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) control-style planner that determines optimal trajectories and passes these waypoints to a pretrained low-level reinforcement learning (RL) controller. Rather than drawing from an explicit cost map, our MPPI planner leverages the value function of the RL controller as an implicit cost representation. In this formulation, MPPI serves as a trajectory exploration mechanism, while the low-level controller’s value function guides the search. To account for the distribution shift seen by the value function between training and evaluation, we propose an online policy evaluation process that adapts the value function to unseen driving experiences, and we demonstrate this adaptation in unseen off-road simulation environments. We evaluate our approach in a high-fidelity off-road driving simulator across a range of challenging terrain conditions and compare its performance against a baseline MPPI controller. The results demonstrate that our method achieves safer and more effective navigation to goal locations while eliminating the need for explicit cost maps and enabling tighter coupling between planning and control.
introduction:
Autonomous navigation in off-road environments requires vehicles to safely traverse from a start to a goal location while interacting with complex, unstructured terrain. This task is challenging due to both terrain properties, such as low traction in sand or deformability of mud, and terrain geometries, including steep slopes, ditches, and uneven surfaces that can induce unsafe vehicle dynamics such as excessive pitch and roll. While there is substantial prior work on perceiving and modeling both categories of terrain features, in this work we focus specifically on planning and control under challenging terrain geometries. Our goal is to enable a vehicle to safely navigate from start to goal by selecting and executing trajectories that avoid or carefully traverse geometrically hazardous regions.

Central to this work is the notion that the true “cost” of traversing terrain is highly dependent on the control that is deployed. For example, take the situation of a vehicle driving down a steep slope. The vehicle might experience unsafe toppling if it passes over the slope quickly, but it could also feasibly pass over the slope safely at a lower speed. Therefore, the “cost” of this hill is not only dependent on the hill geometry but also on the control law deployed. Results from works such as [12] validate this hypothesis in their findings that velocity observations aid in predicting costs of trajectory traversal.

Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) control [30] is a powerful method that has had much demonstrated success in autonomous locomotion, both in off-road and agile locomotion tasks [13, 11, 9, 23, 1]. Key to MPPI’s success are the parallelizable open-loop dynamics rollouts, the optimization costs for which are generally determined from a learned or predefined cost map of the terrain. These cost maps can be learned via methods such as semantic and geometric assessment [26] or via self-supervised learning [22, 18]. Simultaneously, reinforcement learning (RL) policies have demonstrated strong performance in learning control laws for agile robots [24, 16, 17, 20]. Unlike traditional cost maps, which assign costs based primarily on terrain understanding, RL policies learn value functions that estimate expected return under the control behavior they induce. Consequently, these value functions provide an implicit estimate of trajectory cost conditioned on the control policy. This raises a natural question: rather than relying on an explicit cost map, can we instead use a policy’s learned value function as a measure of terrain drivability for navigation?

In traditional hierarchical autonomy stacks, information flows top-down: a high-level planner proposes trajectories, and a low-level controller attempts to track these trajectories, as in [15]. This decoupling can lead to repeated failures when the planned trajectories are not feasible under the true execution dynamics of the controller, and particularly in off-road environments where terrain-vehicle interactions are complex and highly nonlinear [11]. In our hierarchical algorithm, the low-level controller actively informs the planning process. By using the value function of the low-level RL controller to provide an estimate of the expected return under its own control policy, the planner naturally selects trajectories that the robot is expected to be able to traverse. This enables the planner to favor trajectories that not only meet navigation goal requirements but also are realizable by the low-level tracking controller.

Our hierarchical algorithm effectively induces an implicit cost map, shaped by the controller’s learned understanding of terrain difficulty and vehicle limitations, without requiring explicit terrain labeling or cost map learning. By leveraging the value function as an execution-aware cost signal, we enable planning to account for the coupled effects of terrain and control without explicitly modeling them. This perspective frames cost maps not as standalone learned representations of the environment but as quantities that can be implicitly derived from the capabilities and limitations of the control policy itself.

We summarize our main contributions as follows:

The first formulation of MPPI that uses, as a cost function, the negative expected return estimated by a pretrained RL value function.

A hierarchical planning framework with bidirectional feedback between planning and control, enabling online adaptation that mitigates repeated control failures.

An off-road navigation algorithm that can plug into a real autonomy stack with ease, as the algorithm does not use privileged information from the simulator that cannot be adequately replicated using sensory inputs from onboard systems.

A new perspective on the form and role of cost maps for off-road driving.

Prior work in off-road navigation has focused on learning terrain representations for planning and control, typically through costmaps, traversability estimation, or learned dynamics models. These methods differ in their observation modality, how they are trained, and in the type of information they aim to predict.

Explicit Terrain Representations. Approaches such as [26] and [22] learn dense bird’s-eye view (BEV) representations from sensor data using offline supervision. [26] constructs traversability costmaps from sparse LiDAR and uses inpainting for occluded regions. [22] extends this approach to camera-based perception, predicting multi-layer terrain representations for both ground and ceiling structure. While [22] incorporates self-supervised depth completion and pseudo-labeling, it relies on manually annotated data. These BEV maps integrate well with planning but require curated datasets and do not adapt online.

Recent work reduces reliance on manual labels by leveraging self-supervision from onboard sensing and interaction. [9] learns BEV elevation and traversability maps using hindsight labels, while works such as [19] learn terrain affordances directly from real-world experience. [4] extends this to online adaptation by continuously updating a visual traversability model using LiDAR supervision. Other approaches include using proprioceptive feedback to aid in visual understanding [5], or contrastive learning for traversability estimation [18]. Uncertainty-aware traversability estimation has also been explored [7, 4]. While these methods improve scalability and generalization, they typically produce static cost predictions not explicitly conditioned on the controller. Some works [3] partly account for this gap directly by predicting traversal speed in their cost maps.

Our approach assumes that 3D elevation data is sufficient for estimating terrain traversability. In practice, terrain semantics may provide additional information about properties such as deformability (e.g., mud or sand). In this work, however, we focus on the planning–control interface rather than perception. Our framework is compatible with richer perceptual inputs, which could be incorporated into the RL policy observations without changing the overall algorithm.

Learning Costmaps from Demonstration and Interaction. In [29], an explicit discretized costmap is learned by minimizing the discrepancy between expert and MPPI-generated state visitation distributions, favoring routes from MPPI that are similar to those taken by the expert. WVN [8], which addresses traversability for quadrupedal robots, also uses human trajectory data but in a different manner. The robot learns from a few minutes of human data and correlates poor velocity tracking with lower traversability scores. After the inital data collection phase, the robot navigates by itself using its learned costmap. Thus, both of these approaches learn where the robot should travel, whereas ours jointly considers the terrain and the control policy that influences how robot executes the route.

SALON [28] uses self-supervision to associate BEV terrain features with costs measured during prior traversal. It learns a velocity-conditioned costmap that predicts expected “roughness” (quantified by IMU and suspension readings) and a speedmap that estimates the maximum speed allowable under a user-specified roughness limit. Similar to SALON, METAVerse [25] also uses self-supervised learning from physical vehicle-terrain interactions to continuously adapt cost predictions in real time. METAVerse associates LiDAR geometry and speed with traversability cost quantified by vertical acceleration and then adapts a neural costmap predictor using gradient updates from recent experience. Our work is similar in motivation to both of these works; however, our MPPI cost formulation captures a tradeoff between terrain difficulty and goal progress. By training the value function with a reward that jointly considers progress as well as controller and terrain penalties, our planner may select a rougher yet feasible route for goal-reaching tasks.

Learned Dynamics for Planning. An adjacent line of work learns predictive models of vehicle dynamics for use in planning. Methods such as [23] predict dynamics from proprioception and local terrain geometry as part of their MPPI framework. Other works, such as [11], rely strictly on odometry and proprioception by using a “hybrid” architecture. Works such as [10] improve upon this category of approach by incorporating visual terrain information in the dynamics model predictions to better capture terrain interactions. These methods implicitly capture terrain difficulty and are useful for predictions over short horizons while cost maps serve as a method for longer-horizon cost analysis.

Online Adaptation of Learned Models. Several works address the challenge of adapting to novel or out-of-distribution environments through online learning. In perception, methods such as [4] and [5] use self-supervision to continuously update visual models during deployment. In contrast, other approaches such as [21] adapt the control model itself to allow model-based controllers such as MPPI to better reflect the current terrain conditions. In our method, we adapt the value function of our RL policy to better predict the costs experienced during deployment.

Overall, prior work either learns explicit traversability maps or short-horizon dynamics models to assess costs. In contrast, our approach does not learn a model and instead uses a learned value function to provide a control-aware estimate of terrain difficulty that directly shapes trajectory optimization, bridging control and planning without requiring explicit costmap supervision or dynamics modeling.

Recent work has explored incorporating value functions into model predictive control (MPC) to mitigate the myopic behavior induced by short planning horizons. TD-MPC [14] learns a parametric Q-value function via temporal difference learning alongside a latent dynamics model, and uses this value function to estimate the terminal return of sampled trajectories. To assess the costs of non-terminal waypoints, TD-MPC uses a jointly-learned reward function that is separate from the value function. In contrast, [15] proposes a non-parametric alternative by treating a sampling-based planner as an approximate value function, where each node encodes a cost-to-go estimate that can be queried during control. Both approaches use value functions to bootstrap the terminal cost of trajectories, improving long-horizon reasoning without increasing planning complexity. However, these methods either rely on learned reward models and extensive training [14] or assume access to a global planning structure or map [15], which may not be available in unseen environments. In contrast, our approach uses a learned value function not only as a terminal bootstrap but also as a dense, waypoint-wise cost that shapes the trajectory over a local horizon rather than across a global map.

1. The first formulation of MPPI that uses, as a cost function, the negative expected return estimated by a pretrained RL value function.

2. A hierarchical planning framework with bidirectional feedback between planning and control, enabling online adaptation that mitigates repeated control failures.

3. An off-road navigation algorithm that can plug into a real autonomy stack with ease, as the algorithm does not use privileged information from the simulator that cannot be adequately replicated using sensory inputs from onboard systems.

4. A new perspective on the form and role of cost maps for off-road driving.

title: Quantize by Doing: Task-Guided Mixed-Precision Quantization of Vision-Language-Action Models
authors: Jiuyi Xu,Xiao Hu,Meida Chen,Song Wang,Yang Ye,Yangming Shi
abstract:
Post-training quantization (PTQ) reduces the memory footprint of vision-language-action (VLA) models, but lowering bit widths while maintaining task performance remains challenging.
Existing work has used sensitivity estimates from calibration data to assign bit widths to different model components.
However, using task success directly to guide mixed-precision allocation is underexplored because closed-loop evaluations are costly and the effect of quantizing one component depends on the precision of other components.
To this end, we propose QbD-VLA, a task-guided mixed-precision quantization method that uses task success from short closed-loop evaluations to assign weight and activation bit widths while accounting for interactions between model components.
Experiments covering four VLA models and all four LIBERO suites show strong task performance at average precisions of approximately 4 bits for weights and fewer than 6 bits for activations. On SIMPLER, the gain over uniform quantization is small. On a Franka Research 3 robot arm, simulation-selected allocations show no detected success-rate loss on X-VLA but fail on π0.5\pi_{0.5}.
These findings support using task success to guide mixed-precision VLA quantization, while highlighting the need for real-world evaluation before deployment.
Code is available at github.com/jiuyixu25/QbD-VLA.
introduction:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models map camera images and a language instruction to robot actions with backbones of several billion parameters (Kim et al., 2024; Black et al., 2024; Physical Intelligence et al., 2025; Zheng et al., 2025).
Post-training quantization (PTQ) is the standard way to fit such a policy onto an on-robot GPU, and the practical question is a mixed-precision allocation: which groups of layers must stay at higher precision while the rest run at lower bit width.
Existing methods choose the allocation from a sensitivity score computed per layer or per group on calibration data, such as Hessian-based sensitivity (Dong et al., 2019; Deng et al., 2025), a reconstruction error  (Nagel et al., 2020; Li et al., 2021; Frantar et al., 2022), or the deviation of predicted actions on fixed inputs  (Xu et al., 2026c; Akbari et al., 2026; Ranjan and Savakis, 2026; Xu et al., 2026b).
Such scores are cheap, but what matters for a robot policy is closed-loop task success, and the two do not agree in general (Xu et al., 2026a).
They also score one group at a time, whereas the effect of quantizing a group depends on the precision of the others.
For example, two groups of the π0.5\pi_{0.5} action head cost 1.0 and 5.5 success points when quantized alone and 97.5 points together.
Selecting the allocation from task success itself would capture both effects, but closed-loop evaluation is costly, and this problem remains underexplored.

To fill this knowledge gap, we propose QbD-VLA, which selects weight and activation bit widths from closed-loop task success at a bounded cost.
Starting from full precision, it lowers one group by one level at a time. Each candidate is evaluated in simulation with the other groups at their current bit widths, for one to three batches of one episode per task. A sequential test on the Wilson
bounds of the success estimate keeps the move only if the estimate stays above a floor set compared with the full-precision policy.
The allocation ends when no move passes.
On four policies, QbD-VLA finds allocations with nominal weight bit widths of 4.00 to 4.16 and activation bit widths of 4.47 to 5.94.
On π0.5\pi_{0.5} (Physical Intelligence et al., 2025), OpenVLA-OFT (Kim et al., 2025), and X-VLA (Zheng et al., 2025), uniform W4A4 yields 0% success, whereas the selected allocations reach 98.5%, 97.5%, and 97.0% against 99.0%, 100.0%, and 97.0% at full precision on LIBERO benchmark (Liu et al., 2023).
At the same time, allocations chosen by action error, activation kurtosis,
or reconstruction error at the same cost reach 27.5%, 0.0%, and 52.0% on π0.5\pi_{0.5}.
A factorial experiment shows why: lowering the π0.5\pi_{0.5} action-expert MLP from A6 to A4 costs 23.5 points when three other groups are at A6 and 0.5 points when they are at A4.
Across all four LIBERO suites, the allocations
stay within 5 points of full precision on average.
On SIMPLER (Li et al., 2024), the best allocation reaches 66.8% against 64.8% for uniform W4A6.
On a Franka Research 3 robot arm, the frozen allocation succeeds on 13 of 30 layouts for X-VLA against 11 for full precision, but on none of six layouts for π0.5\pi_{0.5}, where full precision succeeds on all six.
Task success is therefore a practical selection criterion for mixed-precision VLA quantization at a few hundred simulation episodes, while success in simulation does not guarantee execution on hardware.
Our contributions are the following:

We propose QbD-VLA, which selects bit widths for VLA models from closed-loop task success, evaluates each candidate within the current mixed-precision configuration, and bounds the simulation cost with a sequential test.

We conduct an evaluation on four VLA policies and all four LIBERO suites against uniform quantization, sensitivity-based allocators, a two-stage allocator, and released VLA quantization methods under the same settings.

We analyze why sensitivity-based allocation fails on these policies and test the transfer of simulation-selected allocations to a real robot with two fine-tuned policies.

1. We propose QbD-VLA, which selects bit widths for VLA models from closed-loop task success, evaluates each candidate within the current mixed-precision configuration, and bounds the simulation cost with a sequential test.

2. We conduct an evaluation on four VLA policies and all four LIBERO suites against uniform quantization, sensitivity-based allocators, a two-stage allocator, and released VLA quantization methods under the same settings.

3. We analyze why sensitivity-based allocation fails on these policies and test the transfer of simulation-selected allocations to a real robot with two fine-tuned policies.
