title: Explore Where It Matters: Targeted Exploration for Efficient Rover Adaptation
authors: Jacob Levy,Arthur Bouton,Tristan D. Hassler,Hari Nayar,David Fridovich-Keil
abstract: Future planetary rovers will traverse steep, deformable terrain where slip, sinkage, and terrain deformation can threaten mobility. Although simulation can capture some wheel-soil effects, unmodeled deformable-terrain phenomena create sim-to-real gaps requiring deployment-time adaptation. Yet, rover operations leave little room for extensive trial-and-error. We introduce TERRA (Targeted Exploration for Reward-Relevant Adaptation), an online adaptation framework that efficiently seeks deployment data exposing task-relevant model errors and corrects them. TERRA adapts a simulation-trained world model with a reward-weighted prediction loss and trains a loss predictor to estimate where future performance-relevant errors are likely to occur, using this signal to guide exploration during MPC. In simulation, TERRA reaches approximately 90% slope-climbing success within five trials under severe out-of-distribution pretraining conditions, outperforming exploration baselines in reward, completion time, and energy to first success. On the ERNEST rover, TERRA recovers coordinated active-suspension locomotion on a deformable Mars-simulant slope within three to five real-world trials. Project website: https://terra-explore.github.io
introduction:
Future Mars and lunar rover missions are increasingly motivated by science targets in steeper, rougher, and more deformable terrain than previous missions traversed. On Mars, compelling sites tied to habitability, geology, and climate history include mid-latitude regions with steep slope exposures [1, 2, 3], while on the Moon, permanently shadowed regions within steep-walled polar craters may host near-surface water ice with scientific and resource value [4, 5, 6]. These terrains may be covered by loose granular regolith, for which steep slopes can amplify wheel slip and sinkage, increasing the risk of entrapment [7]. Such hazards have already affected rover operations: Opportunity suffered substantial slip and sinkage while traversing sandy terrain toward Endeavour Crater [8], while Spirit became permanently immobilized in weak soil at Troy, ending the mission [9].

The ERNEST rover (Fig. 1) is a 75 kg75\text{\,}\mathrm{kg}, four-wheeled platform developed to study and address these mobility challenges [10]. It features a two degree-of-freedom (DoF) Active Gimbal Suspension (AGS) connecting the front bogie to the main chassis. This mechanism has two collocated revolute joints that are actively controlled: a yaw joint that rotates the bogie about a vertical axis relative to the chassis, and a roll joint that rotates it about the bogie’s longitudinal axis (Fig. 2). Together, these joints enable steering, wheel reconfiguration, active load redistribution, and wheel lifting. Through coordinated actuation, ERNEST can execute crawling-like locomotion: the roll joint alternately shifts load to create anchoring wheels, while the yaw joint repositions the bogie to pull the chassis forward, enabling traversal of soft, steep slopes that can immobilize passive-suspension rovers.

However, effectively using these additional DoFs is challenging because successful locomotion depends on appropriate coordination of the suspension under complex, terrain-dependent wheel-soil interaction. Reinforcement learning (RL) is a natural framework for discovering such strategies in contact-rich systems [10, 11, 12, 13, 14]. Yet, because large-scale real-world trial-and-error is infeasible for planetary rovers, policy learning must rely predominantly on simulation. This creates a critical sim-to-real gap: classical terramechanics models capture basic wheel-soil effects such as slip and sinkage, but not soil yielding, flow, excavation, and the resulting terrain deformation during aggressive maneuvers [15, 16, 17]. For example, they cannot capture failure modes in which the rover digs itself into a rut. These effects can substantially alter rover mobility, but high-fidelity simulators that resolve them remain computationally prohibitive for RL-scale training [18, 19, 20, 21]. Consequently, policies trained in simulation inevitably face unmodeled dynamics when deployed in real environments, even when those environments are terrestrial Mars or lunar analogs.

Planetary rovers with articulated mobility mechanisms therefore require not only simulation-trained locomotion strategies, but also mechanisms for rapid deployment-time adaptation to out-of-distribution terrain dynamics at the target site. This adaptation must occur onboard and be highly efficient: rover surface operations are constrained by limited energy, communication delays, bandwidth restrictions, and operational planning workflows, leaving little room for prolonged trial-and-error or human-in-the-loop iteration [22, 23, 24, 25]. Accordingly, the challenge is not merely to collect more data, but to collect the right data: in steep, deformable terrain, not all sources of uncertainty matter equally for control, and the most important ones directly determine whether the rover makes progress or becomes entrapped. In this work, we ask: how can online adaptation and exploration be coordinated so that limited real-world interaction yields the greatest improvement in rover mobility on previously unseen terrain?

To answer this question, we build on the paradigm of using a simulation-trained world model for real-time planning and adapting it to the deployment environment, rather than direct policy finetuning [26]. Our key idea is that adaptation should be guided by control relevance, not prediction error alone. We introduce TERRA (Targeted Exploration for Reward-Relevant Adaptation), a performance-aware online adaptation framework for coordinating exploration and model updates under deployment-time dynamics shift. TERRA uses a reward-weighted dynamics loss to prioritize model errors with the greatest impact on control performance, and trains a loss predictor to forecast where such errors are likely to occur over the same candidate action sequences evaluated by the planner. This prediction becomes a targeted exploration signal, directing data collection toward interactions where reducing model error should yield the largest task-performance gains. We validate TERRA through extensive simulated slope-climbing experiments and onboard hardware deployment on ERNEST, demonstrating rapid adaptation to severe out-of-distribution terrain conditions.

title: A Multi-Layer Navigation System for Smart Wheelchairs with a Limited Input Interface
authors: Piero Simonetto,Anna Polato,Francesco Pasti,Muhammad Rameez ur Rahman,Sebastiano Vascon,Nicola Bellotto,Emanuele Menegatti,Stefano Tortora,Luca Tonin
comment: . Presented at IROS 2026 (IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems); to appear in the conference proceedings
abstract: Smart wheelchairs are robotic devices that gather information from the surroundings and allow people to safely drive through various environments. They usually rely on the interpretation of high-level user’s intentions, typically decoded through  hri (hri) or  bmi (bmi). However, navigating in an unknown environment and accurately understanding user commands remain significant challenges. Misinterpretation of commands or the environment can lead to user frustration, distrust of the system, or even unsafe situations. In this paper, we present a novel  mlns (mlns) for a smart wheelchair that enables navigation in unknown environments while interpreting and safely contextualizing user’s intentions even in the case of limited and faulty commands. The stack relies on a  apf+vs (apf+vs) method for obstacle detection that accounts for the wheelchair’s actual size, a  mpc (mpc) module for trajectory generation, and an open-vocabulary computer vision algorithm for target identification. Finally, a system based on  pq (pq) was implemented for target selection. We validated our system on a real smart wheelchair with experiments involving 10 participants without disabilities, including scenarios with faulty input interfaces. The results demonstrate the robustness and effectiveness of our system in real-world environments, proving its potential for practical applications in assistive technologies.
introduction:
at (at) refers to any device and software designed to maintain and improve the functional capabilities of an individual, enabling their inclusion and participation in all areas of society. Recently, several studies have focused on the development of intelligent powered wheelchairs and on implementing appropriate hri to enable people with severe motor or cognitive disabilities to control these systems [1, 2, 3].

Researchers have focused on hardware and software solutions that provide alternative interfaces to the traditional joystick and that allow end-users to communicate their intentions to the navigation system without using their upper-limbs. The most common approaches rely on deep learning techniques for detecting and interpreting user commands—e.g., hand gestures [4, 5], eye movement [6], and voice commands [7]. Other methods are based on the use of a joystick controlled by the lips [8], tongue [9], or head-neck [10]. Recently, similar commands have been generated by decoding brain activity using bmi [2].

Despite these advances, the integration of robotics in the assistive technology field is still at its infancy. Indeed, many solutions remain at the research or early validation stage, often demonstrating incremental improvements under controlled laboratory conditions. Their robustness and generalizability in real-world assistive scenarios are still limited. In practice, hri for at are highly sensitive to noise, environmental variability, sensor occlusions, and user-specific motor and cognitive fluctuations. As a consequence, they typically support discrete, high-level commands (e.g., left, right, stop, move) rather than continuous, intention-rich control signals. Although such abstractions simplify command decoding, they strongly constrain the interpretation of user intent. This limitation becomes particularly critical in navigation tasks involving close interaction with objects or people, where fine-grained adjustments, continuous modulation, and context awareness are required. In these situations, even small misclassifications or latency-induced errors may propagate into large trajectory deviations, reducing usability and increasing cognitive load. Therefore, understanding how to integrate such a limited input interface in the control of at devices is not merely a performance optimization, but a prerequisite for effective navigation.

Furthermore, safety is a priority in these applications. Indeed, over the last few decades, many obstacle avoidance algorithms for smart wheelchairs have been evaluated. Among these,  apf (apf) have gained particular attention due to the ability to generate smooth trajectories and the straightforward implementation where attractive and repulsive forces are combined to guide the robot away from obstacles while steering it toward free spaces [11].

In this work, we introduce a novel semi-autonomous navigation system for smart wheelchairs to operate in unknown environments with limited user input while maintaining adaptability and safety. The proposed architecture combines reactive obstacle avoidance, predictive trajectory planning, and computer vision algorithms for target identification within a framework designed for assistive mobility.

The remainder of the paper is structured as follows. Section II reviews related works, identifies the limitation of current approaches, and defines the aim of this research. Section III presents the assistive platform and the developed navigation system, as well as the experimental protocol. Section IV reports the results of the experiments followed by discussion, future work, and conclusions in Sections V-VI.

title: Force-Driven Hook Disassembly via Constraint-Aware Object-Centric Reinforcement Learning
authors: Nadeen Elhadad,Takuya Kiyokawa,Kensuke Harada
abstract: This work was motivated by the need to automate disassembly of end-of-life products such as outdoor air-conditioning units for material recovery and reuse. Their hook-type connections are hidden inside the housing and vary between units, preventing camera-based systems and pre-programmed routines from determining which direction a panel should be pulled without breaking it.
introduction:
Electronic waste (e-waste) refers to any discarded device that operates using a plug or battery. Driven by rapid technological advancement, increased consumption, and shorter product lifespans, global e-waste generation increased by 82% between 2010 and 2022. In 2022 alone, e-waste reached 62 million tonnes and is projected to rise further to approximately 82 million tonnes by 2030 [1].

To address this challenge, increasing efforts have been directed toward remanufacturing to enable the recovery of materials from end-of-life (EoL) products for reuse in new production cycles, thereby supporting sustainable manufacturing practices.
To mitigate labor shortages, automation and human-robot collaboration of disassembly processes has become increasingly important[2]. In this context, the robotic disassembly of tightly constrained connections, such as internal hook mechanisms with unseen geometries, is essential for effective remanufacturing.

As a representative case study, we consider the front cover of the commercial outdoor air-conditioning unit in Fig. 1. The cover is retained by two dissimilar constraint types: two downward hooks on one side and two lip-style fasteners on the opposite side. This mixed fastening configuration introduces distinct geometric constraints on the disassembly motion, motivating its treatment as a constraint-aware manipulation problem. Furthermore, the cover exhibits mild structural compliance, allowing local elastic deformation under load. Consequently, the feasible extraction path depends on the interaction between the cover’s elastic deformation and the coupled constraint mechanisms rather than a single fixed geometric direction. The combined actions of these two constraint types produce a coupled multi-stage disassembly process in which releasing one set of constraints depends on the motion permitted by the other.
Since the exact material properties of end-of-life products are not known a priori, the feasible disassembly direction cannot be reliably derived from CAD geometry alone. This motivates a force-driven approach that infers feasible extraction directions from real-time contact interaction rather than relying on a fixed, precomputed motion primitive.

More generally, robotic assembly and disassembly remain challenging due to contact-rich interactions and variability in part geometry, pose, and surrounding environments, a difficulty that continues to motivate dedicated contact-rich manipulation frameworks [3, 4, 5]. Furthermore, end-of-life products often exhibit wear, deformation, and structural irregularities that deviate from their nominal CAD models, limiting the reliability of purely model-based approaches [6, 7], an issue compounded by geometry preprocessing pipelines that can fail to preserve fine-grained features [8] such as hooks. In addition, many critical connections are occluded within assemblies, reducing the effectiveness of vision-based perception, motivating recent force and tactile-based alternatives that recover task-relevant contact information under occlusion [9, 10, 11].

Existing methods typically rely on explicit geometric reasoning or predefined motion primitives to guide disassembly. Although effective in structured settings, these approaches struggle to capture the complex and evolving constraints present in tightly coupled assemblies, particularly when small but critical features or contact interactions are difficult to model accurately.
In contrast, this work leverages contact-rich interaction as a source of informative sensory feedback rather than a challenge to avoid. In tightly constrained assemblies, contact forces implicitly encode information about feasible motion directions and underlying structural constraints as illustrated in Fig. 2. By incorporating this feedback into a reinforcement learning framework, the proposed method learns continuous disassembly policies that infer feasible extraction strategies directly from interaction, without requiring predefined joint types or explicit geometric sequences.

Industrial disassembly of such products therefore requires addressing three challenges: (1) inferring feasible disassembly directions under unknown and partially observable constraints, (2) exploiting contact interactions to achieve stable and non-destructive manipulation, and (3) learning policies that generalize across diverse products without product-specific modeling or reconfiguration.

To address (1) and (2), we learn extraction behavior from contact forces in a physics-based simulation that provides rich contact feedback while avoiding repeated exploratory contact that EoL parts cannot sustain. To address (3), the policy is trained on a simplified peg-in-hole pair in a robot agnostic, object centric environment, so that it learns a force following behavior based on interaction dynamics rather than product-specific geometry or a particular robot. However, instantaneous contact force signals are inherently noisy and locally ambiguous, particularly for multi-stage joints where the feasible axis changes as the connection transitions between constraint states. A policy conditioned only on momentary force feedback can therefore act inconsistently, producing jitter and redundant exploratory motion (quantified in Section V via direction reversals and path efficiency). To address this, we couple the policy with a particle filter (PF) belief estimator that integrates contact observations over time into a persistent belief over the feasible axis, giving the policy a temporally consistent signal to condition its actions on, rather than merely reacting to instantaneous force readings. In this work, we refer to the feasible axis as the joint axis for consistency with previous work.

The contributions of this paper are twofold:

We propose a constraint-aware, object-centric RL framework for force-driven hook disassembly, trained on a simplified peg-in-hole pair in a robot-agnostic simulation environment, that transfers zero-shot to a physical robot and to unseen sequential constraint structures without product-specific models or demonstrations.

To address the noise and local ambiguity of instantaneous force feedback, we introduce a particle filter-based belief over the feasible extraction direction, integrated into the RL policy through observation augmentation and reward shaping. Across four real-world tasks, the belief-augmented policy achieves the highest path efficiency on every task and raises the success rate on a real EoL air-conditioning cover with occluded, multi-stage hook-and-lip constraints from 45%45\% to 75%75\%.

Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed constraint-aware learning approach enables efficient and non-destructive disassembly of complex hook-type connections while reducing reliance on detailed geometric modeling and task-specific planning. Moreover, because training relies on a generic peg-in-hole model, the framework avoids the need for high-fidelity, watertight assembly models during training in physics engines, thereby significantly reducing modeling effort and mitigating errors introduced by geometric decomposition.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section II reviews related work and identifies assumptions of existing approaches that EoL disassembly violates. Section III presents the framework. Section IV describes the experimental design, implementation, and metrics, and Section V reports results. Section VI discusses failure modes, limitations, and future work, and Section VII concludes this work.

title: OmniQuad: a Wheeled-Legged Hybrid Robot with Omnidirectional Wheels
authors: Francesco Iotti,Alok Ranjan,Franco Angelini,Manolo Garabini
abstract: Combining wheeled and legged locomotion within a single robotic platform offers the potential to harness the advantages of both systems. The development of such hybrid systems remains an active area of research. While legged robots exhibit remarkable adaptability for traversing uneven and rugged terrains, their relatively low speed limits their practicality in indoor environments. Conversely, wheeled robots demonstrate higher efficiency on flat surfaces but often encounter difficulties when navigating obstacles such as steps. This paper introduces OmniQuad, a novel hybrid robot that integrates mecanum wheels with legged locomotion to exploit the benefits of both modalities. Mecanum wheels provide omnidirectional mobility, enhancing the robot’s manoeuvrability by enabling agile movement in confined spaces and the ability to maintain a consistent orientation during task execution. In this work, we first present the design of a custom wheeled-foot featuring mecanum wheels. Subsequently, we describe the complete robot assembly, comprising these wheeled feet and EM-Act actuators. Finally, we detail the control scheme developed to govern the OmniQuad and evaluate its performance through experimental trials conducted in both indoor and outdoor environments.
introduction:
The demand for mobile robots is substantial across diverse applications in logistics, cleaning, search and rescue, and environmental monitoring [1]. Although the designs of these robots differ from one another, they are still limited in their ability to navigate tight spaces and interact with humans and other robots due to their lack of human-like locomotion capabilities.

Wheeled mobile robots, owing to their simple design and implementation, are extensively used in these settings. Their efficacy ensues from the ease of achieving high speeds and executing movements with good efficiency. These machines were originally designed for planetary exploration [2, 3], but in recent years, they have also been utilized in warehouse work [4] and homes. Robots equipped with conventional wheels face a significant limitation in manoeuvrability due to their restricted movement capabilities. These robots are only able to move along a direction that is perpendicular to the centre axis of the wheels, which makes it difficult for them to navigate through tight spaces or turn quickly [5].

Various types of wheels have been developed to facilitate omnidirectional movement, including omni wheels and mecanum wheels. Recent years have seen the integration of omni wheels in different typologies of robots, as referenced in works such as [6, 7]. These wheels are distinctively mounted at a 45-degree angle concerning their fore axis, setting them apart from other wheel types. Their major problems are the low traction and stability. In addition, they are also susceptible to vibrations and slippage. In [8], they reduce these kinds of issues by designing a specific suspension system in a four-wheeled omni-wheelchair.

Mecanum wheels [9] consist of rollers oriented at a 45-degree angle to the fore axis. Their utilization is well-suited for scenarios necessitating high stability and manoeuvrability [10, 11]. Additionally, their capacity to accommodate high load capacities makes them versatile across diverse application domains, such as factories, warehouses and even hospitals, as highlighted in [12, 13]. It is essential to note that while omnidirectional wheels offer advantages, they often generate substantial friction forces due to pronounced vibrations during motion. This can result in slippage, impacting overall efficiency during both forward and lateral movements. Attempts to mitigate these challenges include incorporating springs into wheel designs, as addressed in [14]. Moreover, the optimal performance of these wheels is typically observed in flat terrain scenarios. Novel designs for mecanum wheels have been proposed, aiming to optimize motion in rough terrain [15], whereas in [16] they proposed a novel tracked omnidirectional vehicle to achieve omnidirectional motion on challenging terrains. An inherent limitation of wheeled locomotion lies in the inability of such robots to surmount obstacles, a challenge prevalent in both natural and indoor environments, particularly when encountering steps or uneven terrains.

Quadrupedal robots emerge as more adept solutions for rugged terrains due to their ability to overcome obstacles through climbing or jumping manoeuvres [17, 18, 19]. The major examples of legged robots, also known as quadrupedal robots, are Spot [20], ANYmal [21], Mini Cheetah [22], HyQ [23], Oncilla [24] and Cheeta-cub [25]. However, in some scenarios, their speed may be slower compared to wheeled robots, and their operational efficiency may fall short [26].
Choosing the best locomotion system can be a challenging task. To overcome this, hybrid locomoted robots are being developed to combine the benefits of two different locomotion systems. Currently, there are various types of wheeled-legged hybrid robots [27] that offer the efficiency of wheeled locomotion and the ability to navigate through rough terrains and climb over obstacles.
Vehicles with omnidirectional wheels and legged systems are often viewed as fundamentally distinct due to their specialized use in different scenarios. Designing a system that seamlessly integrates vehicles with omnidirectional wheels and legged systems poses a complex challenge. It entails not only the mechanical merging of the two components but also the development of a control system that accommodates their unique operational environments. The goal is to create a robot that harnesses the unique advantages of both technologies, enabling it to excel in a diverse array of scenarios beyond the capabilities of individual systems. By combining wheeled and legged locomotion, this integrated approach allows the robot to surpass the performance limitations of conventional single-mode systems across diverse and demanding environments. Specifically, the robot could achieve exceptional maneuverability within structured environments, such as warehouses, factories, or urban infrastructures, where omnidirectional wheels provide rapid, precise positioning and the ability to maintain a consistent orientation, beneficial for operations like inventory handling or inspection tasks. Furthermore, the incorporation of legged locomotion extends the robot’s capabilities to negotiate uneven terrains, climb stairs or obstacles, and traverse confined spaces, tasks that are typically challenging for traditional wheeled vehicles. The robot’s legs also allow it to dynamically adjust its height, facilitating passage beneath obstacles or through low-clearance areas, enhancing its overall operational versatility.

The contributions of this paper are as follows: (i) Mechanical design of an Omniwheeled foot that incorporates a motor and a gearbox within the assembly; (ii) a robotic system called OmniQuad, as shown in Fig. 1, which integrates both mecanum wheels and legs; (iii) a control system that enables the use of both legs and omnidirectional wheels; and (iv) an evaluation of the capabilities of the developed robot through a series of tasks in different environments. These tasks focused on navigating obstacles using various methods, such as passing beneath or scaling over them, taking advantage of hybrid locomotion. The robot’s omnidirectional movement capabilities were also examined through tasks requiring fixed orientation while performing various manoeuvres. In outdoor environments, the robot followed a grid-patterned path to simulate an environmental survey.

title: Skeleton-Guided Geometry-Aware Auto-Labeling for Robotic Grasping: From 4-DoF Learning to 6-DoF Execution
authors: Ali Sabzejou,Farbod Azimmohseni,Mehdi Tale Masouleh,Ahmad Kalhor
comment: Published in The International Journal of Robotics Research (IJRR), OnlineFirst, September 2026
abstract:
Robotic grasping relies on large manually annotated datasets, which are costly to create. This work introduces a novel algorithm for generating two-finger grasp keypoints based on straight skeletons, identifying high-potential regions for stable and feasible grasp pose estimation. An automated pipeline is developed to perform grasp auto-labeling without human intervention, facilitating large-scale annotation with consistent quality. Furthermore, an architecture for 4-DoF grasping, named the Skeleton-based Generative Grasp Convolutional Neural Network (SkelGG-CNN), is introduced, which incorporates skeleton-based guidance during training to directly learn geometric grasping features.
Finally, the developed auto-labeling is extended to 6-DoF grasping and applied directly to point clouds via a generalized quasi-3D skeletonization algorithm.
Evaluations demonstrate that SkelGG-CNN achieves accuracies of 95.42%, 96.55%, and 97.1% on the Jacquard V1, Jacquard V2, and Cornell benchmarks, respectively, using 4-DoF auto-generated labels. On GraspNet, the 6-DoF auto-labeling algorithm yields an average precision of 18.33 on the novel split, comparable to state-of-the-art model-based approaches. In simulation, the generalized 6-DoF auto-labeling method yields success rates of 98.4% on the Dex-Net test set and 89.1% on EGAD!. Real-world experiments on a Delta parallel robot confirm 97.4% success on single household objects and 95.0% in cluttered scenes, outperforming state-of-the-art methods without domain adaptation. Experiments show that the framework’s 4-DoF pipeline is adaptable across environments, generating grasp annotations that approximate human-level precision, enabling efficient training of lightweight models like SkelGG-CNN on small datasets for real-world deployment. Additionally, the generalized 6-DoF auto-labeling algorithm extends this automation to point clouds, providing scalable, geometry-aware annotations for cluttered 3D scenes.
Source code and videos are available at https://github.com/Farbod82/SkelGGCNN.
introduction:
Robotic manipulation has been a significant area of research, with the task of grasping objects emerging as one of the most widely studied topics in recent decades.
Although grasping appears simple to humans, it remains a difficult task for robots, and various approaches have been explored to address it.
The difficulty lies in determining appropriate grasp poses for a diverse range of objects, each differing in geometry, gripping force requirements, and weight distribution.
These factors significantly influence how robotic systems effectively grasp objects from specific configurations, making the task highly complex and context-dependent.
In early studies, analytical methods were the primary tools used to determine grasp poses, focusing on geometric approaches to analyze the structure and properties of objects.
These methods typically relied on mathematical models and physical principles, such as force closure and friction modeling, to compute stable and reliable grasp configurations Bohg et al. (2013).
While effective for simple and well-defined objects, these techniques often struggle in complex or unknown scenarios.
Additionally, these methods tend to be computationally intensive and lack the ability to generalize effectively in dynamic environments.

The emergence of deep neural networks and data-driven methods in computer vision has significantly advanced the ability to tackle the complex challenges of robotic grasping Newbury et al. (2023).
By leveraging image processing techniques originally developed for computer vision, grasping models have become increasingly robust, achieving strong performance in unfamiliar environments and real-world applications.
With the help of large-scale grasping datasets, these models can generalize effectively to handle objects with diverse shapes, physical properties, and environmental conditions, resulting in enhanced reliability in grasping tasks.
However, despite the impressive capabilities of these models, significant challenges persist.
One of the most critical issues is the heavy reliance of these data-driven methods on annotated datasets for training.
Creating these datasets often requires substantial human effort, involving extensive manual labeling of grasping points.
This dependence on extensive labeled data not only increases development costs but also limits the adaptability of these models to new, unforeseen tasks or environments where labeled data may be scarce or unavailable Wang et al. (2021a); Fang et al. (2020).
Hybrid methods that combine analytical grasp pose estimation with learning-based refinement have been explored extensively in prior research.
These methods mostly rely on random sampling methods for initial grasp generation, which requires extensive filtering to acquire high-quality grasp data Liang et al. (2019); Mousavian et al. (2019); Gualtieri et al. (2016).

This work proposes a comprehensive framework for robotic grasping, integrating a novel grasp pose estimation algorithm, an automated data pipeline, and a 4-DoF learning approach via the Skeleton-Based Generative Grasp Convolutional Neural Network (SkelGG-CNN) model to deliver an efficient and adaptable solution, alongside a generalization of the auto-labeling algorithm for 6-DoF grasp generation.
The skeleton-based grasp generation algorithm developed in this work is an accurate grasp generation method that eliminates the need for a grasp filtering phase.
Next, the SkelGG-CNN model is introduced as an innovative enhancement to generative grasping approaches.
This new architecture addresses several limitations of the widely used existing models, improving performance and robustness in grasp pose prediction, and thereby making the method more effective for real-world applications.
Figure 1 illustrates the model’s output alongside the predicted grasps for a real-world scene, highlighting its practical effectiveness.

The proposed framework is designed as a unified integration of geometry-driven grasp generation and data-driven learning, rather than treating these components as independent contributions.
Instead of presenting a standalone analytical or purely learning-based method, the framework emphasizes the synergy between automatic data generation and geometry-aware learning.
In particular, the auto-labeling algorithm serves as the foundation of the learning process by generating structured and physically meaningful grasp annotations, while the SkelGG-CNN model leverages these representations to learn robust 4-DoF grasp prediction strategies.
This design is motivated by the observation that data availability remains a primary bottleneck in learning-based grasping methods. By embedding geometric priors directly into both the data generation and learning stages, the framework bridges the gap between analytical and data-driven approaches, enabling scalable dataset creation while maintaining compatibility with modern learning paradigms.

As illustrated in Figure 2, the framework operates as a fully automated pipeline within a simulation environment, enabling large-scale generation of annotated grasp datasets without human intervention.
The auto-labeling algorithm produces structured grasp annotations that directly support the training of the SkelGG-CNN model, ensuring consistent and scalable dataset creation while maintaining compatibility with modern learning-based methods.

As a final addition, the auto-labeling pipeline is extended to operate on point cloud data, enabling more comprehensive annotation of 3D grasping scenarios and further enhancing the framework’s applicability to real-world robotic manipulation.
To process the complex and inherently partial point clouds efficiently, this 6-DoF algorithmic extension employs a generalized quasi-3D approach. Here, quasi-3D refers to a stacked planar strategy that partitions the point cloud into localized horizontal cross sections to apply planar skeletonization.
The main contributions of this work can be outlined as follows:

Introduced a robust and efficient grasp pose estimation algorithm that leverages the geometric skeleton of objects to generate accurate grasp pairs.

Developed a fully automated pipeline capable of simultaneously collecting and labeling data without human supervision, effectively addressing the challenge of manual data collection.

Proposed SkelGG-CNN, a novel generative model for 4-DoF grasp prediction that utilizes geometric features extracted from the skeleton creation algorithm, enhancing the robustness and quality of predicted grasps compared to state-of-the-art grasping methods.

Trained the model with a significantly smaller dataset, demonstrating the efficiency of geometry-aware learning techniques in learning grasp strategies.

Extended the auto-labeling pipeline to work with point clouds using a generalized version of the 2D auto-labeling algorithm, which utilizes a quasi-3D algorithm to generate 6-DoF grasp configurations, showing the capabilities of the skeletonization method in other input modalities.

This paper extends the skeleton-based grasp keypoint generation method proposed in Sabzejou et al. (2023).
The previous work lacked a comprehensive pipeline for grasp annotation and relied on global regions, pairing points from different grasp regions together, which often resulted in failure cases. As a result, the algorithm was computationally expensive and unsuitable for large-scale grasp annotation.

In contrast, the skeleton-based approach presented here has been significantly improved to become a more accurate and efficient algorithm, capable of achieving real-time performance within the automatic pipeline.
This efficiency arises from restricting the pairing algorithm to local point candidates around each skeleton node rather than considering global regions.

Beyond algorithmic improvements, this work introduces the SkelGG-CNN model, which adds a new output head to traditional generative grasping methods.
By leveraging skeleton-based grasping regions, the model enables geometry-aware learning and robust generalization.
This integration of analytical methods with data-driven learning constitutes one of the main contributions of this paper.

Finally, in the mentioned paper, no comprehensive evaluations were conducted, and the experiments were limited to simulation-based grasping tests on a small number of simple objects.
Moreover, the experiments were constrained to 4-DoF grasping, and the generalization of the auto-labeling algorithm was not discussed in the original paper.

Beyond these differences from the earlier work, Table 1 situates the proposed framework among recent grasping approaches by summarizing their dataset-generation capabilities, reported benchmark coverage, cluttered-scene evaluation, and code availability.

1. Introduced a robust and efficient grasp pose estimation algorithm that leverages the geometric skeleton of objects to generate accurate grasp pairs.

2. Developed a fully automated pipeline capable of simultaneously collecting and labeling data without human supervision, effectively addressing the challenge of manual data collection.

3. Proposed SkelGG-CNN, a novel generative model for 4-DoF grasp prediction that utilizes geometric features extracted from the skeleton creation algorithm, enhancing the robustness and quality of predicted grasps compared to state-of-the-art grasping methods.

4. Trained the model with a significantly smaller dataset, demonstrating the efficiency of geometry-aware learning techniques in learning grasp strategies.

5. Extended the auto-labeling pipeline to work with point clouds using a generalized version of the 2D auto-labeling algorithm, which utilizes a quasi-3D algorithm to generate 6-DoF grasp configurations, showing the capabilities of the skeletonization method in other input modalities.

title: When "No Worries" Went Wrong: HRI Lessons for Foundation-Model Robots
authors: Eliahu Khalastchi(The College of Management Academic Studies)
comment: . Submitted to IEEE Robotics & Automation Magazine
abstract: When a person declined our robot’s invitation to play, Alice turned her shoulder away and said “No worries, it’s all good.” Only after a brief pause did she drive off. The words and gestures were plausible but their order changed the message. In another episode, Alice informed a host that his visitor had arrived—while the visitor stood right beside him. Both came from a three-year ROS 2 HRI consortium that integrated large language and vision models as they emerged. Today’s foundation models give robots broader capabilities to perceive their surroundings, reason about situations and generate behavior. Yet capability alone does not ensure that a changed situation shapes the action that reaches a person. Evidence may never be acquired, or a purpose or constraint may fail to survive planning and execution. A system may even report Success when an action no longer serves its intended purpose. Drawing on the consortium’s engineering experience, we develop five design lessons about attention, knowledge, commitments, embodied timing and action authority. We then introduce TRACE, a lightweight review that changes one interaction premise, follows it to a decision or enforcement boundary, and produces an actionable architecture finding. A bounded analysis of a published LLM-generated behavior-tree system illustrates how an available clarification mechanism can go unused. The engineering lesson is to preserve accountability boundaries, not the computational pipelines that once exposed them.
introduction:
A person was looking at his phone when Alice, our office robot, cheerfully invited him to play a game. “Maybe later,” he replied. Alice pivoted away, presenting him with her “shoulder.” Then she stopped and, with impeccable verbal composure, declared “No worries, it’s all good.” She waited another beat before driving away. The pause and turned posture made the reassurance sound remarkably like wounded pride. We had not programmed her to sulk (Fig. 1).

The explanation was engineering. Originally, JSON-configured behaviors sequenced the reply before the disengagement gesture. An LLM made responses more natural and context-sensitive but added generation latency, particularly when run locally. We allowed speech preparation and movement to proceed asynchronously to avoid an awkward wait. The orientation change then completed before the words were spoken, even though Alice did not drive away until afterward. The separate components behaved as programmed; their ordering made the overall interaction convey something else.

An upgraded model can improve a component while changing the social effect of the complete robot. Current foundation models may generate subtler responses and richer movement, yet the executor, scheduler or tool boundary can still determine which effect reaches a person first—or whether the relevant observation is gathered at all. Foundation models expand and relocate robot capabilities; appropriate interaction still depends on acquiring the right evidence and making purpose and constraints actionable at the point of effect. We investigate both breaks: a fact that never becomes usable evidence, and information that cannot change execution when it matters.

title: CSO: Refining Robotic Policies via Skill Distribution Alignment and Skill-Grained Optimization
authors: Zhiyuan Xiang,Xiang Deng,Wanjie Tao,Xu Chen,Zhao Jielun,Weili Guan
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. including appendices and checklist
abstract: Discretizing continuous actions into discrete skills using methods like VQ-VAE has emerged as a powerful paradigm for robotic manipulation. However, quantization errors yield a suboptimal distribution for the skill prior, degrading its performance. While reinforcement learning offers a path for refinement, its direct application faces unstable encoder updates and a granularity dilemma in importance sampling. To address these challenges, we introduce Cascaded Skills Optimization (CSO), a two-stage post-training framework. First, Rejection-Sampling Supervised Fine-tuning aligns the model’s observation-to-skill mapping with the distribution of successful online trajectories via supervised fine-tuning. Second, with the observation encoder frozen, Skills Policy Optimization computes an independent, clipped importance ratio for each complete skill, enabling stable and efficient updates. With a lightweight QueST-style policy, CSO raises overall LIBERO success from 80.1% to 97.5%, improves performance on RoboTwin2.0, and achieves 61.0% success across five physical single-arm tasks. Additional comparisons with FAST, discrete BEAST, and fixed-buffer IQL further validate the effectiveness of our two-stage post-training strategy.
introduction:
Modeling complex manipulation behaviors has long been a central problem in robotics [18, 9]. A promising direction is to learn structured action representations through Transformer-based architectures [3, 29]. Temporal action chunks provide useful abstractions for control [43]; skill-based approaches additionally map continuous trajectories into discrete latent representations [17]. A quantized autoencoder, such as a VQ-VAE [38, 13], learns a vocabulary of fundamental tokens. These tokens are then used to form "skills", which are reusable motion primitives represented as token sequences [28, 19]. This hierarchical framework simplifies the problem, enabling an autoregressive policy to tackle complex tasks by sequentially composing tokens to generate a skill [28].

However, while this discretization paradigm is powerful, policies trained purely via imitation learning (IL) with these discrete skills exhibit a notable limitation. The VQ-VAE’s discretization process introduces inherent quantization errors, meaning the skills are only approximations of the expert’s continuous actions [17]. These reconstruction errors compound with policy errors during online execution. On one hand, the inherent imprecision of the tokens that constitute a skill can cause the decoded action to fail the task. On the other hand, these quantization errors can accumulate over an episode, progressively pushing the agent into states outside the expert data distribution. This resulting distribution shift severely hinders the generalization of the IL-trained policy [15].

To overcome the limitations of the initial policy, a natural remedy is to refine it with online reinforcement learning (RL) [11, 22, 37]. However, directly applying RL to this setting presents several challenges. A primary issue is the unstable update of the observation encoder. Online data collection often yields an imbalanced mix of task outcomes (e.g., many successes on easy tasks, many failures on hard ones). This provides inconsistent gradient signals to the crucial observation encoder, leading to inefficient training and often requiring complex hybrid frameworks to stabilize [11, 6]. A second structural challenge arises from a mismatch between the unit of decision-making (a skill) and the unit of optimization (a token). Token-level methods apply a separate importance ratio to each generated token [34, 24], which treats the components of a jointly executed skill separately. Episode-level methods such as GSPO instead use one length-normalized ratio and a shared clipping decision for the complete sequence [44]. Robotic episodes exhibit length asymmetry: time-outs are often longer than successes. This motivates skill-level optimization, which assigns each complete skill its own ratio and clipping decision while sharing the terminal advantage. We compare token-, skill-, and episode-level optimization from the same R-SFT checkpoint.

To address these key challenges, we propose Cascaded Skills Optimization (CSO), a two-stage post-training framework. Our key insight is that effective refinement requires two steps: first, stabilizing the model on successful online data, and second, aligning the unit of optimization with the unit of decision-making. Specifically:
1) To address distributional shift and encoder instability, we introduce Rejection-Sampling Supervised Fine-tuning (R-SFT) for skill-based policy refinement. This stage aligns the model’s observation-to-skill mapping with the distribution of successful online trajectories via supervised fine-tuning, inspired by similar techniques in LLMs [40]. The encoder is then stabilized and frozen, providing a robust foundation for the subsequent RL stage and avoiding the inconsistent gradients of direct online fine-tuning.
2) To solve the granularity mismatch, we introduce the Skills Policy Optimization (SPO) algorithm. By computing and clipping an importance ratio for each complete skill, SPO aligns optimization with execution and enables stable, data-efficient policy improvement.

We validate our framework through extensive experiments on challenging manipulation benchmarks. In its lightweight instantiation, CSO demonstrates substantial improvements over its underlying imitation-learned policy, boosting the average success rate by 17.4 absolute percentage points across all four LIBERO suites [21]. We further validate the method on RoboTwin2.0 [5] and confirm its real-world applicability by successfully deploying the learned policy on a physical robot.

To summarize, our main contributions are:

To circumvent unstable encoder updates in direct reinforcement learning, we introduce R-SFT. This rejection-sampling fine-tuning stage first stabilizes the observation encoder on successful online trajectories to establish a robust foundation for policy optimization.

To resolve the granularity dilemma between internal tokens and complete trajectories, we propose SPO, a novel algorithm that performs stable and fine-grained policy optimization via skill-level importance sampling.

We design and validate CSO, a complete two-stage framework that systematically refines skill-based policies by decoupling representation stabilization from policy optimization, demonstrating substantial performance improvements on challenging benchmarks and real-world robotic tasks.

title: Proprioceptive Finger Force Estimation for Reliable Box Manipulation
authors: Junha Cha,Chanwoo Kim,Kisang Park,Yeoncheol Jang,Doyoung Kim,Seungmin Kim,Kyungjae Lee,Sungjoon Choi
abstract:
Reliable box manipulation requires successful placement without damage, which depends on maintaining sufficient contact force without excessive loading.
We hypothesize that per-finger force feedback improves manipulation reliability relative to open-loop finger commands.
To this end, we present Finger External-Force Estimation from Proprioceptive SignaLs (FEEL), an uncertainty-aware residual method that estimates per-finger external force magnitude from proprioceptive histories.
Our method combines a calibrated virtual-spring estimate with a residual distribution predicted by a Mixture Density Network (MDN) and requires no dedicated contact sensors during deployment.
The estimated force is used for continuous per-finger adaptation, while predictive uncertainty is evaluated as an empirical signal of ambiguity in proprioceptive force estimation.
Across ten fingers and contact forces spanning 0–20 N, our method achieves a mean RMSE of 0.251 N, reducing the error by 92.8% relative to the virtual spring and by 9.4% relative to an end-to-end MDN.
In box pick-and-place, force adaptation maintains task success at 10/10 and increases both damage-free outcomes and reliability from 7/10 to 10/10.
The project page is available at https://finger-force-estimation.pages.dev/.
introduction:
Box pick-and-place requires enough contact force to maintain a stable grasp without damaging the box.
This task is common in logistics and manufacturing, where robots handle packages with different physical properties [4].
Boxes with similar dimensions can differ in mass, contents, and structural strength.
These properties may be unknown before manipulation, so the same grasping motion can produce different outcomes across boxes.
Insufficient contact force can cause grasp or placement failure.
Excessive force can deform the box or damage its contents, leading to product loss and additional operating costs [5].
Reliable handling therefore requires successful placement without box damage.

Force feedback can help maintain a stable grasp while limiting excessive interaction force [6, 7].
Dedicated force and tactile sensors provide measurements at the contact surface [8].
However, integrating these sensors across multiple fingers requires additional hardware and calibration [8].
These requirements motivate estimating external forces from proprioceptive information already available from the robot [1, 2].
External forces influence how the fingers respond to motion commands.
Proprioceptive measurements of this response may therefore provide useful information for estimating the forces acting on each finger.
This approach can provide per-finger force feedback without dedicated contact sensors during deployment.

The central challenge is to obtain per-finger force estimates that support successful box manipulation without damage.
When a position-controlled finger contacts a box, it may move less than commanded.
The difference between commanded and measured joint positions may provide a useful signal for estimating the contact force.
A virtual-spring model estimates force from displacement using a calibrated stiffness [13].
However, unobserved contact locations can make the relationship between joint responses and interaction forces difficult to capture with a fixed analytical model.
This motivates learning a residual correction to the model-based force estimate from proprioceptive histories.

We hypothesize that per-finger force feedback improves manipulation reliability relative to open-loop finger commands.
To this end, we present Finger External-Force Estimation from Proprioceptive SignaLs (FEEL), an uncertainty-aware method that estimates per-finger external force magnitude by correcting a calibrated virtual-spring estimate with a residual distribution learned from proprioceptive histories.
We collect real-robot data pairing proprioceptive histories with reference force magnitudes measured by a force/torque (F/T) sensor to train the residual model.
The corrected force estimate provides continuous per-finger feedback without dedicated contact sensors during deployment.
The residual distribution also provides predictive uncertainty, which we examine as an empirical signal of ambiguity when force variations are weakly reflected in proprioceptive histories.
We evaluate force-estimation accuracy, the contribution of force adaptation to reliable box pick-and-place, and whether predictive uncertainty reflects this ambiguity.

The main contributions of this paper are twofold: 1) an uncertainty-aware residual method that estimates per-finger external force magnitude from proprioception for reliable box manipulation; and 2) a real-robot evaluation comparing accuracy against virtual-spring and end-to-end MDN baselines, assessing uncertainty as a signal of proprioceptive ambiguity, and testing whether force adaptation reduces box damage while maintaining task success relative to open-loop finger commands.
We used approximately 120 boxes across the real-robot manipulation experiments.

title: What Should a Navigator Remember? Spatiotemporal Memory for Zero-Shot Vision-Language Navigation
authors: Yuhang Peng,Zhikai Wang,Ziyi Wang,Jiaru Zhong,Xiaoji Zheng,Jingzhi Huang,Yi Wang,Jiangtao Gong
abstract: Zero-shot vision-and-language navigation (VLN) requires an agent to use past observations without navigation-specific training. We study what information an 8B-scale navigation system should retain and how it should be organized for subsequent decisions. Our agent combines instruction progress, hierarchically compressed observation history anchored to poses, and accumulated geometry in complementary task, temporal, and spatial memories. An 8B observer summarizes observations, and an 8B reasoner uses the memories to select waypoint intents or request additional views, a geometric controller executes the selected targets. A semantic information perspective motivates the distinction between retaining evidence, making it accessible to the reasoner, and acquiring further observations. On R2R-CE val-unseen, the complete system achieves the highest among the evaluated Qwen3-based zero-shot baselines. Removing temporal memory reduces SR and sharply increases average path length from 16.9 to 39.1 m, removing the spatial-map and planning component reduces SR as well. Real-world experiments on a Unitree Go2 show that our zero-shot method achieves higher success rates than the post-trained baseline in both corridor and office environments, suggesting better transfer to the evaluated real-world settings. As a complementary evaluation, LAW2 uses paired instruction interventions to examine behavioral responses, instruction following ability beyond endpoint success. These results support preserving task progress, observation history, and geometry in structured memory for zero-shot navigation with smaller open models.
introduction:
Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN) requires an embodied agent to follow a natural-language instruction through a previously unseen environment, providing a foundation for higher-level tasks such as object manipulation and human–robot interaction. Post-training methods (Guo et al., 2026; Wei et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026) fine-tune vision-language models on navigation trajectories and achieve strong success rates on R2R-CE (Krantz et al., 2020). Zero-shot methods (Chen et al., 2025; Shi et al., 2025; Yuan et al., 2025; Li et al., 2026a) instead reuse pretrained models without navigation-specific training. Despite their different training requirements and inference resources, both approaches must integrate visual observations, instruction progress, and execution history to make reliable navigation decisions.

A central question is how navigation history should be represented for smaller open models. In our reproduced HSGM configuration (Li et al., 2026a), replacing GPT-5 with Qwen3-VL-8B reduces SR from 0.463 to 0.049 on R2R-CE val-unseen (Table 1). This comparison motivates examining the demands placed on the navigation backbone. We focus on memory representation: the reasoner must connect current observations with instruction progress and earlier evidence, often across many actions.

Our design preserves three complementary kinds of information: what the instruction requires and which subgoal is active, what the agent has observed and executed, and what geometry it has explored. We organize these as task memory, temporal memory with hierarchical summaries anchored to poses, and spatial memory containing an occupancy map and a committed target.

The semantic communication perspective of Lastras et al. (2026) motivates retaining evidence useful for task-relevant judgments and organizing it for a computationally bounded receiver. In navigation, these judgments include whether a subgoal is complete and where to move next. We use this perspective as a design rationale. An 8B observer constructs observational summaries, while a Qwen3-VL-8B reasoner combines them with the instruction and spatial memory. Waypoint intents connect these decisions to geometric control, and a PREVIEW action allows the agent to acquire additional views.

We evaluate this memory design through navigation results, component ablations, and deployment on a Unitree Go2 to experiment real world performance. We also introduce LAW2 as a complementary diagnostic benchmark: paired direction reversals, route-information removal, and paraphrases reveal how behavior responds to instruction changes with the same meaning.

Our contributions are as follows.

We propose a spatiotemporal memory representation for zero-shot VLN that combines instruction progress, pose-anchored observation history, and accumulated geometry.

We evaluate the representation in a navigation system with an 8B observer and an 8B reasoner. Component ablations characterize the effects of temporal memory, spatial memory and active previewing with planning, an integration with CA-Nav and real-world deployment provide additional evidence of utility.

We introduce LAW2 to complement navigation metrics with paired tests of directional responsiveness, dependence on route information, and sensitivity to paraphrasing.

Component ablations characterize the effects of temporal memory, spatial memory and active previewing with planning, an integration with CA-Nav and real-world deployment provide additional evidence of utility.

title: Compositional Diffusion Planning with Chunk Selection and Reachability Measure
authors: Chanyoung Park,Youngjoong Kim,Jaesik Park
abstract: Compositional diffusion planners have demonstrated remarkable success on long-horizon diffusion planning by sampling short trajectories, namely chunks, and composing them into a long trajectory. However, averaging overlapping chunks can induce the mode-averaging problem, resulting in discontinuous trajectories. Several works aim to address this problem, whereas a non-negligible portion of plans remains infeasible. In this work, we propose Selective Compositional Diffuser (SCD), handling this problem by measuring reachability. To this end, we present a self-supervised learning method for the reachability classifier. This is trained on offline data and generated chunks jointly to address potential distributional mismatch, while reducing the bias inherited from the generated data. Based on this, we construct a graph whose edge costs represent whether consecutive chunks are reachable, and traverse the graph to find effective yet efficient routes. Lastly, we generate bridging trajectories and refine the composed trajectory for smooth transitions. We evaluate our method on OGBench stitching tasks. It practically reduces incompatible mode compositions and the mode-averaging problem compared to the studied baselines. Across tasks, SCD improves success rates, reaching state-of-the-art results on HumanoidMaze-Large and Giant tasks.
introduction:
Diffusion models (Song and Ermon, 2019; Ho et al., 2020) have demonstrated remarkable results in robotic planning and decision-making (Ajay et al., 2023; Chi et al., 2023; Janner et al., 2022). These models abstract planning as a network-based generative process and are known to handle multimodality, flexible conditioning, and guidance-style control signals (Dhariwal and Nichol, 2021; Ho and Salimans, 2021). However, since diffusion models are inherently constrained by the training data, diffusion-based planners may require a combinatorial-scale dataset to model all possible plans.

To handle this problem, recent works (Luo et al., 2025; Lee et al., 2026; Sun et al., 2026; Mishra et al., 2026) try to stitch or compose short trajectories into a full trajectory for long-horizon tasks. To this end, they learn short-horizon trajectories, namely chunks, conditioned on boundary states and compose them at inference time. Since short trajectories are more practical to collect in the real world than full ones, compositional diffusion planners represent a promising and practical direction.

Previously, several works (Mishra et al., 2023; Luo et al., 2025) generate multiple chunks and compose overlapping regions by averaging. In particular, when the chunk distribution is multimodal, it is known to suffer from the mode-averaging problem, and it can result in discontinuous trajectories. Recently, Mishra et al. (2026); Sun et al. (2026); Lee et al. (2026) have addressed this problem with iterative resampling (Mishra et al., 2026), conservative score correction (Sun et al., 2026), and overlap consistency guidance (Lee et al., 2026). However, as shown in Fig. 2, we observe that a non-negligible portion of plans remains infeasible, failing to arrange feasibly composable chunks.

To handle this issue, we propose Selective Compositional Diffuser, called SCD. As shown in Fig. 1, we reformulate composition as a composable chunk selection problem over the candidate plans. To find a composable chunk sequence, we construct a graph using chunks as vertices. Edges are constructed between chunks and weighted by a score representing whether the next chunk could be reachable within a fixed time budget. By traversing the graph, we can find the minimum-cost path, which selects the sequence of chunks that are most likely to be reachable, thereby composable. We connect them with a fixed-length trajectory, often called a bridge.

To measure reachability, we present a self-supervised method to train a lightweight MLP network, classifying whether one state can reach the other within a given time lag. Once we find the minimum-cost path with this learned reachability score, we generate bridges and finally stitch the chunks.

We evaluate our method on long-horizon planning tasks from OGBench (Park et al., 2025). We observe that our method reduces infeasible transitions between composed chunks. Our results outperform baseline diffusion planners and goal-conditioned reinforcement learning methods, particularly on the giant-sized HumanoidMaze task, improving the success rate from the previous state-of-the-art result of 67% to 83% in the studied settings.

title: Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI: Mechanisms, Evidence, and Evaluation
authors: Xiaofeng Han,Kaize Luo,Zenghuang Fu,Zichong Zhu,Zhe Feng,Changwei Wang,Rongtao Xu,Weiliang Meng,Xiaopeng Zhang
abstract: Embodied systems can update policies, world models, skills, and executable programs from deployment experience, allowing one interaction to benefit later tasks. When a system also revises and reuses its data-acquisition, feedback, or learning procedures, experience changes the process that produces capability, introducing recursive self-improvement. This paper surveys research in physical AI through the connection between persistent capability and its improvement process. We first explain the functional distinction between learner updates and improver revisions, then compare policy learning, imagined experience, memory and skill accumulation, and executable harnesses. These approaches connect to revisions of curricula, rewards, and research programs in different ways. Contact validity, recovery, retention, and resource costs determine whether the resulting gains accumulate during continued deployment. An L0–L3 rubric distinguishes task-local adaptation, persistent capability gain, inherited process revision, and verified improver gain. Representative benchmarks and within-study contrasts relate these distinctions to existing results. We further propose common-data and interactive comparisons that evaluate reference and revised improvers from shared learner starts, separating the use of experience from its acquisition. This perspective connects the diverse methods, physical operating conditions, and evaluation evidence underlying embodied RSI. A comprehensive list of studies in this survey is available at https://github.com/nkd-lkz/physical-ai-rsi-survey.
introduction:
Robots encounter new objects, contact conditions, and task combinations after deployment. A failed attempt exposes a capability gap and can also supply experience for the next improvement. Failed grasps can inform policy updates, human corrections can become reusable skills, and recurring failures can guide further practice. Self-improvement methods incorporate this experience into continued learning so that later tasks benefit from earlier interaction. RoboCat and RECAP use robot experience to update policies, while Learning While Deploying extends the reuse of deployment experience across robot fleets. [1, 2, 3]

As foundation models generate programs, interpret failures, and organize experiments, the editable parts of a robot system extend beyond its action policy to the learning process. ASPIRE and SHAPER retain changes to skills and harnesses, while ENPIRE exposes policy-development programs to agent-generated revision. This enables a further form of self-improvement: experience changes data selection, feedback construction, or training code, and the revised process produces the next update. We use mechanistic recursive self-improvement (RSI) for such system-generated process revisions that are retained and used in subsequent learning. Experience thereby changes how the system acquires new capabilities. [4, 5, 6]

Current work approaches self-improvement through policy training, world models, skill libraries, harnesses, and automated experimentation. The same terminology often refers to changes at different levels. Continued practice can improve a policy, revised reward code can change its learning objective, and a more effective experimental procedure can improve subsequent learning efficiency. Connecting these approaches requires distinguishing changes in capability, changes in the learning process, and the additional gains produced by those process changes. Embodied systems must also obtain valid feedback, recover from failures, and retain existing capabilities within limited robot time and human assistance.

With robot learning and deployment as the main setting, this paper connects two strands of self-improvement in physical AI: how experience becomes persistent capability, and how it changes the process that produces capability. The first covers policies and values, world models, memory and skills, and executable harnesses. The second concerns revisions to experience acquisition, feedback construction, and learning procedures. Figure 1 summarizes their relationship. The L0–L3 evidence rubric connects advances in these mechanisms to the gains established by their evaluations.

This paper makes four contributions:

Conceptual distinctions and evidence criteria. We distinguish task-local adaptation, persistent capability gain, inherited process revision, and verified improver gain. The L0–L3 rubric connects these claims to observable evidence for a specific system configuration and protocol.

A synthesis of persistent and recursive mechanisms. We organize methods by what experience changes, what is retained, and how the retained change influences subsequent learning. This functional analysis links updates to the learner with revisions to data acquisition, feedback, learning procedures, and update control.

Physical conditions and controlled evaluation. We connect contact validity, recovery, retention, and resource use to the interpretation of improvement. Common-data and interactive comparisons distinguish the use of experience from its acquisition when assessing reference and revised improvers.

Evidence-based research priorities. We derive directions for grounded feedback, lasting gains, reliable recovery, and efficient improvement from the gaps between implemented mechanisms and demonstrated benefits.

Related surveys provide complementary perspectives on self-evolving agents, embodied learning, and world–action models.[7, 8, 9] Embodied self-evolution has been organized around memory, tasks, world models, embodiment, and model design, including changes to optimization and evaluation procedures.[10] Code-based robot-learning surveys distinguish execution feedback, persistent memory, and program search,[11] while continual-learning research develops retention and transfer metrics alongside practical robotics constraints.[12] Recent humanoid surveys connect post-deployment mechanisms and meta-updates to safety constraints and lifetime trajectory evaluation.[13] General RSI surveys also cover embodied applications and controlled comparisons of original and revised improvement mechanisms under matched budgets.[14]

These surveys establish the components of self-evolution. This paper connects the technical approaches through the relationship between experience, retained artifacts, and subsequent learning: how policies, models, skills, and code acquire persistent value, and when those same components participate in revising the improvement process. Decision-centered world-model evaluation similarly relates component quality to its effects on planning and policy optimization. Table I summarizes the related perspectives. This mechanism analysis provides the basis for the evidence rubric and physical evaluation conditions developed here. [15]

The remainder of the review follows this progression. Section II establishes the conceptual framework and evidence criteria. Sections III and IV examine persistent capability updates and inherited revisions to the improvement process, respectively. Section V analyzes the physical conditions for sustained improvement, and Section VI synthesizes the evidence and evaluation protocols. Section VII develops research directions from the resulting gaps, and Section VIII concludes.

1. Conceptual distinctions and evidence criteria. We distinguish task-local adaptation, persistent capability gain, inherited process revision, and verified improver gain. The L0–L3 rubric connects these claims to observable evidence for a specific system configuration and protocol.

2. A synthesis of persistent and recursive mechanisms. We organize methods by what experience changes, what is retained, and how the retained change influences subsequent learning. This functional analysis links updates to the learner with revisions to data acquisition, feedback, learning procedures, and update control.

3. Physical conditions and controlled evaluation. We connect contact validity, recovery, retention, and resource use to the interpretation of improvement. Common-data and interactive comparisons distinguish the use of experience from its acquisition when assessing reference and revised improvers.

4. Evidence-based research priorities. We derive directions for grounded feedback, lasting gains, reliable recovery, and efficient improvement from the gaps between implemented mechanisms and demonstrated benefits.
