title: MATCH: Execution-Aware Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning for Vision-and-Language Navigation in Continuous Environment
authors: Shuhao Ye,Yufei Wei,Demao Wang,Shichao Zhai,Rong Xiong,Yue Wang
abstract: Vision-and-Language Navigation in Continuous Environments (VLN-CE) requires instruction-consistent planning and reliable execution under collision constraints. Yet many hierarchical approaches optimize the planner while keeping execution fixed. We introduce MATCH, a framework that jointly learns a language-conditioned planner and a goal-conditioned primitive-action executor. An execution-aware topological graph represents start-dependent execution options and integrates executor value estimates with realized outcome memory, enabling the planner to select execution requests and refine their targets through bounded continuous offsets. A transition-aware dense macro reward balances ordered progress along the reference route against execution residual, encouraging executable requests without substituting local success for instruction following. A staged curriculum culminates in synchronized on-policy updates, with the executor learning on planner-generated requests and the planner adapting its requests to the executor’s current behavior. With 0.5B parameters, MATCH achieves state-of-the-art performance on the R2R-CE and RxR-CE benchmarks. Preliminary real-robot deployments further demonstrate its practical potential.
introduction:
Vision-and-Language Navigation in Continuous Environments (VLN-CE) [1] requires an agent to follow natural-language instructions through hundreds of collision-constrained primitive actions.
Many approaches address this long-horizon problem by predicting intermediate navigation intents, such as target locations [2, 3, 5], or short waypoint-based trajectories [5, 6], which must then be translated into movement.
We refer to intent selection as macro-level planning and intent realization as micro-level execution.
In the hierarchical Markov decision process (HMDP) view [7], an intent is a macro action whose state transition depends on both environmental dynamics and the executor’s policy.
Selecting an instruction-consistent intent therefore doesn’t ensure that it can be realized under collision constraints.

Some methods bypass this execution challenge through teleportation [6, 5] (Fig. 1a), while some other methods rely on hand-designed controllers [2, 8].
Even when the planner is trained on actual execution outcomes [5], the execution policy remains fixed during that training.
The planner may learn to avoid a difficult doorway and select an alternative target, but the same experience does not teach how to handle that doorway more reliably (Fig. 1b).
Our insight is to extend the learning loop beyond macro-level planning to include micro-level execution: navigation experience should help to co-optimize the planner and executor, not just improve the planner’s ability to work within its limits.

Hierarchical reinforcement learning (HRL) [9] provides a natural framework for this joint adaptation. The planner determines the requests on which the executor learns, while the executor shapes the transitions those requests realize. The challenge is to couple these adaptations so that the executor learns on planner-generated requests and the planner selects requests that produce instruction-consistent progress under the current execution policy, rather than merely favoring easy targets. This calls for grounding macro-action learning both in the current executor and in the task contribution of its realized transitions.

We address this challenge with MATCH (Macro-Action Transition Coupling for Hierarchical RL) (Fig. 1c), which jointly learns a language-conditioned planner and a goal-conditioned executor.
We implement its decision interface within the graph-based VLN-CE architecture [2], where waypoint proposals define candidate frontiers for an online topological planner.
To ground the planner’s requests in the executor’s evolving capabilities, we develop an execution-aware topological graph.
In this graph, edges from different visited nodes to the same frontier represent distinct execution options, since execution outcomes depend not only on the destination but also on the starting location.
Each edge carries the executor’s value estimates over a target neighborhood before execution and records the realized outcome memory afterward.
The planner pairs edge selection with a bounded continuous target offset within this evaluated neighborhood, allowing it to refine an execution request rather than merely accept or reject a fixed waypoint.

To learn which execution requests are useful for the task, we introduce a transition-aware dense macro reward based on their realized transitions.
Each macro action receives credit for the ordered progress along the reference route, minus the execution residual—the remaining target-reaching distance—with both measured in meters.
The progress term encourages the planner to advance along the route, not just choose easier targets.
The residual gives the planner direct feedback on each request’s execution difficulty, rather than leaving it implicit in final task outcomes.
This encourages executable requests without making local success a substitute for instruction following.
The executor is rewarded for progress toward assigned target.
A staged curriculum followed by synchronized on-policy updates lets both policies adapt through shared navigation experience.

Our main contributions are:

We propose MATCH, to our knowledge the first VLN-CE framework to jointly optimize a language-conditioned planner and a primitive-action executor through HRL, with both policies learning from shared on-policy navigation rollouts.

To support joint adaptation during HRL, we develop an execution-aware topological graph that uses executor value estimates and outcome memory to guide the planner’s selection and refinement of execution requests.

We introduce a transition-aware dense macro reward that balances ordered progress along the reference route against execution residual, encouraging executable requests that advance the route.

Using a 0.5B-parameter model, MATCH achieves state-of-the-art performance on R2R-CE and RxR-CE, with real-robot deployments further validating practicality.

1. We propose MATCH, to our knowledge the first VLN-CE framework to jointly optimize a language-conditioned planner and a primitive-action executor through HRL, with both policies learning from shared on-policy navigation rollouts.

2. To support joint adaptation during HRL, we develop an execution-aware topological graph that uses executor value estimates and outcome memory to guide the planner’s selection and refinement of execution requests.

3. We introduce a transition-aware dense macro reward that balances ordered progress along the reference route against execution residual, encouraging executable requests that advance the route.

4. Using a 0.5B-parameter model, MATCH achieves state-of-the-art performance on R2R-CE and RxR-CE, with real-robot deployments further validating practicality.

title: SimRetract: Zero-Shot Sim-to-Real Robotic Assistance for Retractor Take-Over in Open Surgery
authors: Xucheng Wang,Zhizhou Yang,Sung Eun Kim,Romain Hardy,Michael P. Sampson,Aakash Reddy,Ankit Pal,Xiaoman Zhang,Luyang Luo,Pranav Rajpurkar
abstract:
We demonstrate the first zero-shot sim-to-real transfer for a surgeon-robot collaboration task in open surgery: retractor take-over. A robot arm takes a retractor from the surgeon’s hand and preserves retraction at handoff, using a policy trained only on simulated demonstrations, without human demonstrations or real-world fine-tuning. Imitation learning from real demonstrations is limited by collection and labeling costs, and by performance degradation when the environment changes. Our framework, SimRetract, generates simulated demonstrations designed for transfer: the policy observes masked instrument images and grasp geometry, learns to recover from off-nominal states, and acts with margin for execution drift. Deployed zero-shot, it grasps the retractor in 90 % of 50 surgeon-defined phantom presentations and preserves retraction at handoff in 78 %. Results on unseen retractors suggest potential for generalization to instruments with similar grasp geometry. Across ten policy configurations and 1 200 simulated and real trials, we localize the sim-to-real gap to components: in simulation, grasp rates across ablations span 80–96 %, while on the real robot removing the instrument mask alone drops performance to 22 % grasped and 12 % held. Transfer-oriented design thus makes zero-shot sim-to-real transfer feasible for a surgical assistance task without human demonstrations.
Code is available here.
introduction:
Open surgery relies on human assistants to provide anatomical exposure and maintain tissue tension through retraction. Although an experienced assistant can sometimes independently establish effective retraction, the primary surgeon commonly places the retractor to create the exposure and tension needed to operate, after which the assistant takes over and maintains the selected retraction. Here we focus on taking over a surgeon-positioned retractor, with the surgeon responsible for selecting the desired exposure. Because surgical personnel are scarce and unevenly distributed (Holmer et al., 2015), robotic assistance could help extend the capacity of existing teams (Kernbach et al., 2026). The same scarcity limits expert time for collecting robot demonstrations, motivating simulation as a scalable source of training data. This handover requires perceiving an instrument partly occluded by the surgeon’s hand and grasping it without disturbing retraction across unfamiliar environments.

We call this hand-off retractor take-over. The surgeon establishes the desired tissue retraction and holds the instrument under load while the robot approaches and grasps the exposed shaft. A successful take-over requires more than grasping the retractor: the established retraction must be preserved at handoff, after the surgeon releases it.

The instrument is presented at varied positions and orientations and is partly occluded by the surgeon’s hand. Only a limited portion of the shaft is available for grasping. A parallel gripper must align its pads with the shaft’s flat faces and center the grasp site between them. Otherwise, closure can shift or rotate the instrument and alter the exposure even if the grasp succeeds. The robot must also approach without disturbing the loaded instrument and move smoothly and predictably beside the surgeon.

Imitation learning from real demonstrations is a natural route to such a skill (Black et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2026), but prior work documents performance degradation under changes in background, lighting and viewpoint (Xie et al., 2024; Pumacay et al., 2024). Generalization to these shifts benefits from greater demonstration diversity (Lin et al., 2025). Collecting this diversity across differently draped, lit and equipped surgical settings requires substantial expert time.

Simulation supports scalable data generation with precise labels and controlled variation (Tobin et al., 2017; Makoviychuk et al., 2021). However, rendered observations differ from real ones, and surgical sim-to-real studies have largely focused on minimally invasive robotic platforms and surgical training tasks (Xu et al., 2021; Yu et al., 2024; Scheikl et al., 2023; Long and others, 2025). With the arm, gripper and wrist-camera configuration fixed, we ask whether a policy trained for retractor take-over on simulated demonstrations can perform the task in a previously unseen real environment without real task demonstrations or environment-specific policy fine-tuning. Wrist-camera sensing and robot joint state provide the policy input, without external cameras or a model of the room.

We propose SimRetract, a framework for learning zero-shot retractor take-over from simulated demonstrations. The expert selects grasps and generates complete approach and closure trajectories, retaining demonstrations only after physical stability checks. Smooth, aligned approaches leave margin for execution drift, while perturbation-recovery adds corrective trajectories from perturbed poses. In both domains, the policy receives masked RGB-D, robot joint state and the grasp-plane normal. Training-time perception augmentation, including input dropout, mimics sensing imperfections.

We fine-tune π0\pi_{0} (Black et al., 2024) using a dataset of 1 500 synthetic episodes and evaluate it in held-out simulation and on 50 surgeon-defined real presentations, with 1 200 trials including ablations and unseen instruments. On the training instrument, the full policy achieves 90 % grasped and 78 % held at handoff in real-world trials. Masking has the largest effect on transfer, while the recovery-augmented dataset improves preservation of retraction.

The first zero-shot sim-to-real transfer for a surgeon-robot collaboration task in open surgery. A policy trained on synthetic task demonstrations, with no real task demonstrations or real-world policy fine-tuning, grasps the retractor in 90% of 50 surgeon-defined presentations and preserves the established exposure at handoff in 78%.

The first zero-shot sim-to-real transfer for a surgeon-robot collaboration task in open surgery. A policy trained on synthetic task demonstrations, with no real task demonstrations or real-world policy fine-tuning, grasps the retractor in 90% of 50 surgeon-defined presentations and preserves the established exposure at handoff in 78%.

A framework for learning a surgical assistance task in simulation. The framework generates and validates complete retractor take-over demonstrations, combines trajectories with execution margin and corrective recovery, and trains on task-relevant inputs with perception augmentation.

A dissection of the sim-to-real gap for an open-surgery task. Our comparisons cover ten policy configurations, 500 simulated and 700 real trials, including unseen instruments. In the main comparison, simulated grasp rates span 80–96 %, while real rates span 22–90 %; comparing both domains identifies which design choices support transfer.

title: HERON: Real-Time Obstacle-Aware Reachability Maps for Mobile Manipulators
authors: G. Dupoiron,F. Michaud,J.P. Roberge
abstract: Mobile manipulator robots rarely reposition their base during manipulation, because doing so requires real-time knowledge of how well the arm can reach its surroundings among obstacles. Reachability maps (RMs) encode this knowledge, but existing methods are slow, coarse (typically 5 cm), or ignore real obstacles. This article asks whether a neural network can predict an obstacle-aware RM at 2 cm resolution from a live depth camera, on embedded hardware, fast enough for online use. We present HERON, a 3D U-Net trained on RMs computed with the GPU-accelerated inverse kinematics of cuRobo, first on synthetic scenes and then on real depth data, and deployed on a Jetson AGX Orin with TensorRT and INT8 quantization. HERON predicts the RM of a 2.56 m cube around the arm in 115 ms on average, for a measured system rate of 8.57 Hz, close to the 10 Hz update rate of the obstacle map, whereas computing the same map with cuRobo takes about 90 min. Against the cuRobo ground truth, 95% of the voxels lie within ±\pm1 class out of 51 with the FP32 model and within ±\pm3 classes with the INT8 model, with a Pearson correlation of 0.99 and a quadratic weighted kappa above 0.9. Accuracy degrades mainly at the workspace boundaries.
introduction:
Mobile manipulator robots (MMs) combine the mobility of a mobile base with the dexterity of a robotic arm, offering a flexibility that fixed manipulators cannot match. To decide where to place its base, an MM needs to know how well its arm can reach the space around it. A reachability map (RM) provides this knowledge: it divides the space around the arm into voxels and scores each voxel by the fraction of end-effector orientations that the arm can reach there Zacharias et al. (2007). Humans rely on a similar, intuitive sense of what is reachable to position themselves before acting Rabellino et al. (2020).

Yet MMs are often implemented as an arm mounted on a base with little coordination between the two subsystems, which Ghodsian et al. Ghodsian et al. (2023) identify as one of the main barriers to their deployment in industry. Whole-body controllers coordinate base and arm motion while accounting for obstacles Pankert and Hutter (2020), and other approaches optimize physically motivated metrics such as manipulability or distance to joint limits Thakar et al. (2023). However, none of them assesses the quality of the workspace in which they place the robot, with respect to the task and to the surrounding obstacles. For tasks with a large range of motion, such as cleaning or painting, the base must be repositioned as the task evolves, which requires this assessment online.

Current RM methods cannot provide this assessment in real time: they are slow to compute, operate at coarse resolution, typically 5 cm, and largely ignore real obstacles. The cause is computational: evaluating inverse kinematics (IK) with collision checking for every pose of every voxel is prohibitively slow on CPU at fine resolution, and maps precomputed without obstacles become inaccurate near them.

Two recent GPU tools change this situation: cuRobo Sundaralingam et al. (2023) solves batched IK with collision checking, and nvblox Millane et al. (2024) maintains a distance field of the scene from depth images. Together, they make it tractable to compute ground-truth RMs at 2 cm resolution in scenes with real obstacles. Computing one RM still takes about 90 min, far too slow for online use, but such maps can train a network that predicts the RM directly from an obstacle map.

This paper presents HERON, a High-resolution Embedded Reachability Obstacle-aware Network, and addresses the following question: can a neural network predict an obstacle-aware RM at 2 cm resolution from a live depth camera, on embedded hardware, fast enough for online base repositioning and close enough to the cuRobo ground truth? We answer it with two criteria: the prediction rate, which we aim to bring as close as possible to the 10 Hz update rate of the obstacle map so that the RM can later drive a closed-loop base controller, and the agreement with the cuRobo ground truth, measured in several regions of the workspace. We assume a single known arm, obstacles observed by a single depth camera, and a ground truth defined by cuRobo IK over 50 orientations per voxel. Each prediction reflects a single snapshot of the obstacle map, so obstacles that move during the approximately 120 ms of a prediction are not accounted for.

The paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews research on RMs and mobile base placement. Section 3 presents the dataset, the network, and the evaluation metrics. Section 4 describes the hardware, the training, and the real-time implementation. Section 5 presents the results, Section 6 discusses them, and Section 7 concludes.

authors: Jiuyi Xu,Meida Chen,Yang Ye,Yangming Shi
comment: Accepted by the CoRL 2026 Workshop "Oops, I Erred".
abstract:
Robot imitation learning uses demonstrations from operators of varying skill, but selecting training data remains challenging.
Existing methods score demonstrations using smoothness, diversity, or estimated influence on policy performance, but differences in selection and evaluation protocols make it difficult to determine whether they outperform simple baselines.
We introduce CuraEval, a framework combining mathematical analysis of demonstration scores with controlled comparisons against fixed size-matched random subsets and full-data training on mixed-skill robomimic data using Diffusion Policy and BC-RNN.
We show that the evaluated PSD score depends only on episode length and squared position magnitudes, and produces nearly the same ranking as episode length on square (ρ=0.999\rho=0.999).
With Diffusion Policy, selecting the shortest 50% of demonstrations improves square success from 70.7% under random selection to 76.5%.
Compared with random selection, our adapted geometric-entropy LOO selector reduces success at 25% retention from 94.7% to 74.0% on can and achieves 41.7% on square, below the mean success rates of all three independently sampled random subsets (59.8–62.5%).
On the same 3 square Diffusion Policy training seeds, length-based selection at 75% retention improves success over full-data training from 76.7% to 86.7% under the original protocol, but lowers it from 80.5% to 79.5% after checkpoint reporting, rollout count, and evaluation seed change jointly.
No evaluated curated condition significantly outperforms full-data training after Holm correction, although confidence intervals still permit useful gains.
Code is available at https://github.com/jiuyixu25/CuraEval.
introduction:
Imitation learning enables robots to learn manipulation skills from human demonstrations, but performance depends on the quality of the training data [11, 16].
Even successful demonstrations vary in speed, consistency, and operator skill.
Selecting smooth or efficient trajectories may remove useful coverage, making it difficult to identify the demonstrations that best support learning.

Existing methods evaluate demonstrations through trajectory statistics [3, 4], diversity [5, 6], state–action mutual information [8], or estimated influence on policy performance [7].
These criteria already inform robot-data pipelines: JoyAI-RA 0.5 [1] uses spectral and jerk-based metrics, while WARP-RM [2] groups T-shirt-folding demonstrations into quality tiers using episode duration.
However, differences in scoring objectives, selection procedures, and evaluation protocols complicate comparisons.
Although several methods include random-selection controls [4, 6, 7, 8], their behavior under common conditions requires further investigation.
Building on studies of injected demonstration defects [13, 14, 15], we examine natural variation among human operators.

We introduce CuraEval, a framework combining mathematical analysis of demonstration scores with controlled evaluation on state-based, mixed-skill robomimic data [11].
We evaluate trajectory scores, explicit adaptations of diversity measures, and our implementation of CUPID [7], using Diffusion Policy (DP) [12] and selected BC-RNN comparisons [11].
Fixed training budgets and comparisons with random subsets, simple heuristics, and all data distinguish three goals: selecting better data than random, improving over full-data training, and retaining performance with fewer demonstrations.

Our results show why these distinctions matter.
The evaluated power spectral density (PSD) score closely tracks episode length, and simple heuristics can outperform random selection.
Conversely, our adapted geometric-entropy selector based on leave-one-out (LOO) contributions achieves 41.7% on square, below all three tested random-subset means (59.8–62.5%).
No curated condition has a Holm-adjusted advantage over full data, while changing the evaluation protocol reverses an initially positive estimate of curation benefit.
Our contributions are:

Score analysis. We derive the evaluated PSD score’s exact time-domain expression and explain its relationship with episode length.

Controlled selection evaluation. We identify beneficial and harmful selections through comparisons with random subsets, simple heuristics, and full data.

Protocol sensitivity. We show that evaluation choices can reverse the estimated benefit of curation on the same training seeds.

1. Score analysis. We derive the evaluated PSD score’s exact time-domain expression and explain its relationship with episode length.

2. Controlled selection evaluation. We identify beneficial and harmful selections through comparisons with random subsets, simple heuristics, and full data.

3. Protocol sensitivity. We show that evaluation choices can reverse the estimated benefit of curation on the same training seeds.

title: Embodied at Sea: Imitation Learning for Multi-Task Underwater Manipulation
authors: Greta Perez-Haiek(1),Luca Macesanu(1),Kevin Angers(1),Mohammed Imam(1),Timothy Gambin(2),Christopher Clark(1) ((1) New York University, (2) University of Malta)
comment: . For associated files, seethis https URL
abstract: Behavior Cloning has demonstrated promising generalization capabilities for robotic manipulation in terrestrial environments. However, marine visual distortions and dynamic currents create a severe domain shift that remains a key bottleneck in adapting generalist architectures to underwater field manipulation. To address this, 1616 episodes of underwater manipulation data were collected in calm and turbulent waters and were used to train 14 generalist Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models (DynamicVLA) with varying proprioception observation configurations. Across three tasks on 1260 gradable on-hardware rollouts in a pool, 10 models outperformed the baseline, with the highest-performing model achieving a 93.3% overall success rate, including partial successes. Results are also introduced from a case study evaluating the performance of a single-task Action Chunking Transformer (ACT) and a generalist VLA (SmolVLA) policy for two tasks in marine archaeology and conservation: grasping and mooring. Experiments are performed on an ROV on and around the WWII wreck Coralita X127 and at Manoel Island Marina, Malta. Across 748 collected episodes and 508 gradable on-hardware rollouts, the ACT policy substantially outperformed SmolVLA (47.9% vs. 7.9% pooled success rate), earning a 66.7% success rate on the most successful task at the marine archaeological site. To enable further contributions to embodied intelligence in marine field robotics, the BluEmbodied Kit used to collect data, train models, and deploy policies on the ROV has been open sourced.
introduction:
Marine conservationists and archaeologists routinely perform tasks such as environmental monitoring and specimen retrieval, constrained by poor visibility, dynamic currents, and the physiological limits of human divers. At deeper depths, monitoring requires repeated dives that are slow, costly, and risky due to lengthy decompression procedures [1]. Automating these operations, e.g. via robots, could accelerate scientific research and reduce diver risk.

Recent advances in Behavior Cloning (BC) [2] have enabled robust single-task robot policies from relatively little data. While prior works explore the performance of these approaches in aquatic robotics [3, 4], deployment in real marine archaeology and conservation missions remains largely unexplored.

BC-based policies, particularly Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models, have shown remarkable generalization to novel tasks and objects, making them an appealing candidate for underwater manipulation. However, they are trained almost exclusively on terrestrial datasets featuring stable lighting and fixed-base manipulators, while underwater vehicles operating in marine environments experience unconstrained 6-DOF motion, drag, turbidity, visual distortion, occlusion, and distractors (see Fig. Embodied at Sea: Imitation Learning for Multi-Task Underwater Manipulation). Whether these policies retain their generalization capabilities under such conditions and across diverse archaeological sites remains an open question.

By enabling increased levels of autonomy for underwater robotic manipulation tasks, there will be scientific value not just within the field of robotics, but as well in the fields of marine archaeology, oceanography, geology, biology, and environmental conservation. This leads to a motivating question: how can the recent advances in terrestrial behavior cloning be leveraged for underwater environments?

In addressing this driving question, the work presented below yields the following contributions:

To our knowledge, the world’s first instance of successfully implementing a multi-task VLA underwater on real hardware, where a VLA is defined as a single Vision-Language-Action model that can execute multiple tasks and be commanded to execute a specific task via language based inputs.

To our knowledge, the world’s first instance of successfully implementing a multi-task VLA underwater on real hardware, where a VLA is defined as a single Vision-Language-Action model that can execute multiple tasks and be commanded to execute a specific task via language based inputs.

A real-world case study of BC manipulation models deployed on an underwater Remotely Operated Vehicle (ROV) at a Mediterranean shipwreck for archaeology and conservation tasks.

A thorough investigation into how different proprioception configurations and underwater sensor modalities in a model’s observation and action spaces affect generalist model behavior underwater, including a new action space that leverages an underwater robot depth sensor and feedback control for stable motion in the vertical direction.

Introducing the BluEmbodied Kit as an open source repository that enables users to collect underwater teleoperation data, train single (ACT) and multi-task models (DynamicVLA, SmolVLA), and run inference on Blue Robotics’ BlueROV2 while staying compatible with BlueOS.

title: Minimum Sufficient Communication for Independent Behaviour Tree Robot Teams
authors: Sherry Jiang,Oliver Obst
comment: accepted for presentation at the Australasian Conference on Robotics and Automation (ACRA 2026)
abstract:
We present an experimental framework for determining sufficient communication in
robot teams running fixed, independent Behaviour Trees with private blackboards.
Within a declared policy family, we vary message content and admission frequency
and measure traffic in recipient-weighted bits per robot decision. A dense sweep
identifies candidate policies for comparison with full-state communication. We
retest selected candidates and the reference on fresh, paired scenarios, using
one-sided simultaneous confidence bounds to assess whether success remains
within five percentage points of the full-state reference. The bounds also
assess whether tested cheaper policies can be ruled out as insufficient.
Depending on the evidence, the framework reports an exact minimum, a positive
bracket, a sufficient upper bound, or an unresolved boundary. Experiments with
eight content policies across four warehouse conditions identify zero
communication as the exact minimum under low contention. In the scaled
condition, the no-release policy at gate q=0.992222q=0.992222 is confirmed sufficient,
achieving 96.33% success at an estimated rate of 738.55 bits per robot
decision, or 0.544% of full-state traffic. The positive minimum remains
unresolved. These claims apply only to the declared policy family, sampled gate
values and operating conditions.
introduction:
Communication allows a robot to learn that another robot has already claimed or
completed a task, which can prevent repeated travel and work. However, sending
this information is associated with a cost and creates communication traffic.
Therefore, the challenge is to reduce communication while preserving enough
information for the robot team to coordinate successfully.

We therefore investigated how much communication is sufficient, for a fixed team
controller and operating condition, to keep task success within a chosen loss
from full-state communication. We study this question using Behaviour Trees
(BTs), which provide modular and reactive control structures
[\citeauthoryearColledanchise and
Ögren2018, \citeauthoryearIovino et al.2022]. Each robot runs its own BT instance and
maintains private beliefs about tasks and teammates. Throughout the experiment,
the BT structure and task-selection rule remain unchanged. We vary only the
communication protocol, which determines what information is shared between
robots and how ownership information is maintained. This allows us to isolate
the effect of communication while keeping the underlying decision-making process
fixed.

We vary communication along two dimensions, namely message content and admission
probability. Firstly, a content rule determines what information a policy is
allowed to send and when it is generated, such as task completion, ownership
claims, releases, intent, task facts or robot status. Secondly, a gate
q∈[0,1]q\in[0,1] controls the probability that each eligible message is admitted.
The gate therefore controls how often eligible messages are transmitted, but it
does not directly measure the amount of communication. Specifically, different
content rules generate different numbers and sizes of messages, and messages
sent earlier can change later robot decisions and therefore which messages are
generated afterwards. We therefore measure the traffic that is actually
transmitted. For each message, we count its application-level payload once for
every intended recipient, then normalise the total by the number of robot
decisions. This gives the realised recipient-weighted application bits per robot
decision.

A policy is sufficient if its success remains within the chosen tolerance of the
full-state reference. To claim a positive minimum, we would additionally need
evidence that every cheaper policy in the declared family is insufficient. We
therefore distinguish between a confirmed sufficient policy, an unresolved
boundary, a positive bracket, and an exact zero-rate minimum.

Note that our conclusions apply only to the family that we evaluate. Within this
scope, our contribution is a reproducible procedure that combines fixed private
BT control, measured recipient-weighted cost, exploratory frontier search, and
fresh paired confirmation. We apply the procedure to eight content policies
across four controlled task conditions and report the strongest conclusion
supported by the evidence in each case.

title: SKiD-SLAM: Resource-Aware Distributed Multi-Robot LiDAR SLAM for Planetary Missions with Field Deployments at Analog Sites
authors: Hogyun Kim,Juwon Kim,Dongjin Cho,Jiwon Choi,Geonmo Yang,Seokhwan Jeong,Jiyun Lee,Miryeong Park,Hyungtae Lim,Younggun Cho
comment: . Published in IEEE Transactions on Field Robotics. Code and field data:this https URL
abstract:
In future planetary exploration missions, teams of robots will need to collaboratively build maps in unknown environments, from subsurface caves and lava tubes to crater-strewn surface terrains.
Such collaboration enables faster and more robust mapping than a single robot can achieve by sharing observations and computation across the team.
However, this collaboration typically assumes seamless communication and abundant computing resources, whereas planetary environments impose severe communication limits, constrained onboard computation, and the absence of any central infrastructure.
In this field report, we present SKiD-SLAM, a distributed multi-robot light detection and ranging (LiDAR) simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM) system for such communication-constrained planetary environments, and report its deployment across two representative mission concepts, i.e., (i) cave exploration and (ii) scientific surface exploration.
To build the system, we survey the communication and computation budgets of actual planetary missions, and select modules that fit these budgets for each core function of distributed multi-robot LiDAR SLAM.
These core functions are recognizing revisited places across robots’ maps, estimating inter-robot relative poses, and fusing trajectories without a central server.
Before field deployment, we verify the assembled system on public datasets that resemble planetary environments and in a simulator built on the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL)’s Open Source Rover.
We then validate our SKiD-SLAM in both mission concepts through field deployments in South Korea, where (i) a team of wheeled rovers explores the Majang lava-tube cave on Jeju Island, and (ii) quadruped robots carry out a crater-and-rock science scenario on a planetary analog terrain at the Korea Institute of Civil Engineering and Building Technology (KICT) in Yeoncheon.
Across both deployments, our SKiD-SLAM reliably performed distributed multi-robot LiDAR SLAM within the 250 kbps inter-robot communication budget, demonstrating its feasibility under challenging field conditions.
The supplementary materials, including our code and field data, are publicly available at https://sparolab.github.io/research/skid_slam/.
introduction:
The Cooperative Autonomous Distributed Robotic Exploration (CADRE) project of the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) [60, 17, 64, 68] aims to develop and demonstrate distributed multi-robot autonomy for future planetary exploration missions.
In such missions, teams of autonomous robots will need to collaboratively build maps in unknown environments on the Moon and Mars, including caves, lava tubes, and crater-strewn surfaces, to support scientific exploration and resource utilization.
However, achieving robust and efficient multi-robot simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM) in these resource-constrained field environments presents substantial challenges, including limited communication bandwidth, constrained onboard computation, and the absence of any central infrastructure [73, 74, 50, 80, 36, 43, 24].

Recently, distributed multi-robot light detection and ranging (LiDAR) SLAM systems have achieved remarkable progress, demonstrating accurate inter-robot loop closing and globally consistent mapping across robot teams [9, 40, 23, 15, 38, 84, 54, 30, 85, 92, 48, 57, 82].
However, most of these systems have been developed and validated on urban and indoor benchmarks, where distinctive geometric structure, high-bandwidth wireless links, and supporting infrastructure are often available.
These assumptions do not hold in planetary environments.
Consequently, their behavior under the kilobit-class, intermittent, and infrastructure-free conditions of planetary missions remains largely unexamined.

This gap motivates our field report.
Rather than proposing another algorithm, we select each module of distributed multi-robot LiDAR SLAM to fit the communication and computation budgets of actual planetary missions, and report on the operation of the resulting system in the field.
Concretely, we organize our study around two representative planetary mission concepts.
These two concepts, distinguished by terrain, platform, and team composition, recur throughout the report, from the mission concepts and field deployments to the simulation, evaluation, and lessons learned.
Drawing on these deployments, we further distill lessons for operating distributed multi-robot LiDAR SLAM beyond benchmark conditions.

Here, we describe the two mission concepts that frame our study of distributed multi-robot exploration, along with the operating assumptions they share.
The first is cave exploration [20].
A team cooperatively maps a confined, lightless lava tube, a type of subsurface environment that may shelter future habitats but that no planetary robot has yet entered.
The entire team shares a single objective, i.e., to build one consistent map of the passages.

The second is scientific surface exploration [2].
A team explores open, cratered terrain, with the robots divided across complementary roles rather than sharing one objective.
In a representative scenario, one robot traverses the crater field to map its geometry, while another inspects scattered rocks for science-oriented observations.
Here, the team size follows from the division of labor in the scenario, not from platform availability.

Both concepts share the same starting condition.
A team of NN robots is deployed in an unknown environment, and each robot starts in its own local coordinate frame, with no shared global reference established a priori [30, 85, 92, 48, 57, 82].
Satellite imagery and orbital depth maps may provide a coarse initial estimate of each robot’s pose in a global frame.
However, they lack the resolution required for precise localization or for inter-robot map alignment on the surface [47, 61].
Therefore, a consistent global map must be constructed on site, from the robots’ own onboard observations.

Beyond this starting condition, both concepts share two operating assumptions.
First, the robots explore without any fixed infrastructure.
There is no fixed localization infrastructure (hereafter referred to as a base station), no positioning system such as the global positioning system (GPS), and no central server with abundant compute for SLAM.
Instead, each robot carries an embedded-class onboard computer and a short-range radio, processes its observations onboard, and exchanges mapping data with the team over short-range wireless links [78, 1].
Robots cannot assume continuous connectivity, and they may operate beyond line of sight of one another for extended periods.
Therefore, each robot runs its SLAM pipeline onboard, and the team shares only the information needed to align and merge maps within the available budgets [12].

Second, the robot platform may differ across mission concepts.
Each terrain demands a different form of mobility, e.g., wheeled rovers where the ground is smooth and traversable, and legged robots where the terrain is rough and uneven [69].
As the platform and LiDAR mounting change with the terrain, the system must remain robust to the resulting viewpoint differences [38, 54].

Within these concepts, the role of SKiD-SLAM is narrow but critical.
It must reconcile the robots’ independent local maps into a single globally consistent map of the explored environment.
This must be achieved using only budget-compliant communication, without a central server, and without operator intervention in the mapping process.

We next describe how the two mission concepts were realized in the field, at two analog sites in South Korea.
For cave exploration, the site is the Majang lava-tube cave on Jeju Island, a subterranean environment analogous to lunar and Martian lava tubes.
The traversed section spans roughly 20 m ×\times 40 m, with ceiling heights ranging from 1 m to 5 m, and contains narrow and rugged passages that are difficult to traverse even for humans.
Critically, the cave receives no natural light, reproducing the permanently dark conditions of planetary caves and the lunar polar shadows that challenge vision-based perception.
We deployed three wheeled rovers from UEL11
1
https://uel.co.kr (N=3N=3), whose drivetrains remain stable over the rough and uneven lava floor (Fig. 1) [51].

For scientific surface exploration, the site is a planetary analog terrain at the Korea Institute of Civil Engineering and Building Technology (KICT) in Yeoncheon.
The site measures roughly 40 m ×\times 60 m and reproduces a lunar surface through scattered rocks and impact-crater-like depressions, the deepest of which reach about 1 m.
We deployed two Unitree22
2
https://www.unitree.com GO2 quadruped robots (N=2N=2), whose legged mobility can negotiate the steep crater walls and scattered rocks of the site (Fig. 2).

As shown in Fig. 3, in both deployments, each robot was equipped with an Ouster OS1-64 LiDAR sensor33
3
https://ouster.com, a MicroStrain 3DM-GX5-25 inertial measurement unit (IMU) sensor44
4
https://www.hbkworld.com, and an Intel NUC Pro Mini PC55
5
https://www.intel.com for running SKiD-SLAM.
Furthermore, the robots were teleoperated for safety, while our SKiD-SLAM performed distributed mapping onboard without any operator input.

For experimental transport and monitoring, the robots used a TP-Link66
6
https://www.tp-link.com Omada Wi-Fi access point, and each robot streamed its scans to a monitoring workstation for joint visualization using Rerun [65], as shown in Fig. 4.
The access point emulated the physical inter-robot network for the field tests, while the workstation was used only for human supervision and was not part of the SLAM architecture.
All SLAM computation was performed onboard the robots in a fully distributed manner.

title: Minimum-Time Escape from the Conic Field of View of a Reeds--Shepp Pursuer: the Faster Evader
authors: Ubaldo Ruiz
abstract: We continue the study of minimum-time escape of an omnidirectional evader from the forward conic field of view of a Reeds–Shepp pursuer, now for a faster evader, and solve the game for every speed ratio ν>1\nu>1 and every half-angle 0<α<π/20<\alpha<\pi/2: the escape time is characterized by explicit characteristics and the selection of roots of a scalar equation, and it is the value of the game in nonanticipative strategies at every state. Above the end EE of the evader’s dispersal line on the front axis, the evader chases the reversing pursuer along a universal line fed by tributaries. The characteristic from the boundary of the usable part is an involute of a circle of radius ν\nu ending at a cusp, and two explicit thresholds decide whether it reaches the axis before the cusp and whether the jump of the escape time across it ends before the cusp or runs to it; in the latter case primaries fold back next to the barrier. The pursuer’s optimal strategy is the relay of the slower case. The evader follows the tributaries and switches once to a primary, or commits in advance to a heading certified by the scalar equation of the primaries. Level-set and semi-Lagrangian computations are compared with the value.
introduction:
A directional sensor on a moving vehicle observes only part of the plane, so escaping surveillance means leaving its field of view rather than outrunning the observer. In Part I (Ruiz, 2026b) we studied minimum-time escape of an omnidirectional evader from the unbounded forward cone of half-angle 0<α<π/20<\alpha<\pi/2 of a Reeds–Shepp pursuer, a car that can drive forward or in reverse but cannot rotate in place (Reeds and Shepp, 1990). The evader minimizes the exit time and the pursuer maximizes it. Part I proved the escape/holding classification for every ratio ν=Vemax/Vpmax\nu=V_{e}^{\max}/V_{p}^{\max} of the evader’s and the pursuer’s maximum speeds. Straight reversal holds the whole cone for ν≤sin⁡α\nu\leq\sin\alpha; for sin⁡α<ν≤1\sin\alpha<\nu\leq 1 escape is confined to a dart bounded by a barrier; for ν>1\nu>1 escape is possible from every state. For the slower or equally fast evader, Part I constructed the escape time with Isaacs’ characteristics (Isaacs, 1965; Lewin, 1994), verified it in feedback form and identified it with the value of the game in nonanticipative strategies at every state except one corner of the holding region.

This paper treats the faster evader, ν>1\nu>1. The closest forward-only model is the conic surveillance–evasion game of Lewin and Olsder (1979); related surveillance games and differential-drive variants are surveyed in Part I (Dobbie, 1966; Lewin and Breakwell, 1975; Lewin and Olsder, 1989; Greenfeld, 1987; Ruiz, 2026a; Braun et al., 2025; Weintraub et al., 2023; Ruiz, 2023; Saavedra and Ruiz, 2024). A faster evader changes the problem in three ways. First, the evader’s axis dispersal line of the slower case ends at a point EE, where the viscosity test on the axis fails (Part I, Proposition 4). Second, above EE a singular arc appears: the evader runs straight at the pursuer, which backs away in a straight line, so the front axis becomes a universal line in Isaacs’ sense, fed from both sides by tributaries. Third, the characteristic issued from the boundary of the usable part (the BUP\mathrm{BUP} characteristic) no longer closes a holding region. It is a semipermeable curve that ends at a cusp, and across part of it the escape time jumps by a finite amount.

The main results are the following.

For ν>1\nu>1 we give the characteristic families in closed form (Section 3): the point EE (Proposition 1), the universal line and its tributaries, whose value is an explicit classical solution of the Isaacs equation on the whole upper half-plane (Proposition 2), and the BUP\mathrm{BUP} characteristic, an involute of the circle of radius ν\nu about the pursuer’s turning centre that ends at a cusp on that circle (Proposition 3).

The condition ν​sin⁡(α+cos⁡α/ν)≤1\nu\sin(\alpha+\cos\alpha/\nu)\leq 1 defines a regime F1 in which the BUP\mathrm{BUP} characteristic reaches the front axis at or before its cusp. In F1 the primaries, the tributaries and their dispersal lines are explicit (Proposition 4, Lemma 4).

In F1, the synthesis is verified in feedback form (Theorem 4.1), and its escape time WW is the value of the game in nonanticipative strategies at every state of the cone (Theorem 4.2). The pursuer uses the relay of Part I. The evader follows the tributaries and switches once to a primary. Both guarantees can be realized by sampled state feedback, so the value is the same whether or not a player observes the opponent’s current control.

In the complementary regime F2, primaries fold before reaching the axis. Whether the tributary value undercuts the barrier before the cusp is decided by comparing the tributary value at the cusp with the retro-time of the cusp, which splits F2 into F2a and F2b (Section 5). In F2a the results of (iii) hold unchanged (Theorem 5.1); the evader’s argument needs only margins at the axis and the barrier that hold before the cusp, not the sign condition on the primary headings used in F1. In F2b the synthesis has folded primaries next to the barrier and a jump with square-root decay at the cusp (Appendix B). It is the value of the game (Theorem 5.2): the evader commits to the heading of a primary, which guarantees its time against every pursuer control, and an auxiliary envelope gives the relay bound before the covering of the tributaries is known. The same holds on the curve that separates F2a from F2b, so the conic escape game is solved for every ν>1\nu>1 and every α∈(0,π/2)\alpha\in(0,\pi/2).

Independent level-set computations agree with the value in F2b away from singular lines. In F1, level-set and semi-Lagrangian computations are compared with the proved value, which identifies their persistent offsets on the universal line as errors of the discretizations (Section 6).

Section 2 recalls the formulation and Section 3 constructs the characteristics. Sections 4 and 5 solve regimes F1 and F2, Section 6 gives the numerical comparisons and Section 7 the comparison with the Dubins game.

title: Same Label, Different Interface: Beyond Action-Space Labels in Robot Learning
authors: Arshia Sangwan,Zhongyang Zhang
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Machine Learning (cs.LG); Systems and Control (eess.SY)
abstract: Robot-learning studies often compare position and velocity actions as though each label identified a single experimental treatment, yet the label alone does not determine what the robot executes. Before affecting robot motion, bounded policy output passes through filtering, physical scaling, reference construction, feedback, timing, and effort limits. We study how these omitted properties affect attribution under one shared learner and training budget. Across three contact-rich Factory tasks (PegInsert, GearMesh, and NutThread), we compare five joint-space interfaces, with ten independently trained policies per condition. We first remain within the same position-feedback law and vary the executed interface: substituting only the physical action scale as the directly modified component changes sample-median evaluation success by 0.645–1.000 across tasks, while removing an exponential moving average produces task-dependent changes. We then move to a cross-law comparison and choose a velocity scale that exactly matches the position interface’s local raw-torque command gain. This calibration raises the sample median on GearMesh and NutThread, with no median change on PegInsert. Yet clear residual sample-median gaps remain on PegInsert and GearMesh, while the NutThread interval includes zero. Thus, even this explicit equality leaves feedback and held-action dynamics unmatched and does not establish position–velocity trained-outcome equivalence. Action-interface comparisons should therefore report the executed pathway and state the physical quantity they match.
introduction:
Two systems can both expose “joint-position actions” while mapping the same normalized policy output to very different target changes. One may request a small calibrated joint increment. Another may request an increment based on the distance from the nominal pose to each joint limit. The label is accurate in both cases, yet it omits a physical difference that can change the robot trajectories used for learning.

At each policy step, the system samples a~t∼πθ(⋅∣ot)\tilde{a}_{t}\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid o_{t}) from observation oto_{t} and bounds it as at=ℬ⁡(a~t)=clip⁡(a~t,−1,1)a_{t}=\mathcal{B}(\tilde{a}_{t})=\operatorname{clip}(\tilde{a}_{t},-1,1). The implemented pathway then filters the bounded action, applies command coordinates and physical scale, constructs and holds a reference, evaluates feedback, and limits motor torque. These operations determine how a normalized output changes the robot state. Position, velocity, torque, and impedance name only selected parts of that pathway.

Figure 1 introduces the tested interfaces and tasks. The three position conditions show how one nominal label can contain different physical scales or temporal processing. The velocity conditions test a stronger cross-law matching hypothesis. Figure 2 shows the actual order of operations. Filtering precedes coordinate mapping and reference construction. The resulting reference is latched once per policy decision, while feedback and effort limiting are evaluated on each physics substep.

Existing work shows that action representation, temporal persistence, gains, and controller choice affect learning [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7]. The unresolved experimental-design question is what an observed difference can be attributed to when a nominal label leaves several of these properties unspecified.

We study this question through controlled substitutions on Factory PegInsert, GearMesh, and NutThread. We first preserve the position feedback law while changing physical action scale or exponential moving-average processing. We then change to velocity feedback and match a precisely defined local raw-torque command gain. This calibration equalizes the action-driven raw-torque coefficient while leaving the feedback terms and held-action state evolution different. The required matching level follows from the attribution being made. A position-versus-velocity claim needs different controls than a claim about physical scale. Our estimand is interface substitution under one shared learner configuration and budget. Separate retuning answers the complementary optimization question. The paper makes three contributions.

An attribution framework for action interfaces. We separate the operations between bounded policy output and applied torque, which makes each controlled substitution and its licensed interpretation explicit.

An attribution framework for action interfaces. We separate the operations between bounded policy output and applied torque, which makes each controlled substitution and its licensed interpretation explicit.

Controlled within-law evidence. With position feedback fixed, directly changing only the physical action scale produces large outcome differences across all three tasks. Removing the moving average produces task-dependent changes.

A controlled test of local command-gain matching. We match the local raw-torque command gain across position and velocity feedback. The calibration changes some observed outcomes but neither matches the remaining feedback dynamics nor equalizes the observed trained-policy outcomes.

The methodological rule is direct: state what is physically matched and report what remains different. We use one learner and one training budget so that interface substitution remains the experimental treatment. Retuning the learner for each interface asks the complementary question of what performance each interface can reach after separate optimization. Our evidence covers one robot, one simulator family, and three contact tasks within the same stack.

title: Efficacy of Monocular Depth Estimation in Lunar Environments
authors: Michael W. Lanighan,Kenji Brameld,Seth Gee
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
comment: Accepted at the International Conference on Space Robotics (iSpaRo) 2026
abstract: Recent advances in monocular depth estimation have demonstrated highly accurate 3D reconstructions within in-distribution terrestrial domains. This study investigates the efficacy of several state-of-the-art approaches to reconstruct out-of-distribution lunar environments using the NASA Ames Polar Optical Lunar Analog Reconstruction (POLAR) stereo dataset and Apollo 17 surface imagery. By leveraging these datasets, we establish a robust analog-to-field validation pipeline that evaluates quantitative performance against ground-truth physical analogs and qualitative performance against historical field data. Our results indicate that select state-of-the-art techniques can successfully generalize to produce high-fidelity relative 3D reconstructions of the unstructured lunar surface.
introduction:
Humanity has decades of experience in conducting and overseeing remote space operations, both in terms of human spaceflight and remote robotic assets. Even with this extensive experience, low Earth orbit (LEO) operations on the International Space Station (ISS) for the Mobile Servicing System (MSS) present challenges for operators related to situational awareness. NASA Astronaut Nick Hague recently outlined the state of operations in LEO:

Robot operations from mission control at NASA JSC use a similar control station as that on station, but face further challenges brought by downlink/bandwidth constraints. Due to the finite number of downlinks and fixed bandwidth available, not all camera views needed to support a remote operation may be available. While tools to support operations, including 3D views [3] and special purpose capability for docking, have been developed [4], integrated 3D solutions to handle general operations are lacking. In upcoming Artemis missions, NASA envisions extended periods of uncrewed activity on the lunar surface. During this time, NASA aims to use robotic assets to perform post-crew-departure activities, carry out scientific and exploration objectives, and relocate themselves and supplies to future landing sites to support crewed missions. Compared to LEO operations, it is anticipated that lunar operations will have decreased available bandwidth and downlinks, which will only further exacerbate issues surrounding situational awareness for remote operators. New tools are required to support both remote operators and autonomous systems to maintain sufficient situational awareness to execute at the envisioned goal cadences.

A promising emerging area that can help address these issues is monocular depth estimation (MDE). These approaches consume a 2D image and reconstruct a 3D scene for operators to inspect. Moreover, relying on a single camera reduces the need for stereo pairs or time of flight sensors to reconstruct 3D representations of the remote scene, providing the additional benefit of lowered bandwidth requirements. However, state of the art MDE approaches are trained using massive image datasets of terrestrial images. The efficacy of such approaches in domains that are out-of-distribution with these large training datasets, such as the lunar surface, is currently unknown. To address this, this study evaluates several state-of-the-art techniques to determine their efficacy in lunar environments, leveraging images from the NASA Polar Optical Lunar Analog Reconstruction (POLAR) stereo dataset [5] and Apollo 17 mission operations [6] (see Fig. 1).

title: EARS-Info: Information-Aware Event-Driven Reallocation for Multi-Robot Exploration
authors: Kabeh Mohsenzadegan,Vahid Tavakkoli,Kyandoghere Kyamakya
abstract: 未获取到摘要
introduction:
Multi-robot exploration distributes spatial search across a team, but additional robots also create overlapping sensing, congestion, and avoidable movement. The useful objective is therefore not simply to move faster or visit more cells. A controller must direct the team toward new information while preserving enough energy to return and limiting coordination overhead. Recent exploration research studies asynchronous decisions, macro actions, reinforcement learning, and frontier-led swarming [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6].

Our starting point is Event-Driven Ant Reallocation Search (EARS). Its original local-to-global structure uses an ant-inspired local rule most of the time and invokes relocation when observable search degradation occurs. This structure is interpretable, but a local score can revisit already sensed neighborhoods, a relocation goal can duplicate another robot’s sensing, and repeatedly rebuilding shortest-path fields can dominate runtime. Event triggering alone does not resolve these problems: the value and feasibility of the requested route must also be considered.

We develop EARS-Info to address this complete decision process. The method scores newly sensed area using the simulator’s sensing footprint, compares feasible distant information gain with the best local opportunity, accounts for return travel before accepting relocation, and reserves sensing footprints across robot decisions. It maintains topology-dependent graph fields across steps rather than treating unchanged geography as a new planning problem. The design reads observable uncertainty and visit information; unsensed mission labels are excluded from policy inputs.

This paper makes four contributions. First, it specifies EARS-Info as a new member of our EARS controller family, including the preceding EARS-Safe, negative-pheromone EARS-NP, and hierarchical H-MAPPO-EARS variants. Second, it defines matched local-only, periodic-request, and sensing-reservation controls that clarify what the complete-controller comparison can and cannot identify. Third, it reports a single frozen comparison of all 30 implementations on identical map snapshots, start zones, and step-indexed communication schedules, comprising 168,000 episodes. Fourth, it provides city-level inference, all-method rankings, raw task metrics, and artifact checks rather than relying solely on an aggregate rank.

The main question is whether the complete information-aware controller improves our preceding EARS-Safe implementation. Additional questions concern team-size/dropout behavior, alternate target realizations, and the evidence for individual design choices. The eight evaluation cities are excluded from the current training and checkpoint selection, but their identities have appeared in earlier development. Accordingly, this is an exploratory evaluation on reused geography, conditional on the frozen models. It is not a claim of untouched geographic confirmation or of reproducing every named external MARL algorithm.

title: METATRON: A Promptable Whole-Body Execution Layer for Humanoids
authors: Chen Tessler,Yifeng Jiang,Alec Otto,Yi Shi,Umar Iqbal,Gal Chechik,Xue Bin Peng
abstract: Humanoid controllers often require task-specific training despite sharing the need for balance and whole-body coordination. We present Metatron, a promptable whole-body execution layer combining a generative base policy with a programmable skill layer. The base policy receives partial goals, collectively called a prompt, that can combine timed body-part targets, velocity commands, and style cues. It produces diverse whole-body motions consistent with these goals. Training combines motion capture, synthetic recovery trajectories, and retargeted scene-interaction motions. After training, the policy is frozen. Stateful programs called skills express task intent as prompts at each control step, drawing rough geometric sketches that the policy turns into coordinated movement. Skills are ordinary code, refined by coding agents that analyze motion data and fit compact rules without task-specific policy training. On the physical Unitree G1, one frozen checkpoint supports walking, recovery, teleoperated object pickup, and sitting on furniture. Comparative evaluations show higher reaching success and push robustness than the tested reference-tracking pipelines. The same recipe produces climbing and acrobatics on a simulated character. Metatron enables coding agents to turn learned motor capabilities into new skills through code, without further policy training.
introduction:
Consider a humanoid that must walk to a table in a particular style, grasp a cup at a designated moment, recover after a shove, present it to a human, and shake hands. Today this typically requires separate learned controllers for locomotion [3], manipulation [4], recovery [5], compliant control [6], and motion tracking [7]. These controllers duplicate capabilities such as balance and coordination, and transitions between them demand additional engineering.

We argue that a more scalable recipe is to separate what a motion should accomplish from how to coordinate the body: train one general-purpose whole-body policy with a flexible goal-conditioning interface, and let task-specific programs specify the goals. The policy becomes an execution layer that provides physical coordination; the programs become the controllers that supply intent. Each program specifies a partial motion goal that we call a prompt: a sitting command specifies the shape and location of a nearby object, while a style cue biases the generated motion toward example poses.

We present Metatron, a promptable whole-body execution layer for humanoids (Figure 1). It combines a capable base policy with a programmable skill layer. The base policy builds on MaskedMimic [8], which trains a dense motion tracker and distills it into a generative policy that accepts sparse body-part targets at specified future times.

Once trained, the policy is frozen and a runtime layer runs programs called skills that convert task intent into prompts at each control step (Section IV). Skills are ordinary code, authored by humans or coding agents. We show how LLM agents analyze motion clips and fit compact rules that capture shared motion characteristics, turning task design into a software problem. Reinforcement learning trains the motion experts; on-policy distillation teaches the base policy to imitate them under partial goals, including at states reached by the student itself. This training supports approximate goal sketches rather than requiring exact reference trajectories.

Metatron also extends MaskedMimic in several directions. Forward kinematics reconstructs local body poses from joint and inertial measurements, without external motion capture; world-position goals additionally require localization. Scene elements are represented as geometric primitives specified by measured dimensions and poses. Style conditioning allows operators and skills to select the generated motion’s character. We augment the training data with synthetic push-recovery and get-up trajectories, extending the repertoire beyond what motion capture alone provides. On the modeling side, spherical projection bounds the stochastic latent, while predictive and temporal auxiliary losses regularize its fused representation (Section III-C).

Our contributions are a whole-body policy with a flexible prompt interface, training data augmented with scene interactions and synthetic recoveries (Section V), and a skill layer whose code can be refined by coding agents without policy retraining (Section IV). One frozen checkpoint per embodiment supports the demonstrated tasks on physical G1 and simulated SOMA. Separate G1 comparisons show higher whole-body reaching success and push robustness than the tested reference-tracking pipelines (Section VI).

3. 是否属于 VLA：否  
理由：虽然Metatron使用了提示来驱动动作生成，但这些提示并不包含视觉和语言的输入，而是基于运动目标和风格的指令。因此，它不符合VLA的标准。

4. 是否属于 Humanoid Loco-manipulation：是  
理由：该论文的研究对象是人形机器人，任务涉及到行走（locomotion）和物体操控（manipulation），并且需要全身协调。因此，符合Humanoid Loco-manipulation的定义。

5. 最终标签总结  
该论文属于World Model和Humanoid Loco-manipulation，但不属于VLA。

6. 如果有歧义，请说明最容易混淆的点  
最容易混淆的点在于Metatron的提示机制，它可能让人联想到VLA中的视觉和语言输入。然而，Metatron的提示主要是运动目标和风格指令，而不是视觉和语言的结合，因此不符合VLA的标准。

title: Self-Labeled Preference Transfer for Steerable Robot Manipulation
authors: Kaiwen Hong,Shaoting Peng,Xiangyu Zeng,Pengcheng Wang,Boyuan Tian,Haonan Chen,Yifan Zhu,Yixiao Wang,Katherine Driggs-Campbell
abstract:
Vision-language-action (VLA) policies can learn to follow execution preferences, such as where to grasp an object or how to move around an obstacle, from demonstrations annotated with preference labels. Providing these
annotations for every new task, however, is costly. We study whether learned preference control can transfer to new tasks whose demonstrations contain the desired behaviors but lack preference annotations. We find that a policy trained with preference annotations can follow preferences on a new task before adaptation but achieves limited task success. Fine-tuning on target demonstrations without these annotations improves task success while weakening preference control. Motivated by this finding, we introduce Self-Labeled Preference Transfer (SPT). SPT jointly trains a shared vision-language backbone for preference-conditioned action prediction and preference recognition on annotated source demonstrations. It then freezes the recognizer to preserve its cross-task preference recognition capability and uses it to self-label target demonstrations for policy fine-tuning. Across five types of execution preferences in simulation, the recognizer achieves 96.4% accuracy, and SPT reaches 84.8% preference following and 89.2% task success, compared with 59.4% and 88.0% for naive finetuning. We further extend to multiple preferences, achieving 93.8% preference following compared with 42.5% of baselines. In real-world experiments, SPT increases preference following from 52.5% to 92.5% relative to naive finetuning across two task transfers. These results show that SPT can support preference
adaptation across tasks and objects while maintaining success, without additional manual preference annotations.
introduction:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models trained on large multi-task datasets can now follow language instructions across scenes, objects, and embodiments [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]. Demonstrations in these datasets usually show one way to complete a task, or follow whatever pattern the operator found natural. In reality, a task has several acceptable executions, and which one is wanted depends on the context and on the user. A mug can be grasped near its rim or near its base; an object can be placed at the center of a tray or in a corner; a path can pass close to an obstacle or give it a wide berth. We call such choices execution preferences: they concern how a task is performed rather than what is accomplished, and the desired choice may depend on the user or context. Standard task-level instructions do not specify this choice, leaving the user without explicit control over it. This paper studies how a VLA can follow a stated execution preference on a new task when its target demonstrations do not contain preference labels.

Existing work approaches execution-level control from two directions. One line makes VLAs steerable by enriching training prompts with descriptions of how each demonstration was performed, produced by human annotators or automated pipelines [7, 8, 9, 10]. These works show that VLAs can follow execution-level instructions once such annotations are available, but a new task still has to be annotated before the policy can be steered on it. The other line is preference learning, which infers a reward or policy from comparisons between executions [11, 12, 13, 14].
The output of preference learning is a policy aligned to a user’s preference (often through ranking executions [15]) rather than one that switches on command to a named style.
Preference learning is typically used to adapt a policy toward preferred behavior on a particular task, rather than to provide command-conditioned switching among named execution preferences across tasks. Neither line asks whether preference control learned on labeled source tasks can be preserved when adapting to a new task whose demonstrations lack preference labels. This setting introduces two challenges. First, the source supervision must teach preference semantics that transfer across tasks, so that the behavior shown in a target demonstration can still be recognized. Second, the policy must adapt to the target task without losing its response to the preference command. Finetuning on target demonstrations with the task instruction alone provides no signal tying the demonstrated motion to a preference, so the control learned on the source can be weakened during adaptation.

We study preference transfer without target preference annotations. We assume preference-labeled demonstrations for a set of source tasks and demonstrations with varied execution behaviors, but no preference labels, for a set of target tasks. Our approach, Self-Labeled Preference Transfer (SPT), addresses this setting in two stages. In Stage A, a shared vision-language backbone learns both to execute a stated preference and to recognize the preference expressed in a demonstration. In Stage B, we freeze the Stage-A recognizer and use it to label the target demonstrations, then finetune a trainable copy of the policy on the target actions paired with these inferred preference prompts. These labels associate each target behavior with the corresponding preference command during adaptation. At deployment, only the policy runs, and the user selects a behavior using the same preference vocabulary learned on the source tasks.

We evaluate SPT in simulation and on a real robot. In RoboTwin 2.0 [16], we synthesize pick-and-place demonstrations along five preference axes and transfer to held-out object and receptacle combinations. On a real robot experiment, we transfer across task types: from pick-and-place to pushing and from air hockey to billiards. The Stage-A recognizer labels target demonstrations with 96.4% average accuracy, and SPT raises average preference following from 59.4% to 83.8% in simulation and from 52.5% to 92.5% on the robot, with similar average task success.

Ablations on placement and contact height isolate the roles of source preference transfer and target self-labeling. Before target adaptation, the Stage-A policy reaches 80% and 88% preference following on the two target tasks, but with lower target-task success. Finetuning the same Stage-A checkpoint with bare target instructions reduces preference following to 52% and 50%, whereas SPT retains 83% and 90% while adapting to the target tasks. Shuffling the inferred target labels gives similarly poor preference following, indicating that the benefit depends on correctly associating each target behavior with its preference rather than on adding preference text alone.

In summary, this paper makes three contributions. (1) We formulate transfer of a named execution-preference vocabulary to target tasks whose demonstrations lack preference annotations. (2) We introduce SPT, which jointly learns preference-conditioned action prediction and preference recognition, then reuses a frozen recognizer to label target demonstrations before policy adaptation. (3) We evaluate this approach across five simulated preference axes and two real-robot task transfers, with controls for source initialization and target label assignment, comparisons to target-labeled reference conditions, and an extension to two simultaneous preferences.

   本文提出了一种名为自标注偏好转移（Self-Labeled Preference Transfer, SPT）的方法，旨在解决在没有偏好注释的新任务中如何利用已学习的偏好控制。通过一个共享的视觉-语言骨干网络，SPT能够学习执行偏好和识别偏好，并在目标任务中自标注演示以进行策略微调，从而提高任务成功率和偏好遵循率。
